questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 42-year-old male industrial worker presented to a health centre with complaints of diminished working capacity and debilitating respiratory complaints including chronic irritant cough, severe dyspnea on exertion and occasional pain in chest. He gave an occupational history of working in the same industry since the onset of adulthood till date. An X-ray of the chest showed “snowstorm” appearance in the lung fields. High-resolution radiographic imaging showed dense nodular fibrosis in the lungs. Which one of the following is the most likely diagnosis for this case?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Silicosis

The most likely diagnosis is silicosis, an occupational pneumoconiosis caused by prolonged inhalation of crystalline silica dust.

• Long-standing industrial exposure
• Chronic cough and progressive dyspnea
• Snowstorm appearance on chest X-ray due to multiple small nodular opacities
• HRCT showing nodular pulmonary fibrosis
• Classically involves the upper lobes
• May show eggshell calcification of hilar lymph nodes

Why not the other options?

• A. Asbestosis: Characteristically causes lower-lobe interstitial fibrosis with pleural plaques.
• B. Bagassosis: Hypersensitivity pneumonitis caused by inhalation of moldy sugarcane bagasse.
• C. Byssinosis: Caused by cotton, flax or hemp dust; classically causes Monday chest tightness.
questions.learning: Silicosis — The most likely diagnosis is silicosis, an occupational pneumoconiosis caused by prolonged inhalation of crystalline silica dust. • Long-standing industrial exposure • Chronic cough and progressive dyspnea • Snowstorm appearance on chest X-ray…

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: New A 45-year old man who was a chronic alcoholic presented with confusion, ataxia, and diplopia. What is the treatment protocol?
options: Vitamin B1 injection followed by glucose infusion
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Vitamin B1 injection followed by glucose infusion

The above clinical history is suggestive of Wernicke's encephalopathy. The current standard of treatment for patients with symptoms of Wernicke's encephalopathy is to give thiamine 100 mg intravenously before administering glucose-containing IV fluids.

Thiamine deficiency leads to the following:

1. Wernicke’s encephalopathy: It is more commonly seen in alcoholics with chronic thiamine deficiency. It is characterized by :

* Global confusion

* Truncal ataxia

* Ophthalmoplegia

* Horizontal nystagmus

2. Korsakoff psychosis: symptoms in addition to those of Wernicke's encephalopathy include:

* Memory loss

* Confabulation

3. Beriberi: It can present with sensorimotor peripheral neuropathy, and muscle weakness (dry beriberi) or tachycardia, cardiomegaly, high-output cardiac failure (wet beriberi).

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which of the following events occur immediately when a person changes his/her posture from supine to standing?
options: Vagal output to cardiac fibres increase
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Decrease in firing from baroreceptor

There is a decreased firing from the baroreceptors.

• When a person stands up from a lying down position, it causes pooling of the blood in the legs, due to gravity. This reduces the venous return and causes a decrease in cardiac output.
• Reduced cardiac output, leads to a fall in blood pressure, which in turn causes reduced firing from baroreceptors.
• As a result, the vagal tone is suppressed leading to increased heart rate.
questions.learning: Decrease in firing from baroreceptor — There is a decreased firing from the baroreceptors. • When a person stands up from a lying down position, it causes pooling of the blood in the legs, due to gravity.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.topic: General Physiology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: Regarding the speed of axonal transport, All of the following statements are correct except:
options: Fast anterograde (orthograde) transport occurs at a speed of approximately 200–400 mm/day
Retrograde axonal transport occurs at a speed of approximately 100–300 mm/day
Slow anterograde axonal transport occurs at a speed of approximately 1–5 mm/day
Retrograde axonal transport is slower than slow anterograde transport
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Retrograde axonal transport is slower than slow anterograde transport

Axonal transport moves materials between the neuronal cell body and axon terminals along microtubules using motor proteins.

Types of axonal transport:

●  Fast anterograde (orthograde) transport:

• Speed: \~200–400 mm/day
• Motor protein: Kinesin
• Carries synaptic vesicles, mitochondria, enzymes

● Retrograde transport:

• Speed: \~100–300 mm/day
• Motor protein: Dynein
• Carries endocytosed materials, growth factors, toxins, viruses back to the cell body

● Slow anterograde transport:

• Speed: \~1–5 mm/day
• Carries cytoskeletal proteins (actin, tubulin) Statement D is incorrect because retrograde transport is faster than slow anterograde transport.
questions.learning: Retrograde axonal transport is slower than slow anterograde transport Axonal transport moves materials between the neuronal cell body and axon terminals along microtubules using motor proteins.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 49-year-old woman from Nagaland presents with right-sided hearing loss and tinnitus. Examination reveals a dull tympanic membrane along with enlarged lymph nodes in the posterior triangle of the neck. What is the most appropriate management for this condition?
questions.explanation: The patient’s symptoms—unilateral hearing loss and tinnitus with a dull tympanic membrane—indicate serous otitis media due to Eustachian tube obstruction. In a patient from Nagaland (an endemic area) with enlarged posterior triangle lymph nodes, this presentation is highly suspicious for nasopharyngeal carcinoma (NPC). Radiotherapy is the definitive management for NPC, as the tumor is highly radiosensitive. Regarding the distractors, grommet insertion and steroids (Options A, B, and C) might treat the symptoms of fluid in the ear but would fail to address the underlying malignancy causing the obstruction. A unilateral ear block in an adult, especially from Northeast India, must always be investigated for malignancy. Therefore, because NPC is the primary diagnosis suggested by the clinical cluster, radiotherapy is the standard treatment
questions.learning: The patient’s symptoms—unilateral hearing loss and tinnitus with a dull tympanic membrane—indicate serous otitis media due to Eustachian tube obstruction.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: After a road traffic accident, a patient sustains severe maxillofacial trauma and has an oxygen saturation of 80% on room air. The airway cannot be secured by intubation or ventilation. What should be the immediate next step in management?
options: Do suction and again try intubation
questions.explanation: The patient is in a "cannot intubate, cannot ventilate" (CICV) scenario, which is an airway emergency. Severe maxillofacial trauma often distorts anatomy to the point where standard oral or nasal intubation is impossible. In a rapidly desaturating patient (SpO2 80%), the immediate priority is bypassing the obstruction to establish an airway. Cricothyrotomy is the fastest surgical airway technique, allowing for oxygenation within seconds by accessing the superficial cricothyroid membrane. Tracheostomy (Option B) provides a definitive airway but is a much slower, more complex surgical procedure unsuitable for acute hypoxic arrest. ICD insertion (Option C) addresses chest trauma but does not correct a primary airway obstruction. Repeatedly attempting intubation or suctioning (Option D) wastes critical minutes while the patient remains hypoxic. Therefore, cricothyrotomy is the mandatory life-saving step in this trauma setting
questions.learning: The patient is in a "cannot intubate, cannot ventilate" (CICV) scenario, which is an airway emergency. Severe maxillofacial trauma often distorts anatomy to the point where standard oral or nasal intubation is impossible.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A young patient presents with nasal polyps and rhinosinusitis. X-ray and clinical images are as below. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Kartagener's syndrome

The given clinical scenario along with an X-ray showing dextrocardia, CT showing maxillary polyp, and endoscopy showing nasal polyp is suggestive of Kartagener's syndrome.

Primary ciliary dyskinesia (also called immotile cilia syndrome) is an autosomal recessive disorder affecting ciliary motility. When a patient has bronchiectasis, chronic sinusitis, and situs inversus triad, he is known to have Kartagener syndrome. It occurs due to the absence of protein dynein in the A tubules of the respiratory mucosa.

The disease is usually diagnosed based on the clinical picture and should be evaluated in later stages when a child presents with recurrent lower and upper respiratory tract infections. Other features of primary ciliary dyskinesia include congenital heart diseases and neonatal hydrocephalus. Male patients with this condition tend to be infertile, due to asthenospermia (immotile spermatozoa due to impaired sperm flagella function).

Transmission electron microscopy is the gold standard investigation to analyze cilia. There is no specific treatment for this condition and is managed according to the symptoms.

Other options:

Option A: Churg Strauss syndrome clinically presents with asthma, fever and eosinophilia.

Option C: Young's syndrome clinically presents with infertility (azoospermia) and bronchiectasis.

Option D: Cystic fibrosis is an autosomal recessive condition due to a mutation of the CFTR gene on chromosome 7. Clinical features include recurrent sinopulmonary infection, intestinal obstruction, pancreatic insufficiency, and male infertility. Diagnosis is made by elevated sweat chloride levels, abnormal nasal potential difference, and genetic testing for CFTR mutation.
questions.learning: Kartagener's syndrome — The given clinical scenario along with an X-ray showing dextrocardia, CT showing maxillary polyp, and endoscopy showing nasal polyp is suggestive of Kartagener's syndrome.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A 46-year-old male was recently diagnosed with colorectal cancer after presenting with multiple polyps in his colon during a colonoscopy. There is a strong family history of non-polyposis colorectal cancer (HNPCC). Which of the following DNA repair mechanisms is most likely to be dysfunctional in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Mismatch repair

The given clinical scenario is suggestive of Lynch syndrome or hereditary nonpolyposis colorectal cancer (HNPCC) and is due to defective DNA mismatch repair.

HNPCC is an autosomal dominant genetic condition that is associated with a high risk of colon cancer as well as other cancers, including endometrial cancer (the second most common), cancers of the stomach, ovary, ureters, etc. It is the most common cause of the syndromic form of colon cancer. Colon cancers are seen at younger ages and usually on the right side.

DNA mismatch repair proteins function as spell checkers during DNA replication by correcting the incorrect pairing. In HNPCC, the proofreading function of the mismatch repair systems (majorly MLH1 and MSH2) is lost, leading to the accumulation of errors throughout the genome. The genomes of these patients show microsatellite instability, which is characterised by changes in the length of short repeats.

Other options:

Option A: Defects in the nucleotide excision repair pathway are seen in patients with xeroderma pigmentosum.

Option B: Defects in non-homologous end-joining are seen in patients with subacute combined immunodeficiency syndrome (SCID).

Option C: Defects in DNA base excision repair are seen in patients with MUTYH-associated polyposis (MAP) syndromes.
questions.learning: Mismatch repair — The given clinical scenario is suggestive of Lynch syndrome or hereditary nonpolyposis colorectal cancer (HNPCC) and is due to defective DNA mismatch repair.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: All of the following are components responsible for the countercurrent mechanism in the kidney except _____.
options: Sodium outflow in thick ascending limb
Water outflow in thin descending limb
Sodium outflow in thin ascending limb
Flow of tubular fluid from PCT to DCT
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Sodium outflow in thin ascending limb

Thin ascending limb is not a component of the countercurrent mechanism.

The loop of Henle function as countercurrent multipliers and vasa recta as countercurrent exchangers.

The functioning of the loop of Henle depends upon:

1. High permeability of the thin descending limb to water ( via aquaporin-1)
2. Active transport of Na+ and Cl- from the thick ascending limb
3. Inflow of tubular fluid from proximal tubule and outflow to the distal tubule.

Note: The thin ascending limbs of juxtamedullary nephrons are permeable to Na+ and Cl- and hence do contribute passively to countercurrent multiplication. However, among the options provided, Option C is the best answer as the other options are directly responsible for the countercurrent mechanism.
questions.learning: Sodium outflow in thin ascending limb Thin ascending limb is not a component of the countercurrent mechanism. The loop of Henle function as countercurrent multipliers and vasa recta as countercurrent exchangers.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A patient presented with a slight loss of sensation along the ulnar nerve and a solitary nodule in the forearm. Intradermal antigen was injected. The histopathology image is shown below. Which of the following is true regarding this condition?
options: Lepromatous leprosy with dermal test positive
Tuberculoid leprosy with dermal test positive
Lepromatous leprosy with dermal test negative
Erythema nodosum leprosum with negative skin test
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Tuberculoid leprosy with dermal test positive

The patient’s slight loss of sensation along the ulnar nerve, solitary forearm nodule, and histopathology showing well-defined granulomas indicate tuberculoid leprosy with a dermal test positive.

In tuberculoid leprosy, dermal granulomas, consisting of groups of epithelioid cells with giant cells, are seen. The granulomas are elongated and generally run parallel to the surface, following neurovascular bundles. The granulomas extend up to the epidermis, thereby obscuring the Grenz zone. It also shows high positivity of the lepromin skin (dermal) test.

Leprosy is a chronic granulomatous condition caused by Mycobacterium leprae. It affects the skin, cutaneous and peripheral nerves, and mucous membranes. The most commonly affected peripheral nerves are the posterior tibial nerve, followed by the ulnar, median, and lateral popliteal nerves. The most frequently involved cranial nerve is the facial nerve. It has a long incubation period, usually 2 to 12 years. It commonly presents as an area of numbness on the skin or a visible skin lesion, which could be a hypopigmented or erythematous macule.

The Grenz zone is most prominent in lepromatous leprosy, as there are scarce granulomas to fill up the space. It is also seen in the borderline spectrum.

Cardinal signs for the diagnosis of leprosy:

• Characteristic skin lesions- hypopigmented or erythematous lesions with definite impairment of sensation.
• Peripheral nerve involvement- thickening of the nerve with sensory impairment. Nerve tenderness can also be seen.
• Detection of acid-fast bacilli in slit-skin smear, skin biopsy, or positive biopsy PCR.

The presence of two of the three signs can establish the diagnosis of leprosy. Other tests done for diagnosis of leprosy include nerve biopsy in pure neural leprosy and PGL-1 antibody in cases with low bacterial load.
questions.learning: Tuberculoid leprosy with dermal test positive — The patient’s slight loss of sensation along the ulnar nerve, solitary forearm nodule, and histopathology showing well-defined granulomas indicate tuberculoid leprosy with a dermal test positive.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which method is used to separate Bajra grains from black seeds when they are mixed together?
questions.explanation: The separation of bajra (pearl millet) grains from black seeds is based on the principle of difference in density (specific gravity). When the mixture is placed in a 10% salt solution, the density of the liquid increases compared to plain water. In this medium: 1. 1. Heavier bajra grains have a higher density than the salt solution → they sink 2. 2. Lighter black seeds (impurities/weed seeds) have a lower density → they float This allows easy separation by decantation or skimming off the floating particles. A 10% salt solution is optimal because it provides the right density difference for effective separation. If the solution is too dilute (like water or normal saline), both may sink. If too concentrated, even desired grains might float, reducing efficiency. Why other options are incorrect: (A) 20% salt water: Too concentrated → may float both components (B) Normal saline (~0.9%): Too dilute → ineffective separation (D) Water: No sufficient density difference
questions.learning: The separation of bajra (pearl millet) grains from black seeds is based on the principle of difference in density (specific gravity). When the mixture is placed in a 10% salt solution, the density of the liquid increases compared to plain water.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A patient presented with a black, foul-smelling discharge from the nose. On examination, blackish necrotic mass filling the nasal cavity and eroding the septum and hard palate were seen. What is the most important risk factor for this disease?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Diabetes

The given clinical scenario is suggestive of mucormycosis and the most important risk factor among these is diabetes.

Mucormycosis is an opportunistic mycosis. It is typically seen in patients with diabetes mellitus and/or diabetic ketoacidosis, and immunocompromised patients. Mucormycosis recently emerged as an important superinfection in COVID-19 patients, especially in India. The surge in cases is most likely due to diabetes mellitus and steroid use.

Risk factors for the infection include the following:

* Uncontrolled diabetes

* Acidosis (especially diabetic ketoacidosis)

* Steroid treatment

* Lymphomas and leukemias

* Immunodeficiencies

* Severe burns

The rhino-orbital-cerebral is the most common form of mucormycosis. Patients present with rhinitis, eye or facial pain, and facial numbness followed by the onset of conjunctival suffusion and swelling along with blurry vision.

Patients can have local tissue destruction with blackish nasal discharge typically resembling the presentation of invasive mucormycosis. The blackish discoloration is due to direct fungal invasion causing arterial and venous thrombosis leading to gangrene.

Diagnosis is made by biopsy with histopathologic examination. The biopsy shows characteristic wide, ribbon-like aseptate hyphal elements that branch at right angles.

The below image shows biopsy findings seen in mucormycosis.

Treatment includes intravenous administration of amphotericin B and wide excision of necrotic tissues. Along with the reversal of underlying conditions and risk factors.
questions.learning: Diabetes — The given clinical scenario is suggestive of mucormycosis and the most important risk factor among these is diabetes. Mucormycosis is an opportunistic mycosis.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: During fetal heart rate monitoring, variable decelerations are noted on the CTG trace. What is the most likely cause or mechanism of this finding?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Cord compression

Cardiotocography detects changes in fetal heart rate patterns during labor.

Variable decelerations are abrupt decreases in fetal heart rate caused by Umbilical Cord Compression.

Variable decelerations on CTG indicate umbilical cord compression and are commonly associated with oligohydramnios. Early decelerations indicate fetal head compression, while late decelerations indicate fetal hypoxia from uteroplacental insufficiency.

Mechanism of Variable Decelerations

Umbilical cord compression

↓

Reduced blood flow to fetus

↓

Baroreceptor stimulation

↓

Sudden drop in fetal heart rate

This produces the characteristic abrupt V-shaped deceleration on CTG.

| Type | Cause | Pattern

| ---- | ----- | -------

| Early deceleration | Head compression | Mirror of contraction

| Variable deceleration | Cord compression | Abrupt V-shaped

| Late deceleration | Uteroplacental insufficiency | Delayed after contraction

Conditions Causing Cord Compression

Common causes include:

• Oligohydramnios
• Cord prolapse
• Nuchal cord
• Cord around limbs

Management of Variable Decelerations

Initial steps include:

• Maternal position change
• Oxygen administration
• IV fluids
• Amnioinfusion if severe
questions.learning: Cord compression Cardiotocography detects changes in fetal heart rate patterns during labor. Variable decelerations are abrupt decreases in fetal heart rate caused by Umbilical Cord Compression.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: An adolescent presents with mild localized pain over the lower limb. X-ray shows a well-defined lytic lesion with sclerotic margins located in the metaphysis of the tibia. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Brodie's abscess

Brodie's abscess presents as a well-defined metaphyseal lytic lesion with thick sclerotic margins in adolescents, representing subacute osteomyelitis typically caused by Staphylococcus aureus.

Key Features:

• Oval/round lytic lesion
• Thick sclerotic border
• Located in metaphysis (especially tibia)
• Minimal periosteal reaction

| Option | Verdict | Why

| ------ | ------- | ---

| A. Simple bone cyst | ❌ | Central, metaphyseal but no sclerotic rim, fluid-filled

| B. Aneurysmal bone cyst (ABC) | ❌ | Expansile, “blow-out” lesion, septations, no thick sclerosis

| C. Chondroblastoma | ❌ | Epiphyseal lesion, not metaphyseal

| D. Brodie’s abscess | ✅ | Metaphyseal + lytic + sclerotic rim + mild symptoms

| Feature | Brodie’s Abscess | Simple Bone Cyst | ABC | Chondroblastoma

| ------- | ---------------- | ---------------- | --- | ---------------

| Age | Adolescents | Children | <20 yrs | Adolescents

| Site | Metaphysis | Metaphysis | Metaphysis | Epiphysis

| Margin | Sclerotic rim | Thin | None | Variable

| Nature | Infection | Fluid cyst | Blood-filled | Tumor

| Symptoms | Mild pain | Often asymptomatic | Pain/swelling | Joint pain
questions.learning: Brodie's abscess Brodie's abscess presents as a well-defined metaphyseal lytic lesion with thick sclerotic margins in adolescents, representing subacute osteomyelitis typically caused by Staphylococcus aureus.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A 10-year-old child presents with hair loss. The hair loss is patchy as shown in the image below. Black dots are noted in areas of hair loss. Which of the following types of tinea is this child suffering from?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Endothrix

The given clinical scenario depicting a young child with patchy hair loss and the image showing black dots is suggestive of endothrix type of tinea capitis.

Tinea capitis is a dermatophyte infection primarily occurring in children. Clinical features of tinea capitis are patchy hair loss, scaling, tender lymphadenopathy, and in severe cases, there might be pustules and crusting of the affected area along with sinus formation.

The clinical variants of tinea capitis are:

• Endothrix - a non-inflammatory type in which multiple black dots are present within the areas of alopecia. It is most commonly caused by T. tonsurans and T. violaceum.
• Ectothrix -a mild inflammatory type in which single or multiple scaly patches with hair loss are seen. Microsporum audouinii, M.canis, M.equinnum, and M.ferrugineum cause ectothrix infection.
• Kerion -a severe inflammatory type that presents with an inflammatory mass with thick crusting and matting of hair with pus and sinus formation. It is commonly caused by T. verrucosum and T. mentagrophytes.

• Favus - is characterized by the presence of yellowish, cup‐shaped crusts known as scutula that develop around hair follicles. It is caused by T. schoenleinii

Treatment:

• Terbinafine: <10 Kg- 62.5 mg; 10-20 kg - 125 mg; >20 kg- 250 mg, all given daily for 4 weeks.
• Itraconazole: 2-4 mg/kg/day for 4-6 weeks.
questions.learning: Endothrix — The given clinical scenario depicting a young child with patchy hair loss and the image showing black dots is suggestive of endothrix type of tinea capitis.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A patient presents with recurrent kidney stones. Microscopic examination finding of the urine specimen is shown below. Which of the following is not seen in the urine of this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Histidine

The image shows hexagonal, translucent and white crystals suggestive of cystinuria. Histidine is not seen in the urine of this patient.

Cystinuria is an autosomal-recessive disease due to a defect in renal PCT & intestinal amino acid transporter that is essential for reabsorptive transport of Cystine and the dibasic amino acids Ornithine, Lysine, and Arginine (COLA).

Diagnosis of cystinuria is by the cyanide–nitroprusside test. Initial treatment is with adequate hydration, alkalization of the urine with citrate supplementation or acetazolamide, and dietary modification to reduce salt and protein intake. If this fails then patients are usually started on chelation therapy with penicillamine.
questions.learning: Histidine — The image shows hexagonal, translucent and white crystals suggestive of cystinuria. Histidine is not seen in the urine of this patient.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A primigravida woman in her late 20s reports progressive hearing loss during pregnancy. Audiological evaluation shows bilateral negative Rinne tests, and the Weber test lateralizes to the right ear. Otoscopic examination reveals normal tympanic membranes, while audiometry demonstrates a notable dip in bone conduction at 2000 Hz. Based on these findings, what is the most appropriate management or intervention?
questions.explanation: The patient’s symptoms and findings—progressive conductive hearing loss exacerbated by pregnancy, a normal-looking drum, and the Carhart’s notch (dip in bone conduction at 2000 Hz)—are classic for otosclerosis. Otosclerosis involves abnormal bone remodeling that fixes the stapes footplate. A negative Rinne test indicates conductive loss. While sodium fluoride (Option A) can sometimes be used to slow the metabolic activity of active foci, it is not a primary curative intervention. Tympanoplasty (Option B) is for drum or middle ear reconstruction and is not indicated here. Stapedectomy (Option C) involves removing the entire footplate, but the modern preferred surgical intervention is Stapedotomy (Option D). Stapedotomy involves making a small hole in the footplate and placing a piston-like prosthesis, which carries a lower risk of inner ear damage compared to total removal. Thus, Stapedotomy is the definitive surgical choice
questions.learning: The patient’s symptoms and findings—progressive conductive hearing loss exacerbated by pregnancy, a normal-looking drum, and the Carhart’s notch (dip in bone conduction at 2000 Hz)—are classic for otosclerosis.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: What is the best position for a conscious patient to be in during the insertion of a Ryle's tube?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Sitting with neck flexion

The best position for a conscious patient to be in during the insertion of Ryle's tube (RT) is sitting with neck flexion. The described position helps in directing the RT towards the esophagus and also prevents it from coiling in the oropharynx or entering the trachea.

RT, also known as nasogastric (NG) tube, measures 120-125 cm. It has 4 markings at 40cm (cardia), 50cm (body), 60cm (pylorus), and 70 cm (duodenum) to indicate the approximate position after the placement.

Indications for NG tube:

• Feeding in patients with dysphagia, decreased appetite, or those who are nil per os (NPO) for medical or surgical reasons.
• Aspiration of gastric fluid
• Gastric decompression in cases of intestinal obstruction and paralytic ileus.
• Zollinger-Ellison syndrome
• Bowel irrigation

The absolute contraindications for an NG tube are severe midface trauma, recent nasal surgery, and basilar skull fractures

Steps for the correct insertion of RT in an adult:

1. Examination of the patient’s nostril for any anatomical abnormalities and then instillation with 10 ml of 1% lignocaine
2. NEX method is used to measure the length of the RT:  Place the exit port of the tube at the tip of the nose. Extend the tube to the earlobe, and then to the xiphisternum.
3. The patient is asked to sit upright with partial neck flexion. The tip of the Ryle’s tube is lubricated and passed along the floor of the nasal passage until a resistance is felt(corresponds to nasopharynx)
4. The patient is subsequently asked to swallow water to guide the tube through the esophagus into the stomach until the marked length (based on the NEX method).
5. NG tube is finally taped to secure it in place.

Confirmation of the correct position is done by:

1. Auscultation in the epigastric area while injecting a bolus of air
2. X-ray chest to locate the lead markers
3. Aspiration of contents and subsequently confirming gastric origin (pH <6 indicates gastric placement)
questions.learning: Sitting with neck flexion — The best position for a conscious patient to be in during the insertion of Ryle's tube (RT) is sitting with neck flexion. The described position helps in directing the RT towards the esophagus and also prevents it from coiling…

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A patient with a history of trauma, presented with diplopia, epistaxis, and restricted eye movements. Looking at the CT image given below, what will be your diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Blow out fracture

The given clinical scenario plus the supportive CT image showing the "hanging drop sign" is suggestive of a blowout fracture of the orbital wall.

Blow-out fractures are isolated comminunited fractures caused from direct trauma to the orbit that results in a backward displacement of the eyeball and an increase in the intraorbital pressure. This causes a fracture at the weakest point of the orbital wall which is usually the posteromedial portion of the maxillary bone in the orbital floor. The second most common site for orbital blowout fracture is the medial wall of the orbit.

The patient with blow out fracture usually presents with immediate periorbital edema and blood extravasation in and around the orbit. Proptosis of the eyeball secondary to orbital edema or hemorrhage with paresthesia along the infraorbital nerve are also very common.

Imaging by a plain x-ray in water's view or by CT demonstrates depression of bony fragments and orbital contents herniating through the orbital floor into the maxillary antrum. This is called as the "hanging drop sign" or "tear drop sign".

Definitive treatment is by surgical repair 10-14 days after injury with initial supportive management with analgesics and antibiotics.

Le fort fracture- Is the term used to describe different types of maxillary fractures.
questions.learning: Blow out fracture — The given clinical scenario plus the supportive CT image showing the "hanging drop sign" is suggestive of a blowout fracture of the orbital wall.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 6-week-old male infant presents with post- feeding vomiting and failure to thrive. On abdominal examination, a firm, olive-shaped mass is palpable in the upper abdomen. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The palpation of a firm, "olive-shaped" mass in the upper abdomen of a 6-week-old infant is pathognomonic for Congenital Hypertrophic Pyloric Stenosis. This condition involves hypertrophy of the pyloric sphincter, leading to progressive gastric outlet obstruction. Classic symptoms include non-bilious projectile vomiting after feeding and failure to thrive. Subacute Intestinal Obstruction (Option A) typically presents with abdominal distension and bilious vomiting. GERD (Option C) causes spitting up or "wet burps" but does not feature a palpable abdominal mass or projectile vomiting. Esophageal Atresia (Option D) presents much earlier—immediately after birth—with drooling and choking during the first feed. The metabolic hallmark of pyloric stenosis is hypochloridemic, hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis due to loss of gastric acid. Ultrasound is the preferred imaging modality to confirm pyloric thickening, and treatment is surgical (Ramstedt’s pyloromyotomy)
questions.learning: The palpation of a firm, "olive-shaped" mass in the upper abdomen of a 6-week-old infant is pathognomonic for Congenital Hypertrophic Pyloric Stenosis.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: In the histological section shown, how do the cells in the highlighted cluster most commonly exert their influence on neighbouring pancreatic cells?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Paracrine effect

The marked cluster of cells represents the Islets of Langerhans within pancreatic tissue. The histological image shows the characteristic appearance of pancreatic parenchyma with dark eosinophilic areas representing serous acinar cells (exocrine pancreas) and lighter, less eosinophilic areas representing the islets of Langerhans (endocrine pancreas).
questions.learning: Paracrine effect — The marked cluster of cells represents the Islets of Langerhans within pancreatic tissue. The histological image shows the characteristic appearance of pancreatic parenchyma with dark eosinophilic areas representing serous acinar cells…

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: What is the most prevalent cause of macrocytic anemia among the options provided?
questions.explanation: Macrocytic anemia is characterized by an elevated mean corpuscular volume (MCV > 100 fL). Among the provided options, Vitamin B12 deficiency is the most prevalent cause, specifically when considering megaloblastic anemia. B12 is essential for DNA synthesis; its absence leads to impaired nuclear maturation while cytoplasmic growth continues, resulting in large, immature cells. Alcohol consumption (Option C) is a very common cause of "non-megaloblastic" macrocytosis, but it is often less frequent or severe than B12 or folate deficiencies in general clinical populations. Bone marrow disorders (Option B), such as myelodysplastic syndrome, and drug-induced causes (Option D), like hydroxyurea or zidovudine, are significant but less common than nutritional deficiencies. Therefore, because Vitamin B12 deficiency is a leading global cause of macrocytic megaloblastic anemia, it remains the most prevalent and classically identified etiology in this context
questions.learning: Macrocytic anemia is characterized by an elevated mean corpuscular volume (MCV > 100 fL). Among the provided options, Vitamin B12 deficiency is the most prevalent cause, specifically when considering megaloblastic anemia.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Where will you find the epithelium shown in the image?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Ureter

The epithelium shown in the above image can be found in the ureter.

The ureter is lined by transitional epithelium (also called urothelium), similar to the urinary bladder. This specialized epithelium allows stretching, which is crucial as the urine passes through. The presence of transitional epithelium is characteristic of structures in the urinary system, such as the ureters, bladder, and part of the urethra.

Given below is a cross-section of the ureter showing the transitional epithelium and the layer of smooth muscle.

Other options:

Option A: Gall bladder: The gall bladder is lined by simple columnar epithelium, which facilitates the absorption of water and electrolytes from bile.

Option B: Trachea: The trachea is lined by pseudostratified columnar ciliated epithelium with goblet cells, which helps trap and remove particles from the respiratory tract.

Option D: Duodenum: The duodenum is lined by simple columnar epithelium with goblet cells, aiding in digestion and nutrient absorption.
questions.learning: Ureter — The epithelium shown in the above image can be found in the ureter. The ureter is lined by transitional epithelium (also called urothelium), similar to the urinary bladder.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Arrange the sequence of steps involved at neuromuscular junction endplate potential.
options: Acetylcholine release - Calcium entry- Na+ entry
Calcium entry- Acetylcholine release- Na+ entry
Na+ entry - Calcium entry - Acetylcholine release
Na+ entry - Acetylcholine release - Calcium entry
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Calcium entry- Acetylcholine release- Na+ entry

The sequence of steps involved at neuromuscular junction endplate potential is Calcium entry- Acetylcholine release- Na+ entry.

Events occurring at the Chemical Synapse:

The action potential arriving at the end of the motor neuron increases the permeability of its endings to Ca2+

↓

Ca2+ enters the endings and triggers a marked increase in exocytosis of the acetylcholine-containing synaptic vesicles

↓

The binding of acetylcholine to nicotinic receptors increases the Na+ and K+ conductance

↓

The resultant influx of Na+ produces a local depolarizing potential, the endplate potential

↓

The current created by this local potential depolarizes the adjacent muscle membrane to its firing level

↓

Action potentials are generated on either side of the endplate and are conducted away from the endplate in both directions along the muscle fiber. This muscle action potential, in turn, initiates muscle contraction.

Acetylcholine is then removed from the synaptic cleft by acetylcholinesterase, which is present in high concentration at the neuromuscular junction.
questions.learning: Calcium entry- Acetylcholine release- Na+ entry — The sequence of steps involved at neuromuscular junction endplate potential is Calcium entry- Acetylcholine release- Na+ entry.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: During a routine health check-up camp in a rural community, a 30-year-old woman presents with symptoms of fever and body aches. Where would she most likely seek initial medical assistance?
questions.explanation: In the Indian rural healthcare system, the Sub-centre is the first and most accessible point of contact between the community and the healthcare system. For minor ailments like fever and body aches, a patient would typically visit the local sub-centre staffed by an ANM (Auxiliary Nurse Midwife) and an MPW (Multi-Purpose Worker). If the condition is more severe or requires a doctor's intervention, she would then be referred to the Primary Health Center (PHC, Option A), which serves as the next level. The Community Health Center (CHC, Option B) is a secondary level facility for a larger population, and the District Hospital (Option D) is for tertiary-level specialist care. Therefore, based on the three-tier rural health hierarchy, the sub-centre is the definitive "initial" seek-point for primary care
questions.learning: In the Indian rural healthcare system, the Sub-centre is the first and most accessible point of contact between the community and the healthcare system.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 25-year-old patient sustains a fall from the 2nd floor of a building and is brought to the emergency department. Which of the following is not an adjunct to the primary survey?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. CT abdomen and pelvis

CT abdomen and pelvis are not an adjunct to the primary survey. CT scan is a part of a secondary survey.

The primary survey identifies and manages the most immediately life-threatening pathologies first.

The secondary survey includes investigations that help identify all other injuries, excluding the apparent ones. This includes X-rays of the spine and extremities(limbs) and a CT of the abdomen, head, chest, pelvis and spine.
questions.learning: CT abdomen and pelvis CT abdomen and pelvis are not an adjunct to the primary survey. CT scan is a part of a secondary survey.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Based on the image shown, which nerve is most likely to be injured if a fracture occurs at the site indicated by the arrow?
questions.explanation: The arrow in the image points to the medial epicondyle of the humerus, a prominent bony projection on the inner side of the elbow. The ulnar nerve passes posterior to the medial epicondyle, in a groove often referred to as the “funny bone” region. Because of its superficial position here, the ulnar nerve is highly vulnerable to injury in fractures involving the medial epicondyle. If a fracture occurs at this site, the ulnar nerve may be damaged, leading to symptoms such as tingling or numbness in the little finger and half of the ring finger, along with weakness in hand muscles (ulnar claw hand in severe cases). Why Other Options Are Wrong (A) Radial nerve: Runs along the posterior humerus (radial groove), not at the medial epicondyle. (B) Median nerve: Lies anteriorly in the cubital fossa, not behind the medial epicondyle. (D) Musculocutaneous nerve: Supplies anterior arm muscles and does not pass near this bony landmark
questions.learning: The arrow in the image points to the medial epicondyle of the humerus, a prominent bony projection on the inner side of the elbow. The ulnar nerve passes posterior to the medial epicondyle, in a groove often referred to as the “funny bone” region.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: Radioactive isotope used for teletherapy?
questions.explanation: Teletherapy refers to external beam radiation therapy where the radiation source is located at a distance from the patient. Cobalt-60 is the standard radioactive isotope used for teletherapy in many centers (specifically in Cobalt units). It emits high-energy gamma rays and has a half-life of 5.27 years. Iridium-192 (Option A) and Iodine-125 (Option B) are characteristically used for brachytherapy, where the radioactive source is placed inside or very close to the tumor. Iodine-131 (Option D) is an unsealed isotope used for the diagnosis and treatment of thyroid diseases, not for external teletherapy. While linear accelerators (LINACs) have largely replaced cobalt units in high-resource settings, Cobalt-60 remains a vital isotope for teletherapy globally due to its reliability and simpler maintenance. Understanding the differences between teletherapy and brachytherapy isotopes is a core concept in clinical oncology and radiotherapy
questions.learning: Teletherapy refers to external beam radiation therapy where the radiation source is located at a distance from the patient. Cobalt-60 is the standard radioactive isotope used for teletherapy in many centers (specifically in Cobalt units).

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which graft option is used least often during coronary artery bypass graft (CABG) surgery?
questions.explanation: In coronary artery bypass grafting (CABG), surgeons use various blood vessels to bypass blocked coronary arteries. The internal mammary artery (Option B), specifically the Left Internal Mammary Artery (LIMA), is the "gold standard" graft due to its excellent long-term patency. The long saphenous vein (Option A) from the leg is the most common "venous" graft used when multiple bypasses are required. The radial artery (Option D) is also frequently used as an arterial graft with good patency rates. The intercostal artery (Option C) is virtually never used as a conduit for CABG. Its anatomical position, relatively small size, and importance in providing collateral circulation to the spinal cord make it a poor and risky choice for a coronary graft. Therefore, among the choices provided, the intercostal artery is the "least frequently utilized"—essentially not used at all—in standard cardiac bypass practice
questions.learning: In coronary artery bypass grafting (CABG), surgeons use various blood vessels to bypass blocked coronary arteries. The internal mammary artery (Option B), specifically the Left Internal Mammary Artery (LIMA), is the "gold standard" graft due to its…

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 6-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department with a generalized tonic-clonic seizure after high grade fever. What is the most appropriate immediate treatment for this child?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Diazepam

This is a febrile seizure presenting as a generalized tonic–clonic seizure in a child with high-grade fever. The immediate management is benzodiazepine administration to abort the seizure.

Diazepam (IV/rectal) is the drug of choice for acute control.

Diazepam given

↓

Binds GABA-A receptor

↓

↑ Cl⁻ influx into neuron

↓

Hyperpolarization

↓

↓ Neuronal firing

↓

Seizure stops

Phenytoin, valproate, and ethosuximide are not used for immediate termination of febrile seizures.

| Drug | Role | Use

| ---- | ---- | ---

| Diazepam | ⭐ First-line | Acute seizure

| Phenytoin | Second-line | Status epilepticus

| Valproate | Maintenance | Chronic seizures

| Ethosuximide | Specific | Absence seizures

Febrile Seizure-

| Feature | Finding

| ------- | -------

| Age | 6 months–5 years

| Type | Generalized

| Prognosis | Good

| Recurrence | Possible
questions.learning: Diazepam — This is a febrile seizure presenting as a generalized tonic–clonic seizure in a child with high-grade fever. The immediate management is benzodiazepine administration to abort the seizure.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following statements regarding MgSO4 is false?
options: MgSO4 causes uterine relaxation, but is dose dependant
MgSO4 is continued upto 24 hours after delivery or last attack of seizure
It has inhibitory effect on cerebral cortex thereby preventing seizures and lowering the BP
In renal failure, MgSO4 loading dose can be given, but maintenence dose should be adjusted based on renal function
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. It has inhibitory effect on cerebral cortex thereby preventing seizures and lowering the BP

The false statement regarding MgSO4 (Magnesium sulfate) is option C. It has an inhibitory effect on the cerebral cortex, thereby preventing seizures, but this action is not responsible for lowering blood pressure.

MgSO4 is mainly used in preeclampsia due to its specific anticonvulsant action and neuroprotective action on the cortex. MgSO4 acts as a membrane stabilizer. It reduces motor endplate sensitivity to acetylcholine and blocks neuronal calcium influx. It is not used to treat hypertension, although it shows some hypotensive action by decreasing vascular response to vasopressors.

MgSO4 is used for the management of eclampsia and as prophylaxis in severe pre-eclampsia. The therapeutic level of magnesium in eclampsia is 4-7mEq/L. The two regimens commonly used are Pritchard and Sibai regimen.

Regimen
Loading Dose
Maintenance Dose

Intramuscular (Pritchard)
4g (20% solution) IV over 3-5 minute
followed by 10g (5O%), deep IM
(5 gm in each buttock)
5g (5O%) IM 4 hourly in alternate buttocks

Intravenous (Zuspan or Sibai)
4g IV slow over 15-20 minute
1-2g/h IV infusion

Other actions:

• Cerebral vasodilatation
• Uterine artery vasodilatation
• Uterine tocolytic i.e. inhibits uterine contractility
• Increased production of endothelial prostacyclin
• Inhibits platelet activation

Other options:

Option A: MgSO4 inhibits uterine contractility but is dose-dependent (only above serum values of 8-10 mEq/L).

Option B: MgSO4 has to be administered up to 24 hours after the last seizure (in postpartum seizure) or delivery, whichever is later. For recurrent seizures, 2 g IV bolus is given in the above regimen.

Option D: Magnesium is cleared almost exclusively by renal excretion. But, in renal failure, the initial 4-g loading dose of magnesium sulfate can be safely administered regardless of renal function. Only the maintenance dose needs to be altered according to the renal function. This is because the loading dose is responsible for reaching therapeutic levels, but the maintenance doses are responsible for maintaining steady states.
questions.learning: It has inhibitory effect on cerebral cortex thereby preventing seizures and lowering the BP The false statement regarding MgSO4 (Magnesium sulfate) is option C.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Match the following: Organism: 1. Helicobacter pylori 2. Mycobacterium tuberculosis 3. Chlamydia trachomatis 4. Non-penicillinase-producing gonococci Drug: a. Amoxicillin b. Doxycycline c. Clarithromycin d. Streptomycin
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 1–c, 2–d, 3–b, 4–a

Knowledge of the drug of choice (DOC) for common bacterial pathogens is essential for selecting appropriate antimicrobial therapy and is frequently tested in examinations.

Correct Match:

• 1. Helicobacter pylori → c. Clarithromycin
• 2. Mycobacterium tuberculosis → d. Streptomycin
• 3. Chlamydia trachomatis → b. Doxycycline
• 4. Non-penicillinase-producing gonococci → a. Amoxicillin (historically susceptible strains)

Why is A correct?

• H. pylori eradication regimens include clarithromycin (where macrolide resistance is low) along with a proton pump inhibitor and other antibiotics.
• Streptomycin is a first-line antitubercular drug (now mainly reserved for selected indications such as drug-resistant TB or when injectable agents are required).
• Doxycycline is the drug of choice for uncomplicated Chlamydia trachomatis infection.
• Non-penicillinase-producing Neisseria gonorrhoeae are susceptible to amoxicillin/penicillin; however, due to widespread resistance, ceftriaxone is now the recommended treatment in current practice.
questions.learning: 1–c, 2–d, 3–b, 4–a Knowledge of the drug of choice (DOC) for common bacterial pathogens is essential for selecting appropriate antimicrobial therapy and is frequently tested in examinations.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: The most common organ injuries in air blast shock waves will be?
questions.explanation: In an explosion, air blast shock waves primarily damage gas-containing organs due to the rapid pressure changes at air-tissue interfaces. The Lungs are the most commonly injured internal organ in primary blast injuries. This "blast lung" involves pulmonary hemorrhage, edema, and alveolar rupture, often leading to severe respiratory distress or air embolism. The auditory system (tympanic membrane rupture) is the most frequent overall blast injury, but the lung is the most critical organ affected. The Intestine (Option A) is the second most common gas-containing organ injured, often suffering mural hematomas or delayed perforation. The Kidney (Option C) and Heart (Option D) are solid or fluid-filled organs that are relatively more resistant to primary blast waves compared to the air-filled lungs. Clinicians managing blast victims must have a high index of suspicion for lung injury, even in the absence of external trauma, as symptoms may be delayed for several hours
questions.learning: In an explosion, air blast shock waves primarily damage gas-containing organs due to the rapid pressure changes at air-tissue interfaces. The Lungs are the most commonly injured internal organ in primary blast injuries.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A patient presents with excessive thirst and markedly increased urine output of about 6–7 liters per day, with a history of cerebral trauma one month earlier. What is the most appropriate treatment for this condition?
questions.explanation: Post-traumatic polyuria (6–7 L/day) and polydipsia after head injury are hallmark signs of Central Diabetes Insipidus (CDI). CDI results from damage to the posterior pituitary or hypothalamus, leading to a deficiency of Antidiuretic Hormone (ADH). The most appropriate and first-line treatment is Desmopressin (DDAVP), a synthetic vasopressin analog. Desmopressin binds to renal V2 receptors, promoting water reabsorption and correcting the fluid imbalance. Hydrochlorothiazide (Option A) is used for nephrogenic DI, where the kidneys are resistant to ADH, but is not first-line for CDI. Tolvaptan (Option C) is a V2 receptor antagonist used to treat SIADH (fluid overload), which would worsen DI. Insulin (Option D) is for diabetes mellitus, which is an unrelated disorder of glucose metabolism. Therefore, replacing the missing hormone with desmopressin is the correct clinical intervention
questions.learning: Post-traumatic polyuria (6–7 L/day) and polydipsia after head injury are hallmark signs of Central Diabetes Insipidus (CDI). CDI results from damage to the posterior pituitary or hypothalamus, leading to a deficiency of Antidiuretic Hormone (ADH).

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following are correct in the treatment of cracked nipple? I. Correct attachment (Latch on) will provide immediate relief from pain and rapid healing. II. If pain, mother should use breast pump and the infant is fed with the expressed milk. III. Miconazole lotion is applied over the nipple as well as in the baby’s mouth if there is oral thrush. Select the correct answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. I, II and III

Cracked nipples are a common cause of painful breastfeeding, especially during the first few weeks postpartum. The most common cause is poor attachment (improper latch) of the baby to the breast. Management aims to correct the underlying cause, relieve pain, and continue breastfeeding whenever possible.

All the given statements are correct:

• I. Correct attachment (Latch on) will provide immediate relief from pain and rapid healing: The most important treatment is correcting the baby’s latch and positioning. Proper attachment reduces trauma to the nipple and promotes healing.
• II. If pain, mother should use breast pump and the infant is fed with the expressed milk: If direct breastfeeding is too painful, expressing breast milk with a breast pump and feeding the infant with expressed milk helps maintain lactation while allowing the nipple to heal.
• III. Miconazole lotion is applied over the nipple as well as in the baby’s mouth if there is oral thrush: Candida infection can cause persistent nipple pain and cracking. Both the mother and the infant must be treated simultaneously to prevent reinfection. Miconazole is commonly used for the mother, while the infant receives appropriate antifungal therapy.
questions.learning: I, II and III Cracked nipples are a common cause of painful breastfeeding, especially during the first few weeks postpartum. The most common cause is poor attachment (improper latch) of the baby to the breast.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 70-year-old woman undergoes a routine follow-up examination, during which an ultrasonography (USG) of the liver is performed and shown below. She has a history of mild pain in the hypochondriac region. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The USG image shows classic features of gallstones — hyperechoic (bright white) foci within the gallbladder lumen with characteristic posterior acoustic shadowing, which is the pathognomonic finding of gallstones on ultrasound. Key USG Features visible: 1. Hyperechoic echogenic foci within gallbladder 2. Posterior acoustic shadowing behind the echogenic foci 3. Gravity-dependent movement of stones 4. Patient has mild hypochondriac pain — consistent with biliary colic Why other options are wrong: (B) Amoebic liver abscess is incorrect because it appears as a hypoechoic/anechoic cavity within liver parenchyma with irregular walls — not echogenic foci with acoustic shadowing in the gallbladder. (C) Hydatid cyst is incorrect because hydatid cyst shows a "double wall sign," daughter cysts, or hydatid sand within a cystic structure in the liver — completely different morphology from what is seen here. (D) Acute cholecystitis is incorrect because although gallstones may coexist, acute cholecystitis additionally shows gallbladder wall thickening (>3mm), pericholecystic fluid, and positive sonographic Murphy's sign — features not specifically demonstrated here
questions.learning: The USG image shows classic features of gallstones — hyperechoic (bright white) foci within the gallbladder lumen with characteristic posterior acoustic shadowing, which is the pathognomonic finding of gallstones on ultrasound.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Zellweger syndrome is due to a defect in the biogenesis of:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Peroxisomes

Zellweger syndrome is due to a defect in the biogenesis of peroxisomes.

Zellweger syndrome is also known as cerebrohepatorenal syndrome. It is caused by mutations in the PEX family of genes. This results in defective beta-oxidation of very long-chain fatty acids.

The child presents with

• Dysmorphic facial features.
• Weakness, hypotonia.
• Neonatal seizures
• Eye abnormalities.

Biochemical findings will show :

• Accumulation of very-long-chain fatty acids, phytanic acid
• Abnormalities in the synthesis of bile acids
• Marked reduction of plasmalogens

There is no appropriate treatment for Zellweger syndrome. It is very severe and infants rarely survive beyond a few months.
questions.learning: Peroxisomes Zellweger syndrome is due to a defect in the biogenesis of peroxisomes. Zellweger syndrome is also known as cerebrohepatorenal syndrome.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: According to the Medical Termination of Pregnancy (MTP) Act of 1971, up to what maximum gestational age is medical termination of pregnancy legally permitted?
questions.explanation: The Medical Termination of Pregnancy (MTP) Act was significantly amended in 2021 (updating the 1971 act). Under the current legal framework in India, the maximum gestational age for MTP has been increased to 24 weeks for certain categories of women. These categories include survivors of sexual assault, rape victims, minors, and women with disabilities or mental illness. For standard cases up to 20 weeks, the opinion of one doctor is required; for the 20-24 week window, the approval of two registered medical practitioners is mandatory. Termination beyond 24 weeks is generally only permitted in cases of substantial fetal abnormalities as determined by a State-level Medical Board. Options A, B, and D do not represent the primary legal thresholds defined by the modern act. Therefore, 24 weeks is the current definitive maximum age for the broad application of the law
questions.learning: The Medical Termination of Pregnancy (MTP) Act was significantly amended in 2021 (updating the 1971 act). Under the current legal framework in India, the maximum gestational age for MTP has been increased to 24 weeks for certain categories of women.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: The probability that infection will occur among susceptible persons following contact with an infectious person within the incubation period is known as the_______.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Secondary attack rate

The probability that infection will occur among susceptible persons following contact with an infectious person within the incubation period is called secondary attack rate.

It is calculated by the following formula:

Secondary attack rate (SAR) = (Number of exposed or susceptible persons developing the disease within the incubation period x 100)/(Total number of close or exposed contacts that are susceptible)

Primary cases are usually excluded from the numerator and denominator.

Secondary attack rate measures the communicability of the disease.
questions.learning: Secondary attack rate — The probability that infection will occur among susceptible persons following contact with an infectious person within the incubation period is called secondary attack rate.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 12-year-old boy presented to the OPD with a scald injury of his arm. The lesion was pink, oozing, and painful to moving air and touch. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Collagen dressing

Scald injury (damage from contact with hot liquids) that appears pink in colour, has oozing, and pain is suggestive of a 2nd-degree burn (i.e. partial-thickness burn). Collagen dressing is the most appropriate management for this injury.

The best dressing for burn wounds is skin; collagen is a good substitute for skin, especially in partial-thickness burns. For full-thickness burns, sequential excision and grafting should be considered.

Initial treatment for burns includes cleaning burnt areas and removing loose dead skin. Blisters are de-roofed and an appropriate dressing is applied.

Biological dressing (collagen dressings, amniotic membrane, etc.) is the preferred dressing material, especially in partial thickness burns.

If this is not available then a non-adhesive dressing like paraffin gauze impregnated with silver sulfadiazine (SSD) cream, colloidal silver, ionic silver cream, or silver nitrate cream can be applied. Since increased resistance to SSD has recently emerged, it should be judiciously used and reserved for deep dermal, full thickness, infected, and old neglected burns.
questions.learning: Collagen dressing Scald injury (damage from contact with hot liquids) that appears pink in colour, has oozing, and pain is suggestive of a 2nd-degree burn (i.e. partial-thickness burn).

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which of the following is the half-life of lithium?
questions.explanation: Lithium is a widely used mood stabilizer in the management of bipolar disorder. In adults with normal renal function, lithium has an average elimination half-life of approximately 24 hours. Because a drug typically requires about 4–5 half-lives to reach steady-state levels, lithium concentrations usually stabilize after 4–5 days of regular dosing. This is why serum lithium levels are generally checked after 5 days of initiating therapy or changing the dose. Lithium is excreted entirely by the kidneys, and its half-life can be prolonged in certain situations—up to 36 hours or more in elderly patients or those with renal impairment. Therefore, renal function has a major impact on lithium pharmacokinetics. Options A (8 hours) and B (12 hours) are too short, while Option D (48 hours) is longer than the typical half-life in healthy adults. Because lithium has a narrow therapeutic index (≈0.6–1.2 mEq/L), regular serum level monitoring is essential to avoid toxicity, which can manifest as tremor, ataxia, confusion, seizures, or coma
questions.learning: Lithium is a widely used mood stabilizer in the management of bipolar disorder. In adults with normal renal function, lithium has an average elimination half-life of approximately 24 hours.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Brown sequard syndrome is characterized by _____
options: Fine touch lost on the opposite side
Pain and temperature lost on the same side
Pain and temperature loss on the opposite side
Only pain lost on the same side
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Pain and temperature loss on the opposite side

Hemisection of the spinal cord causes damage to ascending sensory (dorsal column pathway, ventrolateral spinothalamic tract) and descending motor (corticospinal tract) pathways, which is called the Brown- Séquard syndrome.

The lesion to fasciculus gracilus or fasciculus cuneatus leads to ipsilateral loss of discriminative touch, vibration, and proprioception below the level of the lesion.(fibers from the sacral cord are positioned most medially and those from the cervical cord are positioned most laterally. )

The loss of the spinothalamic tract leads to contralateral loss of pain and temperature sensation beginning one or two segments below the lesion.

Damage to the corticospinal tract produces weakness and spasticity in certain muscle groups on the same side of the body.
