questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 45-year-old woman reports postcoital bleeding for the past three months. On pelvic examination, a small friable cervical growth is seen that bleeds on touch. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The image shows a large, red, smooth, rounded cervical growth in a 45-year-old woman with postcoital bleeding. Despite its large size, the growth appears smooth surfaced and pedunculated — characteristic of a cervical polyp. Key Clinical Features: 1. Smooth, rounded, red mass protruding from cervix 2. Bleeds on touch — polyps are highly vascular 3. Postcoital bleeding — common presentation of cervical polyp 4. Surface appears relatively smooth unlike irregular malignant growth Why other options are wrong: (A) Hemorrhagic cyst is incorrect because hemorrhagic cysts appear as smooth bluish-white rounded swellings — they do not protrude as large vascular masses and rarely cause postcoital bleeding. (C) Cervical cancer is incorrect because cervical cancer typically presents as irregular, cauliflower-like, ulcerative, necrotic friable mass with irregular surface — the growth here appears smoother and more rounded suggesting benign polyp. (D) Cervical fibroid is incorrect because cervical fibroids are firm, pale, hard masses arising from cervical stroma — they are not typically bright red vascular pedunculated growths as seen here
questions.learning: The image shows a large, red, smooth, rounded cervical growth in a 45-year-old woman with postcoital bleeding. Despite its large size, the growth appears smooth surfaced and pedunculated — characteristic of a cervical polyp.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Revised A woman presented in her 8th week of pregnancy seeking MTP. What is the appropriate dosage of Misoprostol administered by the mucosal route?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 800 mcg

The dosage of Misoprostol administered by mucosal route in this case, is 800 mcg.

Mucosal misoprostol administration has increased efficacy and minimizes gastrointestinal side effects and is now preferred over the prior oral administration. The mucosal route includes buccal, sublingual, and vaginal.

Medical management protocol for induced abortion for < 12 weeks of gestation (As per WHO 2018 guideline):

* Combined Regimen (Recommended): 200 mg of oral Mifepristone followed 1-2 days later by 800 mcg of buccal, vaginal or sublingual Misoprostol

* Misoprostol-only regimen (Alternative): 800 μg misoprostol administered vaginally, sublingually, or buccally.

Outpatient medical abortion is an acceptable option for pregnancies with a menstrual age < 63 days (9 weeks)

Various regimens for medical termination of pregnancy

First trimester

* Mifepristone/Misoprostol Combined Regimen (Recommended)

* Misoprostol-only regimen (Alternative)

Second Trimester

* Mifepristone/Misoprostol Combined Regimen (Recommended): 200 mg of oral Mifepristone followed 1-2 days later by 400 mcg of buccal, vaginal or sublingual Misoprostol every 3 hours

* Misoprostol Alone(Alternative): 400 mcg of buccal, vaginal or sublingual Misoprostol every 3 hours

* Dinoprostone- 20 mg vaginal suppository every 4 hr

* Concentrated Oxytocin- 50 units of oxytocin in 500 mL of normal saline infused in an incremental fashion through 150, 200, 250, and finally 300 units of oxytocin each in 500 mL of normal saline

Pearl PF1638: Medical Termination of Pregnancy Act - MTP Act 1971

MTP Act with 2021 amendments

Indications:

* Therapeutic - to save the life of the mother

* Eugenic - to prevent the risk of the child being born with serious mental or physical abnormality i.e. first-trimester viral infections, teratogenic drug intake, radiation exposure

* Humanitarian - pregnancy resulted from rape or incest

* Social - pregnancy resulted from failure of contraceptives

Rules:

* Only a registered medical practitioner who is qualified (one who has assisted in the performance of 25 cases of MTP in a recognized hospital) can terminate a pregnancy.

* MTP should be carried out in a government or government-recognized hospital. Private hospitals may take up MTP if they obtain a license from the chief medical officer of the district.

* The termination of pregnancy by a person, who is not a registered medical practitioner (the person concerned), or in an unrecognised hospital (administrative head) shall be punished with rigorous imprisonment for a term not less than 2 years, but which may extend to 7 years.

Consent:

The consent of the woman is required for conducting an abortion. The written consent of the guardian is required if the woman is minor or mentally ill. Consent of the husband or partner is not necessary.

If the woman is not willing, abortion cannot be performed at the request of the husband alone. The woman need not produce proof of her age. It is enough for the woman to say that she was raped, and it is not necessary that a complaint was lodged with the police.

Opinion of doctors:

* Till 20 weeks - 1 doctor's opinion

* 20 to 24 weeks - 2 doctors' opinion

* For substantial fetal anomalies - approval from the medical board consisting of obstetrician, paediatrician, radiologist and a person appointed by the state

Upper limit of MTP:

* Up to 24 weeks of gestation in victims of rape and incest, fetal anomalies, or congenital malformations

* Up to 20 weeks in case of contraception failure (any female with her partner)

* At any gestational age for substantial fetal anomalies decided by the medical board

Confidentiality:

A register for recording the details of MTP must be kept for at least 5 years. The patient's name must not be entered, only the reference number is used. Unlawful disclosure of patient's details is punishable with 1-year imprisonment ± fine.
questions.learning: 800 mcg The dosage of Misoprostol administered by mucosal route in this case, is 800 mcg. Mucosal misoprostol administration has increased efficacy and minimizes gastrointestinal side effects and is now preferred over the prior oral administration.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Consider the following statements regarding inflammatory bowel disease: 1. Ulcerative colitis (UC) involves terminal ileum and rarely causes proctitis. 2. Cobblestone appearance of bowel is seen in Crohn’s disease. 3. Skip lesions are a characteristic of ulcerative colitis but never seen in Crohn’s disease. 4. Ulcerative colitis is more common in smokers than non-smokers. Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 2 only

Crohn disease is characterized by transmural inflammation, skip lesions, and a cobblestone appearance, and can involve any part of the gastrointestinal tract from mouth to anus. Ulcerative colitis (UC) causes continuous mucosal inflammation, beginning in the rectum (proctitis) and extending proximally.

• 2. Cobblestone appearance of bowel is seen in Crohn’s disease ✔️: Cobblestone appearance is a classic feature of Crohn disease.

Why are the other statements incorrect?

• 1. Ulcerative colitis (UC) involves terminal ileum and rarely causes proctitis ❌: UC always involves the rectum and rarely involves the terminal ileum (except backwash ileitis in extensive disease).
• 3. Ulcerative colitis is more common in smokers than non-smokers ❌: Skip lesions are characteristic of Crohn disease, not UC.
• 4. Ulcerative colitis is more common in smokers than non-smokers ❌: Smoking increases the risk of Crohn disease, whereas it is protective against UC.
questions.learning: 2 only Crohn disease is characterized by transmural inflammation, skip lesions, and a cobblestone appearance, and can involve any part of the gastrointestinal tract from mouth to anus.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A firefighter presents with fever and cough. Culture (shown in the image) reveals Gram- negative, oxidase-positive bacilli, with colonies that fluoresce under UV light. Which is the most likely causative agent?
questions.explanation: The clinical presentation and laboratory findings are pathognomonic for Pseudomonas aeruginosa. This organism is a Gram-negative, motile rod that is characteristically oxidase-positive. A defining feature is its ability to produce pigments like pyocyanin and pyoverdin, which cause colonies to fluoresce or transilluminate under ultraviolet (UV) light. Klebsiella (Option A) is Gram-negative but oxidase-negative and typically forms non-fluorescent mucoid colonies. Staphylococcus aureus (Option B) is a Gram-positive coccus that forms golden-yellow colonies and lacks UV fluorescence. Serratia (Option D) is Gram-negative and oxidase-negative; while some species produce a red pigment (prodigiosin), they do not fluoresce like Pseudomonas. P. aeruginosa is a common cause of respiratory infections, particularly in individuals exposed to environmental stressors like firefighters. Its unique biochemical profile, including the positive oxidase test and UV fluorescence, allows for definitive identification from culture samples
questions.learning: The clinical presentation and laboratory findings are pathognomonic for Pseudomonas aeruginosa. This organism is a Gram-negative, motile rod that is characteristically oxidase-positive.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient without any comorbid conditions is found to have a serum potassium level of 3.0 mmol/L, with a normal ECG. Among the available treatment options, which is the most appropriate management choice?
questions.explanation: The patient has mild hypokalemia (serum 3.0 mmol/L; normal 3.5–5.0 mmol/L) and is asymptomatic with a normal ECG. For stable, mild hypokalemia, the preferred treatment is oral potassium replacement using "Potklor" (Potassium chloride). Oral replacement is safer than intravenous administration and more effective for steady correction. Calcium gluconate (Option A) is used to stabilize the myocardium in hyperkalemia, not hypokalemia. Sodium bicarbonate (Option B) and insulin with dextrose (Option D) are both used to shift potassium into cells to treat hyperkalemia; using them here would dangerously worsen the patient's hypokalemia. Identifying the underlying cause of the potassium loss (e.g., diuretics or GI loss) is also necessary. Patients should be encouraged to increase dietary intake of potassium-rich foods alongside supplementation
questions.learning: The patient has mild hypokalemia (serum 3.0 mmol/L; normal 3.5–5.0 mmol/L) and is asymptomatic with a normal ECG. For stable, mild hypokalemia, the preferred treatment is oral potassium replacement using "Potklor" (Potassium chloride).

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A 4-month-old child was brought to the hospital with an abdominal lesion, as shown in the image. What is the appropriate management for this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Observation

The given clinical picture is suggestive of infantile hemangioma. Only observation of the lesion is required as in 50% of cases, complete involution is seen by 5 years of age.

Hemangioma growth frequently peaks before the first year, and then the lesions enter the involuting phase. The involution phase begins in 50% of children by 5 years of age and in 70% by 7 years of age. It continues until 10 years of age.

Indications for immediate treatment are complications such as ulceration or those pertaining to the location of the mass (e.g. visual issues due to large hemangioma over eyelid).

Other treatment options include:

* Beta blockers - oral propranolol

* Steroids - intralesional triamcinolone, topical clobetasol, systemic steroids (Option B).

* Interferon alfa-2a and vincristine - for steroid-resistant lesions

* Local resection with cutting cautery or carbon dioxide laser (Option C).

Other options:

Option A: Betaxolol is a beta-1 selective blocker that is used in glaucoma and has a lower propensity to precipitate bronchial asthma.
questions.learning: Observation — The given clinical picture is suggestive of infantile hemangioma. Only observation of the lesion is required as in 50% of cases, complete involution is seen by 5 years of age.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text:
A 34-year-old woman was brought to the AIIMS emergency following a road traffic accident. She was hemodynamically stable and her GCS score was 3. She was intubated and sent for non-contrast CT which was found to be normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?

GCS- Glasgow coma scale
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Diffuse axonal injury

The clinical scenario of a patient with a poor GCS score and a normal NCCT brain scan following a road traffic accident is suggestive of diffuse axonal injury.

Diffuse axonal injury (white matter shearing) results from shearing forces, typically from a rotational acceleration of the brain within the rigid cranium. This causes damage to microvasculature and disruption of axons in the subcortical parasagittal white matter, cerebellum, fornix, and internal and external capsule.

Most commonly it occurs in automobile accidents. Patients are usually unconscious from the moment of impact and remain the same until death.

Diffuse axonal injury is characterized by multiple focal lesions with a characteristic distribution:

• CT may be normal.
• MRI is the modality of choice for assessing suspected diffuse axonal injury, even in patients with entirely normal CT of the brain. MRI, especially SWI (susceptibility-weighted imaging) demonstrates small regions of susceptibility artifact or hemorrhage.

Other options:

Option A: Subdural hemorrhage is often due to the rupture of veins that cross the subdural space. In subdural hemorrhage, the CT shows concavo-convex opacity.

Option B: Extradural hemorrhage is mostly due to the rupture of the middle meningeal artery. Since the dura matter tends to adhere to the skull the hemorrhage is seen in CT as a biconvex dense area. They usually do not cross cranial sutures.

Option D: Cerebral contusion occurs due to traumatic brain injury, at the sites that come in direct contact with the skull. Imaging may show microhemorrhages and edema. Usually, no treatment is required.
questions.learning: Diffuse axonal injury — The clinical scenario of a patient with a poor GCS score and a normal NCCT brain scan following a road traffic accident is suggestive of diffuse axonal injury.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: During a routine OPD visit, a 3-year-old child’s growth chart is reviewed and shows a Body Mass Index (BMI) between the 85th and 95th percentile for age and sex. How would you classify the nutritional status of this child?
questions.explanation: Nutritional status in children over the age of 2 is typically assessed using BMI-for-age growth charts. According to standardized CDC and WHO definitions, a child is categorized as overweight if their BMI is between the 85th and 95th percentile (Option C). If the BMI is at or above the 95th percentile, the child is categorized as obese (Option D). Moderate wasting (Option A) and Severe Acute Malnutrition (Option B) are categories used for children with low weight-for-height or low mid-upper arm circumference, representing undernutrition rather than excess weight. Identifying a child in the overweight category is important for implementing early lifestyle interventions to prevent progression to obesity and associated metabolic complications later in childhood. Therefore, based on the percentile range provided, overweight is the correct nutritional classification
questions.learning: Nutritional status in children over the age of 2 is typically assessed using BMI-for-age growth charts. According to standardized CDC and WHO definitions, a child is categorized as overweight if their BMI is between the 85th and 95th percentile (Option C).

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 22-year-old patient presents with fever, severe dyspnea, and expectoration of red currant jelly– like sputum. On examination, the patient has altered sensorium and an increased respiratory rate. Laboratory investigations reveal elevated serum creatinine and blood urea nitrogen levels, with a serum potassium level of 5 mmol/L. What is the most appropriate management in this case?
questions.explanation: The patient presents with features of severe community-acquired pneumonia, likely Klebsiella pneumoniae (suggested by “red currant jelly” sputum). There are concerning signs such as tachypnea (RR ↑), altered sensorium, and renal dysfunction, indicating a serious infection requiring hospitalization. However, ICU admission depends on specific severity criteria (e.g., septic shock, need for mechanical ventilation, severe hypoxemia, or multi-organ failure). In this case: 1. No hypotension/shock mentioned 2. No ventilatory support requirement given 3. Renal involvement appears early/mild 4. Patient is serious but not critically unstable Thus, the patient requires: 1. Inpatient (IPD) care for close monitoring 2. IV broad-spectrum antibiotics (e.g., ceftriaxone, piperacillin-tazobactam) 3. Oxygen and supportive therapy Why other options are incorrect: (A) OPD oral → Too severe (C) ICU IV → No clear ICU criteria (D) ICU oral → Inappropriate

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A woman who underwent dilatation and curettage following a missed abortion now presents with amenorrhoea. Urine pregnancy test is negative. Hysterosalpingography shows the findings seen in the image below. What is your diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Asherman syndrome

The history along with the moth-eaten appearance on hysterosalpingography suggests a diagnosis of Asherman syndrome.

In Asherman syndrome, oligomenorrhoea, amenorrhoea, dysmenorrhoea, abortion and infertility are seen with uterine synechiae.

The synechiae are caused by the following factors:

* Vigorous curettage following postpartum haemorrhage or abortion

* Tubercular endometritis

* Uterine infections with or without intra-uterine device

Treatment involves hysteroscopic lysis of the adhesions

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: In the structure given below, what is the joint observed?
questions.explanation: The image points specifically to the pubic symphysis, which is the classic example of a secondary cartilaginous joint, also known as a symphysis. These joints are characterized by a fibrocartilaginous disc connecting the bony surfaces, which are themselves covered by a thin layer of hyaline cartilage. Unlike primary cartilaginous joints (Option B), which involve hyaline cartilage alone and usually ossify with age (like epiphyseal plates), secondary cartilaginous joints are permanent and typically located in the midline of the body. Syndesmosis (Option A) and fibrous joints (Option C) involve ligamentous or fibrous tissue connections, such as the sutures of the skull or the distal tibiofibular joint, but lack the fibrocartilage disc. The pubic symphysis allows for limited movement, which is particularly vital during childbirth to facilitate the passage of the fetus through the pelvic canal

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: This instrument is not used in which of the following conditions?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Acute anal fissure

The instrument given in the above image is a proctoscope and proctoscopy is contraindicated in acute anal fissures.

Due to pain, digital rectal examination and anoscopy are not performed immediately in acute anal fissures. Acute anal fissures are examined under anaesthesia in operating room when needed.

Anal fissure:

Clinical features

* Severe pain associated with defecation resolves spontaneously and reappears during the next evacuation

* It may even be associated with the passage of fresh blood noticed on tissue after wiping

* Most of the fissures are located in the posterior midline, with the rest being located in the anterior midline. Fissures located laterally can be possible due to other diseases like HIV, TB, syphilis, Crohn's disease, or carcinoma.

Treatment of Anal fissure

* The focus is to normalise bowel habits. Bowel softeners, dietary fibres, and adequate water should be recommended

* Medical therapy involves the topical application of glyceryl trinitrate. It releases nitric oxide and relaxes the internal anal sphincter. This reduces spasms and pain and improves vasculature to promote healing

* Surgical therapy is recommended for chronic fissures that have failed medical therapy. Lateral internal sphincterotomy is the procedure of choice. The aim of this procedure is to decrease the spasms of the internal sphincter by dividing a portion of the muscle.
questions.learning: Acute anal fissure — The instrument given in the above image is a proctoscope and proctoscopy is contraindicated in acute anal fissures. Due to pain, digital rectal examination and anoscopy are not performed immediately in acute anal fissures.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A 30-year-old male presents for evaluation, and his MRI brain is shown below. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Meningioma

Meningiomas are extra-axial tumors characterized by broad dural attachment, homogeneous enhancement, well-defined margins, and the "dural tail" sign on contrast-enhanced MRI.

Typical clues on MRI:

• Extra-axial location
• Broad dural attachment
• Homogeneous contrast enhancement
• “Dural tail sign”

Key Imaging Features:

• Well-defined extra-axial mass
• Broad-based dural attachment
• Dural tail sign (thickened enhancing dura)
• Mass effect with buckling of adjacent cortex
• Possible hyperostosis of adjacent skull

| Feature | Meningioma | Glioma | Ependymoma | Pilocytic Astrocytoma

| ------- | ---------- | ------ | ---------- | ---------------------

| Location | Extra-axial | Intra-axial | Ventricular | Intra-axial

| Enhancement | Homogeneous | Heterogeneous | Variable | Nodule enhances

| Special sign | Dural tail | Necrosis | CSF spread | Cyst + mural nodule

| Age | Adults | Adults | Children | Children

| Margins | Well-defined | Ill-defined | Variable | Well-defined
questions.learning: Meningioma Meningiomas are extra-axial tumors characterized by broad dural attachment, homogeneous enhancement, well-defined margins, and the "dural tail" sign on contrast-enhanced MRI.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A mother brought her 2-year-old child to the OPD with complaints of lack of weight gain, abdominal pain on eating, and poor eating habits. The child was advised gluten-free diet after which there was improvement in the general condition and weight gain. What is the probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Celiac disease

The clinical presentation and the histopathological findings are suggestive of celiac disease.

Celiac disease is an autoimmune gluten-induced enteropathy where HLA DQ2 and DQ8 are expressed. In the small intestine, peptides of gluten are presented to helper T cells which mediate mucosal inflammation. Antiendomysial and anti-tTG antibodies are found in serological studies.

Clinical Features:

• Gastrointestinal Symptoms: Chronic diarrhoea, abdominal pain, vomiting, weight loss, and failure to thrive.
• Extraintestinal Symptoms: Anemia, fatigue, elevated liver enzymes, neurologic disorders, short stature, dental enamel defects, arthralgia, aphthous stomatitis.

Investigation:

• Serologic Tests: Initial testing for anti-TG2 IgA antibodies and total IgA. If anti-TG2 is positive and IgA levels are normal, CD is likely.
• Genetic Testing: For HLA-DQ2 or DQ8 haplotypes.
• Endoscopy and Biopsy: Multiple biopsies from the small intestine to check for villous atrophy.
• Biopsy Findings: villous atrophy: flattening of the villi in the small intestine, crypt hyperplasia: enlargement of the crypts, intraepithelial lymphocytosis: Increased number of lymphocytes in the epithelium.

Treatment:

Gluten-Free Diet: To manage celiac disease, patients must strictly avoid all foods containing gluten. Safe alternatives include rice, corn, maize, buckwheat, millet, amaranth, quinoa, sorghum, potato, soybean, tapioca, and teff, along with bean and nut flours.

Biopsy findings can be seen below:

Other options:

Option A: Tropical sprue is another malabsorption disorder seen as diarrhoea, steatorrhea, nutritional deficiencies, and weight loss. It is prevalent in some tropical areas hence the name. It is mostly attributed to infectious agents considering its response to antibiotics. It is diagnosed by a small intestinal biopsy which shows a close resemblance to that seen in celiac disease but it’s not specifically triggered by gluten and is more common in adults.

Option C: Whipple Disease is a multisystemic disease caused by T.whipplei. Small intestinal biopsy shows PAS-positive macrophages.

Option D: Intestinal Malabsorption is a general term used for conditions that cause poor nutrient absorption, which could include celiac disease but is not specific enough to explain the clear response to a gluten-free diet.
questions.learning: Celiac disease — The clinical presentation and the histopathological findings are suggestive of celiac disease. Celiac disease is an autoimmune gluten-induced enteropathy where HLA DQ2 and DQ8 are expressed.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following is not true about the cavernous sinus thrombosis?
options: Loss of sensation around the orbit
Infection spreads to cavernous sinus from the danger area of face via inferior ophthalmic vein
Superior ophthalmic vein serves as a both incoming as well as outgoing channel to cavernous sinus because it is valveless
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Loss of jaw jerk

Cavernous sinus thrombosis typically affects the cranial nerves that run within the cavernous sinus, leading to characteristic neurological deficits. Structures commonly involved include:

• CN III (Oculomotor)
• CN IV (Trochlear)
• CN V1 (Ophthalmic division of trigeminal nerve)
• CN V2 (Maxillary division of trigeminal nerve)
• CN VI (Abducens nerve)
• Internal carotid artery

Clinical Features:

• Loss of sensation around the orbit → due to involvement of CN V1 (ophthalmic division).
• Infection from the “danger area” of the face can spread to the cavernous sinus via facial vein → angular vein → superior/inferior ophthalmic veins, because these veins are valveless.
• Superior ophthalmic vein acts as both inflow and outflow channel because it lacks valves.

Jaw jerk reflex is mediated by the mandibular division of trigeminal nerve (CN V3) via the mesencephalic nucleus. CN V3 does NOT pass through the cavernous sinus, so jaw jerk is not affected in cavernous sinus thrombosis.
questions.learning: Loss of jaw jerk Cavernous sinus thrombosis typically affects the cranial nerves that run within the cavernous sinus, leading to characteristic neurological deficits.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: In a patient with an aortic dissection, hiccups may occur due to irritation or injury of structures near the aorta. Which anatomical structure is most likely responsible for causing hiccups in this scenario?
questions.explanation: Aortic dissection is a life-threatening condition in which blood enters the medial layer of the aortic wall, creating a false lumen. Although uncommon, persistent hiccups are a recognized atypical presentation of aortic dissection. They occur when the expanding dissecting aorta or aneurysmal dilation irritates or compresses the phrenic nerve. The phrenic nerve (C3–C5) supplies motor innervation to the diaphragm, and its irritation results in involuntary diaphragmatic contractions, perceived clinically as hiccups. Thus, the symptom is caused by nerve involvement rather than the aorta itself. The thoracic aorta (Option C) is the anatomical site of the dissection, but it does not directly explain the mechanism of hiccups. The abdominal aorta (Option B) lies distal to the diaphragm and is unlikely to affect the phrenic nerve. The spinal accessory nerve (Option D) innervates the sternocleidomastoid and trapezius muscles and has no role in diaphragmatic movement. Clinicians should recognize persistent or unexplained hiccups, especially when accompanied by chest or back pain, as a possible sign of mediastinal involvement in aortic dissection, warranting urgent evaluation
questions.learning: Aortic dissection is a life-threatening condition in which blood enters the medial layer of the aortic wall, creating a false lumen. Although uncommon, persistent hiccups are a recognized atypical presentation of aortic dissection.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: What ratio of chest compressions to rescue breaths is given during CPR in an adult if 2 rescuers are present?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 30:2

During cardiopulmonary resuscitation of adults, the ratio of chest compression to rescue breaths is 30:2 irrespective of the number of rescuers.

In infants and children, the ratio is 30:2 for a single rescuer and 15:2 if 2 or more rescuers are present.

Pearl PF1780: High quality CPR for adults

* Push hard: 5-6cm depth

* Push fast: 100-120/min frequency

* Allow for complete chest recoil

* Minimize interruptions in compressions <10 seconds

* Avoid excessive ventilation

* Rotate compressor every 2 min or earlier if fatigued

* If no advanced airway, 30:2 compression-ventilation ratio

Attempt to improve CPR quality if :

* Quantitative waveform capnography - PETCO2 <10mmHg,

* Intra-arterial pressure - If relaxation phase (diastolic) pressure <20mmHg

Pearl PF2036: Basic Life Support (BLS) Algorithm

Pearl PF1767: Adult cardiac arrest algorithm (Updated as per 2020 guidelines)
questions.learning: 30:2 During cardiopulmonary resuscitation of adults, the ratio of chest compression to rescue breaths is 30:2 irrespective of the number of rescuers. In infants and children, the ratio is 30:2 for a single rescuer and 15:2 if 2 or more rescuers are present.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A young athlete was diagnosed to have HOCM and has a harsh ejection systolic murmur. Which of the following maneuvers would most likely increase the intensity of the murmur?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Valsalva maneuver

HOCM is characterized by:

• Asymmetric septal hypertrophy
• Dynamic obstruction of the left ventricular outflow tract (LVOT)

This obstruction varies depending on ventricular volume.

Correct answer is B because Valsalva maneuver decreases venous return and left ventricular preload, which worsens left ventricular outflow tract obstruction in HOCM and increases murmur intensity.

Isometric handgrip and squatting increase preload/afterload and reduce obstruction, decreasing murmur intensity. Leaning forward is classically used to accentuate aortic regurgitation murmur.
questions.learning: Valsalva maneuver HOCM is characterized by: • Asymmetric septal hypertrophy • Dynamic obstruction of the left ventricular outflow tract (LVOT) This obstruction varies depending on ventricular volume.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient with diabetes mellitus on glibenclamide is started on gemfibrozil. Later, he develops recurrent episodes of hypoglycemia. What is the mechanism of drug interaction?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Gemfibrozil causes inhibition of CYP2C9

Sulfonylureas (glibenclamide, glipizide, glimepiride) are metabolized principally by CYP2C9. Gemfibrozil — and more potently its glucuronide metabolite — is a strong inhibitor of CYP2C8 and also inhibits CYP2C9 and OATP1B1 transport. Inhibition reduces the hepatic clearance of glibenclamide, raising its plasma concentration and prolonging half-life. The result is exaggerated insulin secretion → recurrent hypoglycemia.

Other options:

• A. Enzyme induction: Would do the opposite — increased metabolism → loss of glycemic control, not hypoglycemia. Inducers = rifampicin, phenytoin, carbamazepine.
• B. Increased renal excretion of glibenclamide: Would lower drug levels → hyperglycemia; also glibenclamide is largely hepatically cleared.
• D. Reduced GI absorption: Again lowers bioavailability → hyperglycemia.

Pearl:

• Inhibitor → ↑ effect of substrate.
• Inducer → ↓ effect.
• Gemfibrozil + repaglinide is the classic dangerous CYP2C8 pair (contraindicated).

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: In a town with one lakh population (1,00,000) there are a total of 2500 live births in a year. There were 75 total deaths of children before the age of one month, total 200 deaths before the age of one year, and a total 300 deaths before the age of three years. Which of the following statements regarding Infant Mortality Rate (IMR) of the town for the given year are correct? 1. The denominator is 1,00,000. 2. The IMR of the town is higher than the current national average of IMR for India. 3. The numerator is the number of children dying before the age of one month. 4. The IMR of the town is 80 per 1000 live births. Select the correct answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 2 and 4 only

Infant Mortality Rate (IMR) is defined as: Number of deaths of infants (<1 year of age) during a year ÷ Number of live births during the same year × 1000

Calculation:

• Infant deaths (<1 year) = 200
• Live births = 2500

IMR = (200 ÷ 2500) × 1000 = 80 per 1000 live births

Why are the statements correct/incorrect?

• 1. The denominator is 1\,00\,000❌: Incorrect. The denominator is 2500 live births, not the total population.
• 2. The IMR of the town is higher than the current national average of IMR for India✔️: Correct. 80/1000 is much higher than the current national average.
• 3. The numerator is the number of children dying before the age of one month❌: Incorrect. The numerator is deaths before 1 year of age (200).
• 4. The IMR of the town is 80 per 1000 live births:✔️: Correct.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Determine the classification of the myoma denoted as '4' in the provided image.
questions.explanation: A pedunculated submucosal myoma is a type of fibroid that arises beneath the endometrium and projects into the uterine cavity, remaining attached by a thin stalk. These fibroids can sometimes extend toward or even through the cervix. Because of their intracavitary location, they commonly cause heavy menstrual bleeding (menorrhagia), infertility, and recurrent pregnancy loss. In contrast, a submucous myoma (option D) refers to a broad-based lesion beneath the endometrium without a stalk. The presence of a distinct pedicle in the image confirms that this is not a simple submucous fibroid but a pedunculated variant. Why other options are wrong: (B) Subserous myoma → grows outward from uterus (C) Parasitic myoma → detached and vascularized externally (D) Submucous myoma → no stalk

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: What is the recommended treatment for nephrotic syndrome in children?
questions.explanation: Corticosteroids, such as oral prednisolone, are the first-line and mainstay treatment for nephrotic syndrome in children. This is because Minimal Change Disease (MCD) accounts for about 80% of pediatric cases and typically shows a high response rate to high-dose steroids. Remission of edema and proteinuria often occurs within 10–14 days of therapy. Steroids and cyclophosphamide (Option B) or cyclophosphamide alone (Option C) are second-line treatments reserved for children who are steroid-resistant or frequent relapsers. ACE inhibitors (Option D) are adjunctive therapies used to reduce residual proteinuria and control blood pressure but are not the primary treatment for the underlying disease. Therefore, standard initial management always begins with a steroid regimen, only escalating to immunosuppressants like cyclophosphamide if resistance develops

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Identify the structure passing through the foramen marked.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Abducens nerve

The marked foramen is the superior orbital fissure and the abducens nerve passes through it.

The abducens nerve is the 6th cranial nerve and arises from the brainstem at the pontomedullary junction. It runs through the Dorello's canal which is present at the medial most end of the petrous ridge and then enters the cavernous sinus where it lies lateral to the internal carotid artery. It enters the orbit through the superior orbital fissure within the common tendinous ring and supplies the lateral rectus.

Other options:

Spinal accessory nerve passes through the foramen magnum along with the medulla oblongata and the verterbral arteries

Ophthalmic artery passes through the optic canal along with the optic nerve.

Middle meningeal artery and vein pass through the foramen spinosum along with the meningeal branch of mandibular nerve.

questions.topic: Renal Electrolytes · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 60-year-old man with chronic congestive cardiac failure (CCF) presents with jugular venous distention, ascites, and bilateral pedal edema. Laboratory evaluation reveals elevated atrial natriuretic peptide (ANP) levels. ANP promotes natriuresis by decreasing sodium reabsorption predominantly at which of the following nephron segments?
options: Thick ascending limb of loop of Henle
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Medullary collecting duct

Atrial natriuretic peptide (ANP) promotes natriuresis primarily by inhibiting sodium reabsorption in the medullary collecting duct.

Why Medullary Collecting Duct Specifically?

The medullary collecting duct (MCD) is the primary site of ANP action because:

| Feature | Detail

| ------- | ------

| Receptor density | Highest concentration of NPR-A receptors in the entire nephron

| Transport target | Inhibits ENaC (Epithelial Sodium Channels) on luminal side

| Net effect | ↓ Na⁺ reabsorption → Na⁺ stays in tubule → osmotic water retention in lumen → natriuresis + diuresis

| Aldosterone antagonism | ANP opposes aldosterone action at this same segment

ANP Actions Across the Nephron

| Site | Action | Significance

| ---- | ------ | ------------

| Medullary Collecting Duct ⭐ | ↓ ENaC → ↓ Na⁺ reabsorption | Primary natriuretic effect

| Glomerulus | ↑ GFR (dilates afferent, constricts efferent arteriole) | ↑ filtered Na⁺ load

| Proximal tubule | Mild ↓ Na⁺ reabsorption | Minor contribution

| Inner medullary CD | ↓ Urea transporters | Reduces medullary tonicity → impairs concentrating ability

| Adrenal gland | ↓ Aldosterone secretion | Indirect natriuresis

| Vasculature | Vasodilation | ↓ BP, ↓ venous return

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which of the following is responsible for the phase marked C to D in the given nerve action potential?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. K+ efflux

The phase C to D in the given nerve action potential is caused by K+ efflux as a result of the opening of the  K+ channels, resulting in repolarization.

The sequence of events occurring during an action potential is shown below

• Point A represents the resting state where both channels are closed.
• Na+ channels open in response to depolarizing stimulus resulting in Na+ influx (option A). The initiation of action potential occurs only after a certain potential is reached, which is called the threshold potential represented by point B.
• After this, the sodium influx causes the opening of more Na+ channels through a positive feedback mechanism. Rapid depolarization occurs to reach point C.
• At point C, Na+ channels close and K+ channels open, causing repolarization due to K+ efflux.
• Point D represents continued depolarization due to K+ efflux.
• At point E, Na+ channels are reset and are ready to respond to another depolarizing stimulus. During this phase, the K+ channels remain open and slowly return to the closed state, causing after-hyperpolarization. As a stronger stimulus is required to reach the threshold potential, the excitability of nerve fibre is reduced at point E.
• As both channels close, the membrane returns to resting membrane potential back to point A.

Point B-D is a part of the refractory period. During this period, the application of even a stronger stimulus will not elicit an action potential.

The refractory period is divided into an absolute refractory period and a relative refractory period. During the absolute refractory period, the nerve will not be excited no matter how strong a stimulus is given. However, during the relative refractory period, stronger than normal stimuli can cause excitation.
questions.learning: K+ efflux — The phase C to D in the given nerve action potential is caused by K+ efflux as a result of the opening of the K+ channels, resulting in repolarization.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text:
What is the mechanism of action of methotrexate in osteosarcoma?

UMP- Uridine monophosphate

DHFR- Dihydrofolate reductase
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Competitive inhibitor of DHFR

The anticancer activity of methotrexate is by inhibition of dihydrofolate reductase (DHFR).

Methotrexate belongs to the antimetabolite class of anticancer drugs. The antifolate action of the drug is responsible for its anti-cancer properties.

Mechanism of action:

It is a folic acid analog and binds to the active catalytic site of dihydrofolate reductase(DHFR). This would inhibit the formation of tetrahydrofolate(THF) which is needed for purine nucleotides, thymidylate, and the amino acids serine and methionine. This would interfere with the production of DNA, RNA, and important cellular proteins.

Low doses of methotrexate are used in the management of rheumatic diseases. It is due to the inhibition of amino-imidazole carboxamide ribonucleotide (AICAR) transformylase and thymidylate synthetase. This results in increased levels of adenosine that inhibits inflammation.

Adverse effects:

Common side effects are nausea and mucosal ulcers. Others include anemia, leukopenia, stomatitis, GI ulcerations, and alopecia. Dose-related hepatotoxicity is also seen. The GI effects and hepatotoxicity can be reduced by the use of leucovorin or folinic acid.
questions.learning: Competitive inhibitor of DHFR — The anticancer activity of methotrexate is by inhibition of dihydrofolate reductase (DHFR). Methotrexate belongs to the antimetabolite class of anticancer drugs.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: In a cardiac arrest patient with more than one rescuer present, what is the recommended compression-to-ventilation ratio during CPR?
questions.explanation: According to the American Heart Association (AHA) and global resuscitation guidelines, the recommended compression-to-ventilation ratio for adults in cardiac arrest is 30:2, regardless of whether there is one rescuer or more than one rescuer present. This means the rescuers perform 30 high-quality chest compressions followed by 2 rescue breaths. The 15:2 ratio (Option A) is used only in pediatric (children and infant) CPR when two or more healthcare rescuers are present. Ratios like 15:1 (Option C) or 30:1 (Option D) are not part of standard modern Basic Life Support (BLS) protocols. The goal of the 30:2 ratio in adults is to maximize the amount of "hands-on" time for chest compressions to maintain coronary and cerebral perfusion pressure, while still providing some oxygenation. Rescuers should switch roles approximately every 2 minutes to prevent fatigue and ensure high-quality compressions are maintained

There were 50 deaths between the age of 1 month to 6 months of life and 30 of them died in utero. What is the neonatal mortality rate in this population?

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: What is the appropriate timing for taking a blood sample to diagnose neonatal hypothyroidism?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 72 hours after delivery

The appropriate time for taking a blood sample to diagnose neonatal hypothyroidism is 72 hours after delivery.

After birth, there is a temporary elevation in TSH levels due to physiological neonatal surge, which remains elevated for the first 2-3 days of life. If sampling is done during this period, falsely elevated TSH values may be obtained. Therefore, the ideal time for sampling through a heel prick is after 72 hours of life.

Screening for children for congenital hypothyroidism is very important, as early diagnosis and treatment can help in normal intellectual development. Otherwise, congenital hypothyroidism is known as the most common preventable cause of mental retardation. Children diagnosed beyond the neonatal period have a poor outcome.

The most commonly used strategy is to screen for TSH first as that has have higher sensitivity compared to the T4-based approach. Although the TSH-based approach is better, it doesn't identify central hypothyroidism, which can be identified by the T4-first approach. However, the T4-based approach misses out on the cases of compensated hypothyroidism.

The incidence of congenital hypothyroidism seems to be 4 times higher in India compared to Western countries. Thyroid dysgenesis has emerged as the most common cause of congenital hypothyroidism in India accounting for about 75% of all cases. Interestingly, an Increased incidence of thyroid dysgenesis is noted in Down syndrome.

Clinical features of hypothyroidism:

Congenital
Acquired

Open posterior fontanel
Growth retardation

Umbilical hernia
Delayed skeletal maturation

Characteristic edematous facies
Delayed dental development

Constipation
Delayed puberty

Pallor
Myopathy and pseudohypertrophy

Hypothermia
Enlarged sella

Large tongue
Pseudotumor cerebri

Rough dry skin

Hypotonia

Large abdomen

Management: Thyroid replacement soon after the diagnosis. Thyroxine of dose 10-15 μg/kg/day should be started and adjusted to achieve normal free T4 range. TSH may be elevated up to 2 years of age with reset of the hypothalamic-pituitary axis.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A 60-year-old male patient is brought to the ER due to a suspected stroke. The patient has difficulty forming words but can make noises and give expressions as if he understands the questions asked. Which type of aphasia is most likely present in the patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Broca’s aphasia

The given clinical scenario is suggestive of Broca's aphasia.

In Broca's aphasia/ Motor aphasia / Non-fluent aphasia, areas 44 and 45 in the prefrontal and premotor facial regions of the cerebral cortex are affected. The affected individuals will have difficulty forming verbal or written words. The comprehension aspect of speech is preserved but the person cannot repeat or name the words and lacks fluency.

Other options:

Option A: Wernicke's aphasia is a type of fluent aphasia in which comprehension is impaired. The speech is easy and fluent but it is full of jargon and neologisms(non-existent words) that make little sense. Damage to the posterior part of the superior temporal gyrus(area 22) or blockade of the inferior division of the middle cerebral artery causes Wernicke's aphasia.

Option C: Global aphasia- In this, both understanding and speaking are impaired. It is also non-fluent aphasia.

Option D: Conduction aphasia is seen in lesions of the arcuate fasciculus, the bundle of nerve fibres connecting the Wernicke and Broca's areas. Repetition of words is impaired and paraphasias are observed, though not as much as in Wernicke aphasia.

Broca's and Wernicke's areas can be seen in the image below:

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 17-year-old tall male presents to OPD for a routine checkup. He has long limbs, arachnodactyly, and hypermobile joints. 2D echocardiography revealed mitral valve stenosis, and an eye check-up revealed subluxation of the lens. Workup showed the defects are due to an abnormal FBN1 gene mutation. Which of the following is the most likely cause?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Marfan Syndrome

The above clinical scenario of a 17-year-old tall male with long limbs, arachnodactyly, hypermobile joints, and 2D echocardiography revealed mitral valve stenosis and subluxation of the lens with an abnormal Fibrillin 1 gene mutation/ FBN1 gene mutation is highly suggestive of Marfan's syndrome.

It is a clinical diagnosis based on skeletal, cardiovascular, and ocular manifestations. Ghent criteria are used for diagnosing Marfan syndrome.  The main features are tall stature, ectopia lentis, and aortic root dilatation.

Skeletal manifestations:

* Tall stature and long limbs

* Pectus carinatum or pectus excavatum

* Long and slender fingers (arachnodactyly), contracture of fingers (camptodactyly)

* Scoliosis

Cardiovascular manifestations:

* Thickened atrioventricular valves, valvular prolapse (mitral regurgitation)

* Aortic valve dysfunction due to an aortic root aneurysm

* Aortic dissection and rupture due to cystic medial necrosis of the aorta

Ocular manifestations:

* Ectopia lentis with upward and outward displacement of the lenses due to weakening of the ciliary zonules

* Myopia with blurred vision

* Retinal detachments

* Early cataracts and glaucoma

The images below show two important signs seen in Marfan's syndrome:

* Image A shows a positive wrist sign - the ability to join the thumb and fifth finger around the wrist

* Image B shows a positive thumb sign - the thumb tip extends from the palm in a closed fist.

Other options:

Option A: Homocystinuria caused by a deficiency of the cystathionine β-synthase. The deficiency of this enzyme leads to an accumulation of homocysteine in the blood and a clinical syndrome of intellectual disability, subluxated ocular lenses, long and slender extremities, arachnodactyly, and arterial and venous thrombi with megaloblastic anemia.

The image below shows lens subluxation (infero-nasal quad).

Option B: High Myopia usually presents with diplopia, ectopic lens, secondary cataract, or glaucoma with retinal detachment.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Deficiency of which vitamin is most commonly linked to cognitive decline in elderly individuals?
questions.explanation: In geriatric medicine, Vitamin B12 (cobalamin) deficiency is a frequent and reversible cause of cognitive impairment and dementia-like symptoms. The elderly are particularly susceptible due to a high prevalence of atrophic gastritis, which reduces the production of intrinsic factor and gastric acid needed for B12 absorption. Clinically, it presents as "megaloblastic madness," involving memory loss, irritability, and depression, often preceding the classic hematological finding of megaloblastic anemia. Vitamin C deficiency (Option A) causes scurvy but not primary dementia. Vitamin B6 (Option C) is involved in neurotransmitter synthesis, but its isolated deficiency is rare. Vitamin B1 (thiamine) deficiency (Option D) causes Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome, which involves severe amnesia and confabulation, typically in the context of chronic alcoholism rather than general aging. Screening for B12 levels is a standard step in the workup for any elderly patient presenting with new-onset cognitive decline, as timely supplementation can halt or reverse neurological deterioration

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A patient who underwent surgery for a lipoma 5 weeks back, now presents with a scar at the incision site that is limited to the original wound boundaries. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Hypertrophic scar

The given clinical vignette is of a hypertrophic scar as it stays within the confines of the original wound. Hypertrophic scars rise above the skin level but stay within the confines of the original wound and often regress over time.

Accumulation of excessive amounts of collagen during repair may give rise to hypertrophic scar or keloid. The accumulation of excessive amounts of collagen→ raised scars known as a hypertrophic scars. If the scar tissue grows beyond the boundaries of the original wound and does not regress → keloid formation. Formation of excessive amounts of granulation tissue, which protrudes above the level of the surrounding skin and blocks re-epithelialization → Exuberant granulation

Inadequate formation of granulation tissue or formation of a scar → wound dehiscence and ulceration. The contraction in the size of a wound is an important part of the normal healing process. An exaggeration of this process gives rise to contractures, which are particularly prone to develop on the palms, the soles, and the anterior aspect of the thorax and are commonly seen after serious burns.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A pregnant woman with deafness is evaluated and found to have a 50 dB hearing loss. What is the most likely cause of her hearing impairment?
options: Ossicular fixation with an intact tympanic membrane
Ossicular fixation with a damaged tympanic membrane
questions.explanation: The presentation of progressive hearing loss in a pregnant woman is a high-yield clinical trigger for Otosclerosis. This condition involves abnormal bone remodeling in the labyrinth, frequently causing stapes footplate fixation. Pregnancy is known to accelerate the progression of otosclerosis due to hormonal influences. The resulting conductive hearing loss is typically around 50-60 dB, while the tympanic membrane remains normal and intact. Options B and C are incorrect as otosclerosis is not an inflammatory disease that damages the drum. Option D (erosion with an intact drum) can occur in cholesteatoma, but the specific association with pregnancy makes stapes fixation much more probable. On clinical examination, a pinkish "Schwartz sign" might be seen through the intact drum. Management during pregnancy is typically conservative, such as hearing aids, while definitive surgery (stapedotomy) is postponed until after delivery
questions.learning: The presentation of progressive hearing loss in a pregnant woman is a high-yield clinical trigger for Otosclerosis. This condition involves abnormal bone remodeling in the labyrinth, frequently causing stapes footplate fixation.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 24-year-old woman who is being treated for infertility with human menopausal gonadotropin came with complaints of sudden abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, and breathlessness. The finding of the ultrasound is shown below. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome

The above clinical scenario and the sonogram showing enlarged ovaries having large cysts are suggestive of ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome.

Ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome (OHSS) is characterized by multiple ovarian follicular cysts accompanied by increased capillary permeability. It happens most often as a complication of ovulation induction therapy for infertility. It occurs due to the stimulation of vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) expression in granulosa-lutein cells by hCG.

They often present with shortness of breath, abdominal pain, and gastrointestinal disturbances like nausea, vomiting, and oliguria.

Abdominal pain occurs due to ovarian enlargement and accumulation of peritoneal fluid. Increased vascular permeability and loss of fluid, protein, and electrolytes into the peritoneal cavity cause ascites and result in hemoconcentration. Hemoconcentration causes hyperviscosity and leads to hypercoagulability.

Hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, leukocytosis, pleural effusion, and pericardial effusion can be associated with OHSS.

Some of the risk factors for OHSS:

• Polycystic ovarian syndrome
• Young age
• High estradiol during ovulation induction
• Pregnancy

This condition can be prevented by

• Using lowered FSH dose to decrease follicular stimulation
• Coasting- withholding FSH administration for 1 or more days prior to the hCG trigger injection,
• Prophylactic treatment with volume expanders,
• Substitution of hCG for FSH during the final days of ovarian stimulation.

OHSS is primarily managed with general supportive care. Paracentesis is performed to ameliorate abdominal discomfort and relieve respiratory discomfort.

Other options:

Option B- Polycystic ovarian syndrome (PCOS) is the most common endocrine disorder of the reproductive age group. Patients with PCOS present with menstrual irregularities, hirsutism, acne, infertility, sleep apnea, and depression/anxiety. These are all short-term consequences of PCOS. The long-term consequences of PCOS include diabetes mellitus, endometrial cancer, and cardiovascular disease.

According to the American Society of Reproductive Medicine (ASRM) and the European Society of Human Reproduction and Embryology (ESHRE), sonographic criteria for PCOS include

• >20 follicles and/or
• Increased ovarian volume (>10 mL), or both

The ultrasound examination image shown below is of PCOS showing enlarged ovaries with multiple cysts.

Option C - Theca lutein cysts are a type of follicular cysts. Hyperreactio luteinalis is a condition in which one or both ovaries develop multiple large theca lutein cysts. They typically occur after the first trimester due to luteinization and hypertrophy of theca interna layer in response to exceptionally high hCG or luteinizing hormone.

They are commonly seen in

• Gestational trophoblastic disease
• Multiple gestational pregnancy
• Fetal hydrops
• Placentaomegaly

Most patients are asymptomatic and the above symptoms are not seen in this condition. Surgical management is only required if it is complicated by torsion or hemorrhage.

The below image shows bilaterally enlarged ovaries with multiple theca luteal cysts as in hyperreactio luteinalis.

Option D - Most women are diagnosed with adult granulosa cell tumors after the age of 30 years, and the average age is roughly 55 years. Heavy, irregular menstrual bleeding and postmenopausal bleeding are frequent and are caused by the endometrium's extended exposure to estrogen. Breast soreness and enlargement are also seen in this condition. Instead of hormones, the mass of the ovary may be the cause of the symptoms. Abdominal pain and distension that is brought on by an expanding tumor that could potentially be hemorrhagic.
questions.learning: Ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome — The above clinical scenario and the sonogram showing enlarged ovaries having large cysts are suggestive of ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: The most appropriate description of vasomotor reversal of Dale is
options: Repeated administration of ephedrine decreases its effect on blood pressure
A patient pretreated with phentolamine develops severe hypotension on administration of adrenaline.
High dose of acetylcholine after pretreatment with atropine produces increase in blood pressure and heart rate
Increase in pulse pressure is produced by intravenous administration of isoprenaline
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. A patient pretreated with phentolamine develops severe hypotension on administration of adrenaline.

A patient pretreated with phentolamine develops severe hypotension on the administration of adrenaline is the most appropriate description of the vasomotor reversal of Dale. (Option B)

Vasomotor reversal of Dale is a blockade of alpha (α1) followed by stimulation of beta (β2) receptors.

Normally, a high dose of epinephrine injected produces α1 mediated rise in BP followed by β2 mediated fall in BP.

Vasomotor reversal of Dale: Administration of adrenaline after administration of α blockers(phentolamine) produces only a fall in BP. This is because the α mediated response is abolished and hence, only the β-mediated response is seen, i.e., a fall in BP.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A study finds that exercise reduces the incidence of cardiovascular disease. However, it was found that people who exercise also tend to consume a healthy diet. What does a healthy diet act in this context?
options: There is no association, it can be ignored
Diet is a mediator for reducing cardiovascular disease
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Confounding factor

A confounder is a variable that:

1. Is associated with the exposure (exercise)
2. Is independently associated with the outcome (CVD)
3. Is not on the causal pathway between exposure and outcome

✔ A healthy diet is associated with exercise

✔ A healthy diet independently reduces CVD risk

✔ Diet is not caused by exercise in the causal pathway being tested

This fulfils all criteria for a confounding factor.

An effect modifier:

• Alters the strength or direction of the association between exposure and outcome
• Is identified by stratified analysis, showing different effect sizes in different strata

In the question: There is no mention of stratified effects; Only co-existence of diet with exercise is described. So, effect modification is not demonstrated.

Example:

Exercise may reduce CVD more strongly in young people than elderly.

Healthy diet in this question does not modify the effect, it distorts it.

In Conclusion,

Confounding = Mixing of effects

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: A patient is brought in to the casualty with maxillofacial trauma after an RTA. He is unconscious with a dropping SpO2. The ER doctor decides to intubate him. What is the preferred method of intubation for this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Tracheostomy

Patients with severe maxillofacial trauma are very likely to experience severe airway compromise or obstruction. Hence to maintain airway competency, intubation is necessary and in the above case, the presence of facial trauma, tracheostomy is ideal.

Tracheostomy involves making an opening and placing a stoma in the anterior wall of the trachea.

Functions:

* Provides an alternative pathway for breathing by bypassing the obstruction.

* Improves alveolar ventilation by reducing dead space by 30-50% and reducing airway resistance

* Uses a cuff to protect the airways from secretions and blood

* Allows suction of secretions in the setting of the impaired cough reflex.

* Allows positive pressure respiration

* Allows administration of anesthesia

Indications:

* Respiratory obstruction due to

* Infections (laryngo-tracheo-bronchitis, epiglottitis, diphtheria)

* Trauma due to external injury, mandibular or maxillofacial fractures

* Neoplasms

* Foreign bodies or edema

* Bilateral abductor paralysis

* Congenital anomalies

* Retained secretions

* Inability to cough due to coma, spasm, or paralysis of respiratory muscles

* Aspiration of pharyngeal secretions

* Painful cough

* Respiratory insufficiency due to emphysema, chronic bronchitis

Other options:

Option A and B: Mask ventilation and LMA are not enough as the patient has severe airway compromise.

Option D:  In cases of facial trauma, nasotracheal intubation is avoided due to the risk of the tube entering the brain through an undiagnosed basal skull fracture.

questions.text: If a simple muscle twitch has a latent period of 10 milliseconds, a contraction period of 40 milliseconds, and a relaxation period of 50 milliseconds, what is the tetanizing frequency?

Correct answer: C. 25HZ

Tetanizing frequency = frequency at which next stimulus arrives before relaxation completes → sustained contraction (tetanus).

• Latent period = 10 ms
• Contraction period = 40 ms
• Relaxation period = 50 ms
• 1 / contraction period = 1 / 40 ms = 1 / 0.040 s = 25 Hz ✔

| Contraction | 40 ms | Cross-bridge cycling

| Relaxation | 50 ms | Ca²⁺ reuptake

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following features are characteristic of the Bezold–Jarisch reflex? 1. Hypotension 2. Bradycardia 3. Hypopnea 4. Tachycardia Which among the options are correct?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 1, 2, 3

The Bezold–Jarisch reflex is triggered by ventricular mechanoreceptor stimulation, often during inferior wall ischemia. Classic triad-

• Bradycardia

• Hypotension

• Hypopnea (reduced respiration)

It causes increased vagal tone leading to bradycardia and hypotension.

There is also hypopnea due to reflex inhibition of respiration.

The Bezold–Jarisch reflex increases vagal tone, which causes: Bradycardia

Tachycardia is not a feature of this reflex.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 30-year-old married woman presents for infertility evaluation. Investigations reveal intramural fibroids measuring 7 × 5 cm and 5 × 3 cm at the right and left cornual ends of the uterus. Her husband’s semen analysis is normal. What is the most appropriate management?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Laparoscopic Myomectomy

Intramural fibroids, especially those large or located near the cornual region --> can impair fertility by distorting uterine architecture, affecting tubal patency, and interfering with implantation.

• In women with infertility and significant intramural fibroids (>4–5 cm), the preferred treatment is myomectomy to restore normal uterine anatomy and improve fertility.

Why not other options:

A) Uterine artery embolization: Used for symptomatic fibroids, but not preferred in women desiring fertility (may impair uterine blood supply).

C) Assisted reproductive techniques: Structural uterine pathology should be corrected first before ART.

D) GnRH analogues: Cause temporary fibroid shrinkage only; fibroids recur after stopping and do not improve fertility long-term.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: During a routine examination, a young asymptomatic male is found to have a wide, fixed split of the second heart sound (S2) on auscultation. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: A wide, fixed split of the second heart sound (S2) is the pathognomonic physical finding for an Atrial Septal Defect (ASD) (Option A). Normally, S2 splits slightly during inspiration. In ASD, the continuous left-to-right shunt increases right ventricular volume throughout the entire respiratory cycle, causing the pulmonic valve to close consistently later than the aortic valve, regardless of breathing. VSD (Option B) typically presents with a pansystolic murmur. Tetralogy of Fallot (Option C) presents with cyanosis and a single S2. Bicuspid Aortic Valve (Option D) is characterized by an early systolic click. Because the finding of a "fixed split" is so uniquely specific to the physiology of an interatrial shunt, ASD is the definitive clinical diagnosis. Most young patients are asymptomatic initially, which is why this auscultatory finding is often discovered during routine screening. Management may involve percutaneous or surgical closure
questions.learning: A wide, fixed split of the second heart sound (S2) is the pathognomonic physical finding for an Atrial Septal Defect (ASD) (Option A). Normally, S2 splits slightly during inspiration.

questions.text: A hypertensive patient who is non-compliant with medication presents to you with sudden onset breathlessness. A chest X-ray was done, which is shown below. How will you manage this patient?

Correct answer: B. Intravenous nitroglycerin

Sudden breathlessness in a non-compliant hypertensive with chest X-ray showing pulmonary edema (bat-wing appearance) indicates acute cardiogenic pulmonary edema.

↓

↓

↓

↓

Fluid leaks into alveoli

↓

↓

Intravenous nitroglycerin rapidly reduces preload and afterload, lowering pulmonary capillary pressure.

Bronchodilators and antibiotics do not address the primary hemodynamic cause.

| A. IV salbutamol | β₂ bronchodilator | Asthma/COPD | ❌ Not bronchospasm | No role in edema

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: 30,000 women were followed up for 10 years for the development of breast cancer. 1200 women developed cancer and were given a questionnaire to assess possible risk factors. Additionally, 2000 women from the same study were used as controls and were also given the questionnaire. What is this type of study called?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Nested case control

The type of study described in the question is a nested case-control study.

A nested case-control study is essentially a case-control study that is present inside a cohort study. The cases are all the cohort members who developed the disease being studied at a given point in time during the follow-up period. However, each case is matched to one or more controls — individuals who did not develop the disease but are otherwise comparable to cases in terms of age and gender. Cases and controls are then compared in terms of their respective exposures to the risk factor. Nested case-control studies thus represent an interim analysis of the exposure and outcome data of a cohort study.

A case-cohort study (option A) involves selecting a subset of the entire cohort at the beginning of the study. This sub-cohort acts as the control group for making comparisons with multiple case groups. For example, if a cohort study is being done to assess smoking as a risk factor for ischemic heart disease and lung cancer, the same sub-cohort can be used as the control group for both outcomes. If it was a nested case-control study, it would require two separate control groups. Case-cohort studies are more efficient than nested case-control studies when multiple outcomes are being studied.

In a retrospective cohort study (option B), the outcomes have already occurred before the study begins. The investigator has to analyze the history of prior exposures and the duration of such exposures. Even though the exposure and the outcome have already occurred, the investigator goes from the exposure → outcome in a retrospective cohort study. This is in contrast to case-control studies, where the investigator goes from outcome → exposure.

Cross control cohort (option D) is not a type of study design.
questions.learning: Nested case control — The type of study described in the question is a nested case-control study. A nested case-control study is essentially a case-control study that is present inside a cohort study.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 7-year-old boy is brought to the pediatric clinic with multiple soft, pedunculated masses scattered over his torso and limbs. His parents report recent learning and reading difficulties. Examination reveals hyperpigmented macules with irregular borders on his back, and ocular findings as shown. What is the most likely diagnosis in this child?
questions.explanation: The child presents with classic features of Neurofibromatosis Type 1 (NF1), an autosomal dominant neurocutaneous syndrome. The "pedunculated masses" are neurofibromas, and the "hyperpigmented macules with irregular borders" are café-au-lait spots. Learning disabilities are also common in NF1 patients. The ocular image shows Lisch nodules, which are pigmented hamartomas of the iris pathognomonic for NF1. NF2 (Option A) is characterized by bilateral vestibular schwannomas and typically lacks Lisch nodules and extensive café-au-lait spots. Tuberous Sclerosis Complex (TSC1 and TSC2, Options B and C) presents with ash-leaf spots, shagreen patches, and facial angiofibromas, but not neurofibromas or Lisch nodules. The diagnosis of NF1 is clinical, requiring at least two of the seven NIH diagnostic criteria. Given the cutaneous and ocular findings, NF1 is the definitive diagnosis
questions.learning: The child presents with classic features of Neurofibromatosis Type 1 (NF1), an autosomal dominant neurocutaneous syndrome. The "pedunculated masses" are neurofibromas, and the "hyperpigmented macules with irregular borders" are café-au-lait spots.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: The X-ray of a 65-year-old man is given below. Clinical examination, and hematological and urinary tests were normal. Which of the following is the probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Langerhans cell histiocytosis

The given image showing a solitary punched-out lytic lesion without a sclerotic rim with a beveled edge appearance, along with the age of the patient with history of normal hematological and urinary tests is suggestive of Langerhans cell histiocytosis.

Langerhans cell histiocytosis occurs due to the proliferation of a special type of immature dendritic cells, called Langerhans cells. Their normal function is to present antigens.

It is characterized by single or multiple osteolytic bone lesions. It can also infiltrate the skin (of the scalp), lungs, liver, spleen, bone marrow, or the central nervous system.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 65-year-old woman underwent elective surgery five days ago and received intravenous clindamycin postoperatively. She now presents with profuse watery diarrhea. Which organism is the most likely cause?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Clostridioides difficile

Clostridioides difficile is the most common cause of antibiotic-associated diarrhea and pseudomembranous colitis. Broad-spectrum antibiotics, particularly clindamycin, cephalosporins, fluoroquinolones, and amoxicillin/ampicillin, disrupt the normal colonic flora, allowing C. difficile to proliferate and produce toxins A and B, leading to colonic inflammation and diarrhea.

Why not the other options?

• B. Enterotoxigenic Escherichia coli (ETEC): Causes traveler’s diarrhea after contaminated food or water, not antibiotic-associated diarrhea.
• C. Salmonella enteritidis: Causes inflammatory diarrhea associated with contaminated poultry or eggs, often with fever.
• D. Staphylococcus aureus: Causes rapid-onset food poisoning (1–6 hours) due to ingestion of preformed enterotoxin, presenting with vomiting rather than post-antibiotic diarrhea.
