questions.subject: ENT
questions.text:
A patient presents with vertigo associated with horizontal nystagmus. The slow component is towards the left. What is the most likely diagnosis?

BPPV- Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Left hypoactive labyrinth

The most likely diagnosis for a patient presenting with horizontal nystagmus and fast component towards the right (slow component towards the left) is left hypoactive labyrinth.

Nystagmus is an involuntary oscillatory movement of the eyes, which can occur in horizontal, vertical, or torsional directions. The direction of nystagmus is determined by the fast component.

In horizontal nystagmus, the direction of nystagmus (fast phase) is always away from the hypoactive lesions and towards the active or hyperactive lesions of the labyrinth. Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (BPPV) is a hyperactive disease while vestibular neuronitis and vestibular Schwanomma are hypoactive diseases.

The involvement of the vertical semicircular canals (superior and posterior) leads to vertical or mixed vertical-torsional nystagmus, ruling out posterior canal BPPV (Option A) and superior canal BPPV (Option B).

Alternatively, if the right hypoactive labyrinth was one of the options, it could be considered as a differential for horizontal nystagmus with the slow component towards the right.

BPPV is a condition characterized by recurrent episodes of transient vertigo (<1 min) triggered by changes in head position relative to gravity. It is caused by dislodged calcium carbonate crystals (otoconia) from the utricular macula into one of the semicircular canals, usually the posterior semicircular canal. A diagnosis of BPPV can be made by Dix-Hallpike test and the condition is treated by repositioning maneuvers for the otoconia such as the Epley maneuver.
questions.learning: Left hypoactive labyrinth — The most likely diagnosis for a patient presenting with horizontal nystagmus and fast component towards the right (slow component towards the left) is left hypoactive labyrinth.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: For a female patient planned for laparoscopic surgery, what is the most appropriate pre- operative instruction that should be given?
options: Drink plenty of water before surgery
Enema on the night before surgery
NPO for specific hours before surgery
questions.explanation: The most critical pre-operative instruction for a patient undergoing general anesthesia for laparoscopic surgery is to remain NPO (nil per os), meaning nothing by mouth, for a specific period (Option D). Standard guidelines usually mandate fasting from solids for at least 6–8 hours and clear liquids for 2 hours before the procedure. This is essential to minimize the volume of gastric contents, thereby reducing the risk of pulmonary aspiration during induction and the procedure itself. Instructions to eat fully (Option A) or drink plenty of water (Option B) just before surgery are dangerous and would lead to cancellation of the case. While bowel preparation or an enema (Option C) was historically routine, it is no longer standard for all laparoscopic surgeries unless specifically indicated for bowel-involved procedures. Therefore, adhering to strict fasting protocols is the primary safety requirement for pre-anesthetic preparation
questions.learning: The most critical pre-operative instruction for a patient undergoing general anesthesia for laparoscopic surgery is to remain NPO (nil per os), meaning nothing by mouth, for a specific period (Option D).

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: On January 1, 2024, a community with a population of 10,000 had 100 existing cases of tuberculosis (TB). During the year, 30 patients were cured and 10 patients died. Additionally, 20 new TB cases were reported, of which 5 were cured before December 31, 2024. What is the incidence of TB at the end of the year and the prevalence of TB for the year?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 2/1000,12/1000

Incidence is the number of new cases occurring in a defined population during a period of time. Here, 20 new TB cases occurred in 2024 in a population of 10,000, so:

* Incidence = (Number of cases of a disease in a specified period of time/Population at risk during that time) x 1000

* incidence = (20/10,000) × 1000 = 2/1000

Prevalence is the proportion of all cases, old and new, present during a specified period. At the end of 2024, the community had 100 old cases plus 20 new cases, giving a total of 120 cases. So:

* Prevalence = (Number of all cases of a specified disease at a given point in time/Estimated population at the same point in time)

* prevalence = (120/10,000) × 1000 = 12 per 1000

Pearl PF0953: Incidence and Prevalence

Incidence in Epidemiology:

* Incidence is the number of new cases occurring in a defined population during a period of time.

* Incidence = (Number of cases of a disease in a specified period of time/Population at risk during that time) x 1000

* Incidence rate is expressed in person-time units, usually per 1000 per year.

* It provides insight into the effectives of health services and programs.

* Incidence rate of spells of sickness =  (Number of spells of sickness starting in the specified period/Mean number of people exposed to that risk in the specified time) x 1000

* It is generally used for acute illnesses.

* Special types of incidence rates:

* Attack rate: It is used when there is a risk for a limited period of time.

* Secondary attack rate: It is the number of exposed persons developing the disease within the range of incubation period following exposure to a primary case.

* Incidence can be determined from cohort studies and longitudinal studies.

Prevalence in Epidemiology:

* Prevalence is the proportion of all cases, old and new, of a particular disease at a given point in time or over a period of time in a given population.

* It is a proportion, not a rate or ratio.

* It can be determined from cross-sectional studies.

* Types:

* Point prevalence is the prevalence at a point in time. Usually, prevalence is point prevalence unless otherwise specified.

* Period prevalence is the prevalence over a period of time.

* Prevalence is always expressed in percentage.

* Prevalence = (Number of all cases of a specified disease at a given point in time/Estimated population at the same point in time) x 100

* It is useful to determine the magnitude of health problems.

Relationship between Incidence and Prevalence:

* Prevalence depends upon incidence and duration.

* Prevalence = Incidence x Mean Duration

* Longer the duration of the disease, greater the prevalence.

* In acute diseases,because of rapid recovery/death prevalence will be relatively lower than incidence.This is because in some diseases (eg. food poisoning), the disease is so short lived, there are no "old cases".

* In chronic diseases like TB, prevalence will be higher than incidence.

* If a new treatment for a disease is effective, incidence does not change but prevalence decreases as duration of disease decreases.

* If treatment only prevents death but doesn’t cure the disease, it may cause a paradoxical increase in prevalence.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 16-year-old girl with primary amenorrhoea presents to the gynaecology OPD for evaluation. She has normal secondary sexual characters. Her karyotype is 46,XX and ultrasonography reveals normal ovaries and tubes but absent uterus. What is her clinical diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Mayer-Rokitansky-Küster-Hauser syndrome

• The patient has the classical features:

• Primary amenorrhea
• Normal breast development and secondary sexual characteristics
• 46,XX karyotype
• Normal ovaries and fallopian tubes
• Absent uterus on ultrasonography
• agenesis or hypoplasia of the uterus and upper two-thirds of the vagina

Why are the other options incorrect?

• A.  Androgen insensitivity syndrome (AIS):

• Karyotype: 46,XY
• Testes present, absent uterus, sparse/absent pubic and axillary hair.

• B. Turner syndrome:

• Karyotype: 45,X
• Streak ovaries, absent secondary sexual characteristics, uterus present but infantile.

• D. Primary ovarian failure: Characterized by elevated FSH, absent ovarian function, and poor secondary sexual development if occurring before puberty. The uterus is present.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Which of the following is a cause of bilateral sudden painless loss of vision?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Diabetic retinopathy

Diabetic retinopathy is a cause of bilateral sudden painless loss of vision due to vascular complications.

Bilateral sudden painless loss of vision is a hallmark of advanced diabetic retinopathy, particularly when associated with complications such as:

• Vitreous haemorrhage: Leakage of blood into the vitreous cavity due to rupture of fragile neovascular vessels.

• Tractional retinal detachment: Occurs when fibrovascular tissue pulls the retina away from its underlying structures.

• Macular oedema: Severe swelling in the macula can lead to central vision loss.

These conditions can cause sudden and significant visual impairment, often affecting both eyes in patients with long-standing, poorly controlled diabetes.

Other options

Option A: Acute congestive glaucoma: Typically causes sudden vision loss, but it is painful and unilateral in most cases.

Option C: Keratoconus is a progressive condition that leads to gradual vision loss due to corneal thinning and irregular astigmatism, not sudden or bilateral loss.

Option D: Iridocyclitis is associated with pain, redness, and photophobia, and it is usually unilateral.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A 30-year-old man presented with choking episodes after ingestion of a fish bone. The fishbone was impacted at the T4 level in the oesophagus. Which is the most likely site of obstruction?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Arch of aorta

The most likely site of obstruction in the case of a fishbone impacted at the T4 level is the arch of the aorta.

Normally, the oesophagus shows 3 constrictions at the following levels measured from upper incisors:

* At the pharyngo-oesophageal junction (C6)—15 cm from the upper incisors.

* At the crossing of the arch of the aorta (T4)—25 cm from the upper incisors.

* Where it pierces the diaphragm (T10)—40 cm from the upper incisors.

Foreign bodies in the oesophagus can be held up at these constrictions.

Acute dysphagia is common with foreign body obstruction. They might also experience odynophagia, regurgitation of food, neck pain, or chest pain. Esophageal obstruction can cause complications such as esophageal perforation and lung aspiration.

When impaction of a foreign body occurs in an adult esophagus, it usually occurs in the presence of underlying structural abnormalities (such as a web or stricture), functional abnormalities resulting from abnormal esophageal peristalsis, or when the swallowed object is too large to navigate the anatomic constrictions of the normal esophagus. The two most common causes are eosinophilic oesophagitis and Schatzki rings. Esophageal webs, tracheo-oesophageal fistula/esophageal atresia (TOF/OA), and peptic strictures are conditions that predispose to food bolus obstructions.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Graft from identical twin is called:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Isograft

A graft from an identical twin is called isograft.

Isograft is defined as an organ or tissue that is taken from an individual (donor) and is placed on another individual (recipient) who has the same genetic constitution as of the donor. Example, graft between identical twins.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A particular community population has been consuming Maize as a staple diet for years. The vitamin deficiency most likely to be seen in this population is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Niacin

A maize-based staple diet is classically associated with niacin (vitamin B3) deficiency, leading to pellagra.

Maize is deficient in tryptophan and contains niacin in a bound, poorly absorbable form, especially when not processed by alkali treatment.

This results in the characteristic triad of dermatitis, diarrhea, and dementia, making niacin deficiency the most likely outcome.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: During the puerperium, what is the accurate order of vaginal discharge?
options: Lochia serosa > Lochia rubra > Lochia alba
Lochia rubra > Lochia alba > Lochia serosa
Lochia alba > Lochia rubra > Lochia serosa
Lochia rubra > Lochia serosa > Lochia alba
questions.explanation: Lochia is the vaginal discharge occurring after childbirth, consisting of blood, mucus, and placental tissue. It progresses through three distinct stages based on its color and composition. Lochia Rubra is the first stage (Days 1–4), appearing bright red due to high blood and decidual content. Lochia Serosa follows (Days 5–9), appearing pinkish or brownish as the discharge becomes thinner and contains more serous fluid, leukocytes, and cervical mucus. The final stage is Lochia Alba (Day 10 to about 4–6 weeks), which is yellowish-white or pale and consists primarily of leukocytes, epithelial cells, and fat. Options A, B, and C provide incorrect sequences that do not follow this physiological progression. Understanding the normal order and duration of lochia is essential for healthcare providers to distinguish healthy postpartum recovery from complications like secondary postpartum hemorrhage or endometritis (infection)
questions.learning: Lochia is the vaginal discharge occurring after childbirth, consisting of blood, mucus, and placental tissue. It progresses through three distinct stages based on its color and composition.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: True statement regarding Ayushman Bharat scheme?
options: Rs 5 lakh/per family per year is given
Rs 10 lakh/per family per year is given
Rs 6 lakh/per family per year is given
Rs 2 lakh/per family per year is given
questions.explanation: The Ayushman Bharat Pradhan Mantri Jan Arogya Yojana (AB-PMJAY) is the world's largest government-funded healthcare program. Its primary feature is providing a health cover of Rs 5 lakh per family per year for secondary and tertiary care hospitalization. This benefit is available to over 12 crore poor and vulnerable families based on Socio-Economic Caste Census (SECC) data. Options B (10 lakh), C (6 lakh), and D (2 lakh) are incorrect amounts for the standard annual coverage. The scheme is "portable," meaning a beneficiary can receive treatment in any empaneled public or private hospital across India. It covers pre-hospitalization, medicines, and post-hospitalization expenses. The program aims to reduce catastrophic out-of-pocket expenditure that often pushes families into poverty. By providing cashless and paperless access to services, Ayushman Bharat is a critical step toward achieving Universal Health Coverage in India, specifically targeting the bottom 40% of the population
questions.learning: The Ayushman Bharat Pradhan Mantri Jan Arogya Yojana (AB-PMJAY) is the world's largest government-funded healthcare program. Its primary feature is providing a health cover of Rs 5 lakh per family per year for secondary and tertiary care hospitalization.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Where is the Bartholin gland located?
questions.explanation: The Bartholin glands (greater vestibular glands) are a pair of pea-sized glands located in the posterior third of the labia majora, deep within the perineum. Their primary function is to secrete mucus into the vaginal vestibule to provide lubrication during sexual arousal. The ducts of these glands open at the 4 o'clock and 8 o'clock positions relative to the vaginal introitus. Options A, C, and D are anatomically incorrect locations for these specific glands. Clinically, these glands are important because they can become obstructed, leading to the formation of a Bartholin cyst or, if infected, a painful Bartholin abscess. An abscess usually requires surgical management, such as incision and drainage or marsupialization, to prevent recurrence. Precise knowledge of pelvic anatomy is essential for both the diagnosis of vulvar masses and the performance of minor gynecological surgical procedures in this area
questions.learning: The Bartholin glands (greater vestibular glands) are a pair of pea-sized glands located in the posterior third of the labia majora, deep within the perineum.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following was launched to ensure complete immunization of children?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Mission Indradhanush

Mission Indradhanush was launched by the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare in 2014 to fully immunize children (>90%) who are either partially immunized or completely unimmunized by 2020. It was later modified in 2017 to the Intensified Mission Indradhanush, to achieve the same goal by December 2018.

Intensified Mission Indradhanush includes 12 vaccine-preventable diseases (updated from the 7 diseases that Mission Indradhanush focussed on). 4 rounds of immunization are proposed to be held for 7 days each month (from the 7th- 13th of each month).

The diseases included in Mission Indradhanush are:

• TB
• Polio
• Hep B
• Diphtheria
• Pertussis
• Tetanus
• Measles

The diseases included recently in Intensified Mission Indradhanush are:

• Rotavirus diarrhoea
• Rubella (as MR vaccine)
• H. influenzae B diseases (as part of the pentavalent vaccine)
• Pneumococcal meningitis
• Japanese Encephalitis

The Intensified Mission Indradhanush 2.0:

The government of India introduced IMI 2.0 to accelerate the vaccine drive and extend the coverage to children and pregnant women in identified districts and blocks from December 2019- March 2020.

Note: Currently, the government has completed Intensified Mission Indradhanush 5.0:
Intensified Mission Indradhanush (IMI 5.0), the flagship routine immunization campaign of the Union Ministry of Health and Family Welfare concluded all 3 rounds in October 2023. This is the first campaign to be conducted across all the districts in the country and includes children up to 5 years of age (Previous campaigns included children up to 2 years of age). It also had a special focus on improvement of Measles and Rubella vaccination coverage.
questions.learning: Mission Indradhanush Mission Indradhanush was launched by the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare in 2014 to fully immunize children (>90%) who are either partially immunized or completely unimmunized by 2020.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Renal Electrolytes · Acid Base Electrolyte Disturbances
questions.text: Which of the following is seen during rapid ascent to high altitude?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Respiratory alkalosis

High altitude → ↓ O₂ (Hypoxia)

↓

Peripheral chemoreceptor stimulation

↓

Hyperventilation

↓

↓ CO₂ (Hypocapnia)

↓

↑ pH

↓

Respiratory Alkalosis

Rapid ascent to high altitude causes hypoxemia, which stimulates peripheral chemoreceptors.

This leads to hyperventilation, causing excessive CO₂ washout and resulting in respiratory alkalosis.

Renal compensation with bicarbonate loss occurs later.

| Phase | Change

| ----- | ------

| Immediate (hours) | Respiratory alkalosis

| After 2–3 days | Renal compensation → ↓ HCO₃⁻

| Long-term | ↑ RBC, ↑ 2,3-BPG
questions.learning: Respiratory alkalosis High altitude → ↓ O₂ (Hypoxia) ↓ Peripheral chemoreceptor stimulation ↓ Hyperventilation ↓ ↓ CO₂ (Hypocapnia) ↓ ↑ pH ↓ Respiratory Alkalosis Rapid ascent to high altitude causes hypoxemia, which stimulates peripheral chemoreceptors.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Which of the following is not recommended in an 8 yr old child with bilateral sensorineural hearing loss?
options: Sitting in front row of the class
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Adenoidectomy and grommet insertion

Adenoidectomy and grommet insertion is not recommended in bilateral sensorineural hearing loss (SNHL).

Adenoidectomy and grommet insertion is done in the management of serous otitis media.

Serous otitis media is also known as secretory otitis media or mucoid otitis media or glue ear. It is characterized by the accumulation of nonpurulent effusion in the middle ear cleft.

Treatment is mainly aimed at the removal of fluid and preventing recurrence.

• Medical management includes decongestants, antihistamines, antibiotics, and middle ear aeration techniques.
• Surgical management includes myringotomy and aspiration of fluid, grommet insertion, tympanotomy, or cortical mastoidectomy. Adenoidectomy and tonsillectomy may be required and are usually done at the time of myringotomy.

Option B: Cochlear implant is an electronic device which helps in hearing for those with profound sensorineural hearing loss, who cannot benefit from hearing aids. It has two components :

• External component : speech processor and transmitter
• Internal component : receiver / stimulator and electrode array

Sound signals received by the processor is then conducted to the stimulator via the transmitter. It is then decoded and sent to the electrode array which is placed over the scala tympani. Scala tympani then transmits the signal to the spiral ganglion, which in turn stimulates the auditory nerve cells. Thus, sound is conducted to the brain.

Option C: Hearing aids are used in the management of SNHL. Hearing aids are of the following types

• Conventional hearing aids
• Bone-anchored hearing aids (BAHAs)
• Implantable hearing aids (vibrant soundbridge)

Option D: Sitting in the front row of class is recommended in SNHL to help the child hear the class better.
questions.learning: Adenoidectomy and grommet insertion Adenoidectomy and grommet insertion is not recommended in bilateral sensorineural hearing loss (SNHL). Adenoidectomy and grommet insertion is done in the management of serous otitis media.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: A man was found to be lying dead on the ground. His friend saw a snake passing in the area and took a picture of it and showed it to the doctor (image below). What is the most probable cause of death of this man?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Respiratory failure

The snake in the given image with single white bands on the body is a Common krait which is neurotoxic and the most probable cause of death in this patient is respiratory failure.

Bites of Elapidae (Cobras, Kraits, Mambas, Coral Snakes) present with a local bite reaction which is generally mild with minimal swelling, blistering or superficial necrosis. However their neurotoxic effects are prominent and early symptoms usually include vomiting, hypersalivation, headache, the heaviness of the eyelids, blurred vision, tingling sensation around the mouth, hyperacusis, dizziness, vertigo, and ‘gooseflesh’.

Ptosis is the earliest neuroparalytic manifestation followed

by ophthalmoplegia.

This is followed by paralysis of the facial muscles, palate, jaws, tongue, vocal cords, neck muscles. Muscles of deglutition become progressively flaccidly paralyzed.

A respiratory arrest may occur due to obstruction of the upper airway by the paralyzed tongue or inhaled vomitus, or due to paralysis of intercostal muscles and diaphragm.

Other options:

Options A and C: Viper snake bite (hemotoxic) can lead to shock, haemorrhage, and consumptive coagulopathy.

Option D: Sea snake bites (myotoxic) often result in death due to cardiac arrest caused by hyperkalemia from renal failure or due to respiratory failure.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: 1-month-old baby came with complaints of projectile vomiting with an olive-shaped mass. X-ray abdomen was done which is shown. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Pyloric stenosis

Congenital hypertrophic pyloric stenosis is a common cause of non-bilious projectile vomiting in early infancy due to hypertrophy of the pyloric muscle causing gastric outlet obstruction.

• Presents at 2–6 weeks with projectile non-bilious vomiting and an “olive-shaped” mass
• X-ray may show a distended stomach with paucity of distal bowel gas
• Ultrasound is the investigation of choice (elongated, thickened pylorus)

Clinical significance:

• Leads to hypochloremic, hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis
• Management requires fluid and electrolyte correction followed by pyloromyotomy

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following does not classify as locally advanced breast cancer?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Tumor more than 4 cm

A breast tumor of size > 5 cm (not 4 cm) is classified as locally advanced breast carcinoma (LABC).

Invasive breast carcinoma is of 3 types:

1. Early breast carcinoma (EBC) - TNM combination of T1 to T2, N0 to N1, and M0
2. Locally advanced breast carcinoma (LABC) - T4N0M0, T3N1M0, TanyN2-3M0
3. Advanced breast carcinoma (ABC) - TanyNanyM1

Locally advanced breast cancer (LABC) includes:

1. Breast tumors more than 5 cm in diameter
2. Cancers that involve the skin or the underlying muscles of the chest (T4 of TNM staging)
3. Cancers that involve multiple local lymph nodes (axillary or sub clavicular)
4. Inflammatory breast cancer - a rapidly growing type of cancer that makes the breast appear red and swollen

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A patient presents to the emergency and his ocular examination reveals the following. Which of the following is not done initially?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Removal of the foreign body

The above image shows penetrating injury by a metallic fish-hook.

In cases of penetrating injuries, the foreign body is removed only after ascerting it's location through a CT scan.

Hence, Removal of the foreign body is not done initially in these injuries. It is surgically explored & repaired under OT settings.

Management of penetrating injuries of the eye include:

• Primary survey (Option D) of the patient and the wound
• Visual acuity assesment (Option B) in both normal and injured eye
• A CT scan is performed to localize the foreign body and detect any intaorbital or intracranial extensions.
• MRI is contraindicated for metallic foreign bodies.
• Prophylactic intravitreal antibiotics (option C) are prescribed
questions.learning: Removal of the foreign body — The above image shows penetrating injury by a metallic fish-hook. In cases of penetrating injuries, the foreign body is removed only after ascerting it's location through a CT scan.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A neonate born to a mother with well-controlled gestational diabetes was asymptomatic at birth but developed respiratory distress on the fourth day of life, with an oxygen saturation of 80% on room air. What should be the initial step in management?
questions.explanation: A 4-day-old neonate with acute onset dyspnea and severe hypoxia (SpO₂ 80% on room air) requires immediate evaluation and stabilization. The first and most appropriate step is to administer 100% oxygen, not only as a resuscitative measure but also as a diagnostic test. This approach is known as the hyperoxia test, which helps differentiate pulmonary causes of cyanosis from cyanotic congenital heart disease (CCHD). After giving 100% oxygen for about 10 minutes, arterial PaO₂ is measured: If PaO₂ rises significantly (usually >150 mmHg), the cause is likely respiratory. If PaO₂ fails to rise above ~100 mmHg, it suggests a cardiac right-to-left shunt, as seen in CCHD. Options A (21–30%) and C (50%) provide inadequate oxygen for this diagnostic purpose. Observation (Option D) is unsafe in a neonate with marked hypoxemia. Therefore, administering 100% oxygen immediately is the correct initial management to stabilize the infant and guide further diagnostic evaluation

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 38-year-old man presents with bleeding gums for the past 20 days, along with gingival hyperplasia and hepatosplenomegaly. Laboratory findings show hemoglobin 11 g/dL, platelet count 95,000/mm³, and white blood cell count 45,000/mm³. Bone marrow examination reveals 100% cellularity with numerous blast cells that are peroxidase negative and non- specific esterase positive. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The clinical and laboratory findings provide several definitive clues. The presence of gingival hyperplasia and bleeding gums is a classic physical sign associated with the monocytic subtypes of leukemia. Hepatosplenomegaly and leukocytosis ( cells/mm3) further indicate an acute proliferative malignancy. The critical diagnostic hallmark is the bone marrow biopsy result: blasts that are peroxidase negative but non-specific esterase (NSE) positive. According to the FAB classification, AML M5 (acute monocytic leukemia) is defined by its strong NSE positivity and its clinical propensity for extramedullary involvement, such as in the gums. AML M2 (Option A) is typically peroxidase positive. AML M0 (Option B) is undifferentiated. AML M7 (Option D) is megakaryoblastic and would not typically be NSE positive. Therefore, the specific combination of gingival infiltration and NSE positivity confirms the diagnosis of AML M5
questions.learning: The clinical and laboratory findings provide several definitive clues. The presence of gingival hyperplasia and bleeding gums is a classic physical sign associated with the monocytic subtypes of leukemia.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Common carotid artery pulse is taken at the level of?
questions.explanation: The common carotid artery pulse is typically palpated in the neck, lateral to the larynx. Specifically, it is assessed at the level of the cricoid cartilage, which corresponds to the C6 vertebrae level. At this point, the artery can be compressed against the prominent carotid tubercle (Chassaignac's tubercle) of the C6 transverse process. The bifurcation of the common carotid into internal and external branches usually occurs higher, at the upper border of the thyroid cartilage (C4 level), which corresponds to the laryngeal prominence (Option B). The suprasternal notch (Option C) is too low for a reliable carotid pulse, and the angle of the mandible (Option D) is the site for the facial artery or the termination of the external carotid. Clinically, the carotid pulse is the most reliable peripheral pulse to check during cardiopulmonary resuscitation. Understanding these surface landmarks is essential for rapid clinical assessment and procedures such as carotid endarterectomy or central line placement
questions.learning: The common carotid artery pulse is typically palpated in the neck, lateral to the larynx. Specifically, it is assessed at the level of the cricoid cartilage, which corresponds to the C6 vertebrae level.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 35-year-old woman develops wheezing and breathlessness after taking aspirin for a headache. In addition to these symptoms, which other clinical features are most likely to be present in this condition?
questions.explanation: The patient is presenting with Aspirin-Exacerbated Respiratory Disease (AERD), also known as Samter's Triad. This condition is defined by a characteristic clinical triad: Aspirin sensitivity, Asthma (manifesting as wheezing and breathlessness), and the presence of Nasal polyps. Therefore, finding a nasal polyp (Option B) is highly likely in this patient. AERD is not an IgE-mediated allergy (Option A); instead, it results from an imbalance in arachidonic acid metabolism, specifically an overproduction of leukotrienes when the COX-1 pathway is inhibited by aspirin. It is a form of intrinsic, not extrinsic (Option C), asthma. While this is a reaction to a drug, "Nasal polyp" is the specific clinical entity belonging to the diagnostic triad. On examination, these polyps are typically bilateral, pale, and insensitive to pain. Management involves a strict avoidance of NSAIDs, the use of leukotriene modifiers (like montelukast), and often surgical removal of the polyps if they cause significant nasal obstruction

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: What is the treatment plan for this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Split thickness skin grafting

The given clinical image is suggestive of partial thickness burns and the treatment plan for this condition is split thickness skin grafting.

Split-thickness skin graft (Thiersch graft ): Partial-thickness skin grafts consisting of the epidermis and a portion of the dermis are called split-thickness skin grafts. Less dermis in the split-thickness skin graft translates into less primary contraction (the degree to which a graft shrinks in surface area after harvesting and before grafting) and more secondary contraction (the degree to which a graft shrinks during healing). Humby knife is used to harvest split-thickness skin grafts.

Advantages of split skin graft over full-thickness skin graft:

• Large grafts can be harvested.
• In the case of thinner split-thickness grafts, the donor site heals more rapidly and can be reused in severe cases such
as burns.
• Uptake is good.
• Meshing can be done, i.e., small splits are made in graft and any exudates collected can come out through this, improving graft takeup. It also allows the graft to expand.

Other options

Option A: Full-thickness skin grafts (Wolfe graft) include the epidermis and entire dermis, with portions of the sweat glands, sebaceous glands, and hair follicles. More dermis in the full-thickness skin graft translates into more primary contraction and less secondary contraction.

Option C: VAC is a negative pressure dressing. An occlusive dressing is placed over the sore and it is connected to VAC that generates -125mmHg of pressure. It is used in chronic non-healing ulcers, venous ulcers, diabetic ulcers, burn wounds, and bed sores.

Venous ulcers are due to chronic venous insufficiency and are particularly seen in the lower ⅓ of the leg above the ankle on the medial aspect, known as the gaiter zone. Ambulatory venous hypertension is the most acceptable theory in the pathophysiology of venous ulcers. Venous ulcers have a sloping edge and the floor contains granulation tissue covered by slough and exudate. Marjolin’s ulcer is a type of squamous cell carcinoma seen in chronic long-standing venous ulcers.

Option D: Flaps are tissues with a blood supply, providing vascularity to a new area. Types include:

• Random Flaps: Rectangular, with no specific blood supply, length-to-breadth ratio ≤ 1.5:1.
• Axial Flaps: Long flaps based on known blood vessels, suitable for large distances.
• Pedicled/Isolated Flaps: Axial supply allows them to be moved on a stalk or fully isolated.
• Free Flaps: Blood supply disconnected and reconnected via microsurgery.
• Composite Flaps: Combine tissues like skin with bone or muscle.
• Perforator Flaps: Use small vessels from major blood vessels to supply the surface.
questions.learning: Split thickness skin grafting — The given clinical image is suggestive of partial thickness burns and the treatment plan for this condition is split thickness skin grafting.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following are correct regarding pathological findings of placenta accreta? 1. Absence of decidua basalis 2. Absence of Nitabuch’s fibrinoid layer 3. Loss of normal hypoechoic retroplacental myometrial zone in ultrasonography Select the answer using the code given below.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 1, 2 and 3

Placenta accreta spectrum (PAS) is characterized by abnormal adherence of the placenta to the uterine wall due to defective decidualization. It occurs because of absence or deficiency of the decidua basalis and Nitabuch’s fibrinoid layer, allowing chorionic villi to attach directly to or invade the myometrium. Ultrasound is the primary modality for antenatal diagnosis.

• 1. Absence of decidua basalis ✓

• The fundamental pathological defect in placenta accreta is the absence or deficiency of the decidua basalis, permitting abnormal placental attachment.

• 2. Absence of Nitabuch’s fibrinoid layer ✓

• Nitabuch’s layer normally separates the placenta from the myometrium. Its absence facilitates abnormal trophoblastic invasion.

• 3. Loss of normal hypoechoic retroplacental myometrial zone on ultrasonography ✓

• One of the characteristic ultrasound findings is loss of the retroplacental clear (hypoechoic) zone, suggesting placental invasion into the myometrium.
questions.learning: 1, 2 and 3 Placenta accreta spectrum (PAS) is characterized by abnormal adherence of the placenta to the uterine wall due to defective decidualization.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A 50-year-old patient presents with complaints of skin lesions and joint pain. Cutaneous examination reveals erythematous, scaly plaques, while musculoskeletal examination shows a painful, swollen, and tender finger joint with signs of inflammation. Based on these clinical features, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The combination of a chronic skin condition (red, scaly patches characteristic of psoriasis) and inflammatory joint pain involving a specific digit is diagnostic for Psoriatic Arthritis. This seronegative spondyloarthropathy often presents with "dactylitis" (sausage digit) and can involve the distal interphalangeal (DIP) joints, which is less common in rheumatoid arthritis. The provided image further supports the diagnosis by showing pathognomonic psoriatic nail changes, such as pitting, onycholysis, and oil spots. Reactive arthritis (Option A) typically follows a GI/GU infection and presents with a classic triad including uveitis and urethritis. Pseudogout (Option B) is a crystal-induced arthropathy characterized by chondrocalcinosis on X-ray. Osteoarthritis (Option C) is a degenerative "wear and tear" disease that lacks the primary scaly skin rash of psoriasis. Up to 30% of patients with psoriasis will eventually develop psoriatic arthritis. Management involves a combination of NSAIDs, conventional DMARDs like methotrexate, and modern biologic therapies (TNF inhibitors) to control both skin and joint inflammation
questions.learning: The combination of a chronic skin condition (red, scaly patches characteristic of psoriasis) and inflammatory joint pain involving a specific digit is diagnostic for Psoriatic Arthritis.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which of the following dimorphic fungi causes subcutaneous mycosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Sporothrix schenckii

The dimorphic fungus that causes subcutaneous mycosis is Sporothrix schenckii.

Sporotrichosis is caused by Sporothrix schenckii, a thermally dimorphic fungus that lives on vegetation. The infection occurs following traumatic inoculation.

The lesion initially develops as a granulomatous nodule that may progress to form a necrotic or ulcerative lesion. The infection from the lesions in the skin and subcutaneous tissue can spread via the lymphatic channels to the lymph nodes. This condition is known as lymphocutaneous sporotrichosis. This disease is commonly encountered among gardeners and forest workers.

The image below shows lymphocutaneous sporotrichosis.

Other options:

Option B: Histoplasmosis is a systemic fungal infection caused by the dimorphic fungi Histoplasma capsulatum. It is acquired by inhalation and causes a disease similar to tuberculosis and may present as fever, chills, headache, dry cough, dyspnea, and chest pain.

Option C: Blastomycosis is caused by Blastomyces dermatitidis. It is contracted through the inhalation of contaminated soil. Primary infection usually presents as pneumonia.  Chest X-ray reveals consolidation. Disseminated disease may lead to multiple abscesses. Cutaneous lesions present as papules and nodules which progress into large ulcerative lesions.

Option D: T. marneffei is a dimorphic fungus that causes talaromycosis (penicilliosis). It is commonly seen in individuals with advanced AIDS. Clinical features include fever, weight loss, lymphadenopathy, and hepatosplenomegaly. Umbilicated papules that resemble molluscum contagiosum may also be seen.
questions.learning: Sporothrix schenckii — The dimorphic fungus that causes subcutaneous mycosis is Sporothrix schenckii. Sporotrichosis is caused by Sporothrix schenckii, a thermally dimorphic fungus that lives on vegetation.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Which structure is most commonly compressed, affecting the anterior ethmoid nerve and leading to Sluder’s neuralgia?
questions.explanation: Sluder's neuralgia, also referred to as "contact point headache," is a syndrome believed to be caused by physical contact between anatomical structures within the nasal cavity. Specifically, contact between a deviated nasal septum (Option D) and the middle turbinate (Option B) can lead to the compression of the branches of the sphenopalatine ganglion or the anterior ethmoidal nerve. The middle turbinate is the most frequently involved structure in this compression. The superior turbinate (Option A) is located much higher and is rarely a site of such contact. The inferior turbinate (Option C) is involved in congestion but not typically in this specific neuralgia. Symptoms include deep-seated facial pain, headaches, and nasal congestion. Diagnosis is often made by applying topical anesthetic to the contact point; if the pain subsides, surgical correction via septoplasty or partial turbinectomy may be indicated to resolve the contact point
questions.learning: Sluder's neuralgia, also referred to as "contact point headache," is a syndrome believed to be caused by physical contact between anatomical structures within the nasal cavity.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: An adult male presents with a history of intermittent purulent discharge, occasionally tinged with blood, from an external opening in the perianal region. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The clinical presence of an external opening in the perianal region that produces intermittent purulent discharge and blood is the hallmark of a Fistula in ano. This is a chronic abnormal track communicating between the anal canal and the perianal skin, most commonly resulting from a previous perianal abscess. Hemorrhoids (Option A) cause painless bright red bleeding during defecation but not a discharging skin opening. A pilonidal sinus (Option B) is located in the sacrococcygeal (tailbone) region, further from the anus. A perianal abscess (Option C) is the acute, painful inflammatory stage before a fistula forms. Goodsall's rule is used to predict the internal path of the fistula based on the location of the external opening. Diagnosis is clinical but may be aided by MRI to map complex tracks. Management is surgical, involving fistulotomy for simple tracks or specialized procedures like the Seton technique or LIFT for complex fistulas to preserve anal sphincter function and prevent incontinence
questions.learning: The clinical presence of an external opening in the perianal region that produces intermittent purulent discharge and blood is the hallmark of a Fistula in ano.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: A 14-year-old rape victim presents with 26 weeks of pregnancy. What should not be done?
options: A female doctor should examine the patient
Vaginal swab examination is not necessary
No need to confirm pregnancy by UPT
Termination of pregnancy with her consent by a Gynaecologist
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Termination of pregnancy with her consent by a Gynaecologist

According to the MTP Act 2021 amendments, pregnancy beyond 24 weeks of gestation cannot be terminated. Also, the guardian's written consent is required in the case of a minor girl.

• Up to 20 weeks of pregnancy, any qualified practitioner can perform an abortion. However, he must have undergone compulsory training.
• Between 20-24 weeks of pregnancy, the opinion of a second practitioner must be obtained to justify performing the abortion.
• The woman to be wanting an abortion should be above 18 years of age to consent. If not, consent can be obtained from the parents or guardian when she is a minor or mentally unsound.

In the cases of sexual assault of a female child, a female doctor is appointed for the examination (Option A). In case, such a doctor is unavailable, then the head of the institution can nominate a woman for that purpose. These examinations are carried out in the presence of a parent or guardian.

Vaginal swab samples are typically collected within 96 hours (ideally up to 72 hours), as the chances of detecting evidence decrease significantly after this period. (Option B)
questions.learning: Termination of pregnancy with her consent by a Gynaecologist According to the MTP Act 2021 amendments, pregnancy beyond 24 weeks of gestation cannot be terminated.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 5 year old with gradually progressive hoarseness of voice over three months and respiratory distress for 2 weeks. Diagnosis is
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Respiratory papillomatosis

The given clinical scenario of a child presenting with chronic hoarseness (3 months) of voice and respiratory distress for 2 weeks suggests the diagnosis of respiratory papillomatosis (juvenile papillomatosis).

Croup (Option A) and acute epiglottitis (Option D), which cause acute upper respiratory tract obstruction, are ruled out due to the chronic nature of the symptoms. In croup, the upper airway obstruction becomes apparent after 1 to 3 days of low-grade fever, rhinorrhea, and pharyngitis. On the other hand, in epiglottitis, a child experiences respiratory distress within hours of developing a fever.

Vocal nodules (Option C) are not typically associated with respiratory distress.

Respiratory papillomatosis is the most common respiratory tract neoplasm in children. They are simple warts (benign tumors) caused by human papillomavirus types 6 and 11 commonly seen in children aged 3 to 5 years.

The course involves remissions and exacerbations of recurrent papillomas, mostly affecting the glottic area (vocal cords), and supraglottis. The patient presents with progressively worsening hoarseness, sleep-disordered breathing, dyspnea, stridor, and severe airway obstruction if left untreated.

Diagnosis confirmed by direct laryngoscopy, which shows grape-like projections (shown below), and biopsy. Treatment consists of micro laryngoscopy and CO2 laser excision. Antivirals like interferon alpha2a, ribavirin, cidofovir, and acyclovir are used as adjunct therapies.

Other options:

Option A: Croup (laryngotracheobronchitis) is caused by the parainfluenza virus. The patient initially presents with an upper respiratory tract infection (rhinorrhea, pharyngitis, cough, low-grade fever) followed by a characteristic barking cough, hoarseness, and inspiratory stridor.

Option C: Vocal nodule (singer’s or screamer's nodule) occurs as a result of chronic vocal abuse. They appear symmetrically at the junction of the anterior one-third and posterior two third of the vocal cord. The patient presents with chronic hoarseness and voice fatigue.

The image below shows symmetric vocal nodules:

Option D: Acute epiglottitis is caused by streptococcus pyogenes, pneumococci, Hemophilus influenzae, and staphylococcus aureus. It is characterized by an acute rapidly progressive course of high-grade fever, dyspnea, and stridor.
questions.learning: Respiratory papillomatosis — The given clinical scenario of a child presenting with chronic hoarseness (3 months) of voice and respiratory distress for 2 weeks suggests the diagnosis of respiratory papillomatosis (juvenile papillomatosis).

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 45-year-old woman with irregular bleeding is found to have an endometrial thickness of 15 mm. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Endometrial biopsy

In a 45-year-old with abnormal uterine bleeding and ET = 15 mm, the priority is to rule out endometrial hyperplasia or carcinoma.

Even without ultrasound findings, guidelines recommend biopsy in all women ≥45 with AUB.

Normal endometrial thickness varies with menstrual cycle, but in AUB evaluation:

| Patient group | Suspicious ET

| ------------- | -------------

| Premenopausal with AUB
Perimenopausal | >12 mm

| Postmenopausal bleeding | >4 mm

This patient has 15 mm, which is abnormally thick.

Procedure : A catheter is inserted into the uterus to obtain endometrial tissue.

Advantages

• Outpatient procedure
• Quick and minimally invasive
• High sensitivity for endometrial carcinoma

Detects

• Endometrial hyperplasia
• Endometrial carcinoma
• Hormonal endometrial changes

B. Hysterectomy  is not the first step.

It is done only after:

• Confirmed malignancy
• Failed medical treatment

C. MRI Pelvis  is used for:

• Staging endometrial cancer
• Assessing myometrial invasion

D. Hysteroscopy and Fractional Curettage

This procedure is more invasive and usually performed when:

• Biopsy is inconclusive
• Focal lesion suspected
• Persistent bleeding despite normal biopsy

PALM-COEIN

| Structural causes (PALM) | Non-structural causes (COEIN)

| ------------------------ | -----------------------------

| Polyp | Coagulopathy

| Adenomyosis | Ovulatory dysfunction

| Leiomyoma | Endometrial

| Malignancy / hyperplasia | Iatrogenic / Not classified
questions.learning: Endometrial biopsy — In a 45-year-old with abnormal uterine bleeding and ET = 15 mm, the priority is to rule out endometrial hyperplasia or carcinoma. Even without ultrasound findings, guidelines recommend biopsy in all women ≥45 with AUB.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 42-year-old woman presents with a thyroid nodule. FNAC suggests papillary carcinoma. She undergoes total thyroidectomy. Histopathology reveals multifocal tumors with cervical lymph node metastasis. Postoperatively, serum thyroglobulin is undetectable. What is the most likely explanation?
options: Residual tumor suppressed by TSH suppression therapy
Presence of anti-thyroglobulin antibodies interfering with assay
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Presence of anti-thyroglobulin antibodies interfering with assay

Educational objective:

• Thyroglobulin is used as a tumor marker for follow-up in differentiated thyroid carcinoma after total thyroidectomy
• It should be undetectable; detectable levels suggest residual or recurrent disease
• Anti-thyroglobulin antibodies can interfere with assays and cause falsely low or undetectable values
• Always interpret thyroglobulin along with anti-thyroglobulin antibody status
• Undetectable thyroglobulin does not rule out disease if antibodies are present
questions.learning: Presence of anti-thyroglobulin antibodies interfering with assay Educational objective: • Thyroglobulin is used as a tumor marker for follow-up in differentiated thyroid carcinoma after total thyroidectomy • It should be undetectable; detectable levels…

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Steroid hormone receptors bind to specific DNA sequences via which of the following structures?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Zinc finger motif

After binding their hormone ligand, steroid hormone receptors dimerize, translocate to the nucleus (if not already nuclear), and bind to specific DNA sequences (HREs) through the zinc finger DNA-binding domain, thereby activating or repressing transcription of target genes.

Why not the other options?

• B. RNA motif: Involved in RNA binding, not DNA binding by steroid receptors.
• C. Leucine zipper: DNA-binding motif found in transcription factors such as c-Fos and c-Jun (AP-1).
• D. Helix-turn-helix: DNA-binding motif seen in homeobox proteins and many prokaryotic transcription factors, not steroid hormone receptors.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: What does the point labeled C denote?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Onset of symptoms

The given diagram shows the natural history of disease in an individual over time, in which the point labeled C denotes the onset of symptoms. The natural history of disease refers to the progression of a disease in an individual over time, in the absence of treatment.

Exposure (point A): the disease process begins with appropriate exposure to or accumulation of factors sufficient for the disease process to begin in a susceptible host. For example in infectious disease, the exposure is a microorganism. For lung cancer, it is any factor that initiates the process, such as asbestos fibers or components in tobacco smoke.

Pathological changes (point B): after the disease process has been triggered, pathological changes occur without the individual being aware of it. This stage of subclinical disease, extending from the time of exposure to onset of symptoms, is usually called the incubation period for infectious diseases, and the latency period for chronic diseases. During this stage, the disease remains asymptomatic.

The onset of clinical symptoms (point C): it is the beginning of the clinical stage of the disease.

The usual time of diagnosis (point D): the onset of symptoms is followed by a short interval (varies from disease to disease) after which the patient presents to a healthcare setup where a diagnosis of the disease is made. Based on treatment and prognosis, the patient can progress to either recovery, disability, or death.
questions.learning: Onset of symptoms — The given diagram shows the natural history of disease in an individual over time, in which the point labeled C denotes the onset of symptoms.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A child typically achieves the ability to build a tower of 6 cubes, turn a doorknob, and use personal pronouns such as “I,” “me,” and “you” at around 2 years of age.
questions.explanation: A child’s developmental milestones are key indicators of neurological health. The ability to build a tower of 6 cubes and turn a doorknob are significant fine motor milestones typically achieved by 24 months (2 years) of age. At this same age, children also reach a major language milestone: they start using pronouns such as "I," "me," and "you" and begin forming two-word phrases. At 15 months (Option B), a child can build a tower of 2 cubes. At 18 months (Option C), a child can build a tower of 4 cubes and follows simple commands. By 36 months (3 years) (Option A), a child can build a tower of 9 cubes and can ride a tricycle. Therefore, the specific combination of fine motor precision (6 cubes) and emerging self-identity in language (pronouns) identifies 24 months as the correct developmental stage. These standard "checks" are essential for pediatricians during well-child visits to identify early signs of developmental delay
questions.learning: A child’s developmental milestones are key indicators of neurological health. The ability to build a tower of 6 cubes and turn a doorknob are significant fine motor milestones typically achieved by 24 months (2 years) of age.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: The following device shown attached to the baby is used in all except :
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Measure central cyanosis

The image shows a pulse oximeter. It cannot be reliably used to measure central cyanosis.

A pulse oximeter employs spectrophotometry to measure the percentage saturation of oxygen at a peripheral site. In cases of markedly deranged hemoglobin (Hb) levels and abnormal Hb, pulse oximetry doesn't correlate with central cyanosis, which depends on the absolute value of reduced Hb.

A pulse oximeter can be used for assessing response to resuscitation, titrating oxygen therapy in newborns, monitoring apnea (bradycardia and desaturation), confirming endotracheal tube placement, evaluating the effectiveness of bag and mask ventilation, and monitoring for hypoxia during suction and laryngoscopy.

Cyanosis is characterized by a bluish discoloration of the skin and mucous membranes due to elevated levels of reduced Hb (more than 4 g/dL) or Hb derivatives. It is examined in the nail beds and mucous membranes, earlobes, lips, and fingers. It can be classified into central and peripheral types.

Central cyanosis can be due to reduced oxygen saturation or the presence of abnormal Hb derivatives. Causes include high altitudes, impaired pulmonary function, anatomic shunts, and abnormal Hb. Both the mucous membranes and skin will be affected.

The absolute amount of reduced Hb rather than its relative quantity is significant in cyanosis. In severe anemia, even with marked arterial desaturation, cyanosis may not be present. Conversely, polycythemia patients are prone to cyanosis even at higher oxygen saturation levels.

The presence of abnormal Hb species may lead to errors in SpO2 readings. In a patient with methemoglobinemia, the SpO2 will be 80% to 85%, irrespective of arterial saturation (SaO2). A patient with carbon monoxide poisoning will have a falsely elevated SpO2 level. A co-oximeter is a better device to measure abnormal hemoglobins.

Carbon monoxide poisoning does not lead to true cyanosis. It causes cherry red discoloration.

Peripheral cyanosis occurs due to decreased blood flow and excessive oxygen extraction from normally saturated arterial blood. The mucous membranes of the oral cavity and sublingual mucosa are spared. The causes include reduced cardiac output, cold exposure, and arterial and venous obstruction. Here, the degree of cyanosis will generally correspond to SpO2 readings. However, the SpO2 levels may be falsely low despite normal SaO2.
questions.learning: Measure central cyanosis — The image shows a pulse oximeter. It cannot be reliably used to measure central cyanosis.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following is not true about syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion (SIADH)?
options: Patient can be clinically euvolemic to hypervolemic
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Urinary sodium <20 mEq/L

In SIADH, the kidneys retain water, leading to volume expansion and natriuresis. Therefore, urinary sodium levels are typically higher than 20 mEq/L.

Other options:

Option B: SIADH is a condition where there is an inappropriate release of antidiuretic hormone (ADH), leading to impaired water excretion and dilutional hyponatremia.

Option C: ADH promotes the reabsorption of water and not the solutes resulting in concentrated urine. This is depicted as high urine osmolality.

Option D: Patients can be hypervolemic due to water retention. However, persistently elevated ADH levels can induce vasopressin escape mechanism, resulting in the typical euvolemic status.

Patients usually present with hyponatremia with a euvolemic status.

Acute hyponatremia may present with mild headache, confusion, anorexia, nausea, vomiting, coma, and convulsions.

Chronic hyponatremia allows cerebral adaptation, and the patients are asymptomatic despite the hyponatremia.

Laboratory findings in SIADH include:

• Hyponatremia: serum Na+<135 mEq/L
• Urinary Na+ >25 mEq/L
• Urine osmolality >100 mOsm/kg
• Blood urea nitrogen (BUN) levels are low, usually <10 mg/dL
• Serum urate is low
• Serum K+ and serum bicarbonate are normal

Mild and symptomatic hyponatremia can be managed by restricting fluid intake.

Severe, symptomatic hyponatremia can be corrected using hypertonic saline or vasopressin receptor-2 antagonists (tolvaptan and conivaptan).

Other drugs which are useful in the management are demeclocycline and fludrocortisone.
questions.learning: Urinary sodium 25 mEq/L • Urine osmolality >100 mOsm/kg • Blood urea nitrogen (BUN) levels are low, usually <10 mg/dL • Serum urate is low • Serum K+ and serum bicarbonate are normal Mild and symptomatic hyponatremia can be managed by restricting fluid intake.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: In a 12-year-old girl who has reached Tanner stage 4 for breast development and pubic hair growth, which of the following pubertal changes is not exclusively dependent on estrogen?
questions.explanation: Puberty involves two distinct hormonal events: gonadarche (gonadal activation) and adrenarche (adrenal activation). Breast development and the menstrual cycle are primarily driven by ovarian estrogen. Estrogen is responsible for the maturation of the reproductive tract, including vaginal cornification (Option A), cervical mucus production (Option C), and the proliferation of the endometrium leading to menstruation (Option D). However, pubic and axillary hair growth (Option B) is NOT dependent on estrogen; it is driven by androgens secreted by the adrenal glands and ovaries. This process is known as adrenarche and can occur independently of the estrogen-driven thelarche (breast development). Therefore, in a girl with clinical signs of both pathways (breast and hair development), the hair growth is the only component listed that is strictly androgen-mediated rather than estrogen-mediated
questions.learning: Puberty involves two distinct hormonal events: gonadarche (gonadal activation) and adrenarche (adrenal activation). Breast development and the menstrual cycle are primarily driven by ovarian estrogen.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A 34-year-old male whose staple diet primarily consisted of only maize presents with diarrhea, dementia, and photosensitive dermatitis in sun-exposed areas. Which vitamin is most likely deficient in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Niacin

The above history and clinical features suggest niacin/vitamin B3 deficiency.

Excessive consumption of maize-based diets can cause niacin/vitamin B3 deficiency. Maize contains niacin in bound form and is unavailable for absorption. Jowar has high leucine content which inhibits QPRTase, an enzyme in the synthesis of niacin.

Niacin deficiency leads to a disease called pellagra which is characterized by

* Diarrhea

* Dermatitis

* Dementia

Casal’s necklace pattern classically seen in pellagra is an erythematous pigmented skin rash in the distribution of a broad collar.

Pellagra occurs despite an adequate intake of tryptophan & niacin in the case of

* Carcinoid syndrome as tryptophan will be used up in the production of serotonin

* Hartnup disease due to a defect in the tryptophan transporter resulting in intestinal malabsorption and failure of renal reabsorption.

Niacin significantly decreases concentrations of all apoB-containing lipoproteins like VLDL, IDL, LDL, and lipoprotein a. It also increases HDL cholesterol.

Niacin toxicity occurs when it is taken in excess quantity for the treatment of hyperlipidemia and manifests as

* Prostaglandin-mediated cutaneous flushing

* Glucose intolerance

* Fulminant hepatitis (the most serious complication)

* Hyperuricemia

* Macular edema and macular cysts

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: Which of the physiological parameters does the waveform in the image represent?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. End-tidal carbon dioxide

A capnograph is a device that displays and records end-tidal carbon dioxide, usually as a function of time.

The normal waveform has four different phases:

Phase I: Inspiratory baseline, represents the CO2-free gas from the airways (anatomical and apparatus dead space).

Phase II: Expiratory upstroke, mixing of dead space gas with alveolar gas.

Phase III: Alveolar plateau, represents CO2-rich gas from the alveoli. The last of the alveolar gas is sampled to measure ETCO2.

Phase 0: Inspiratory downstroke and the beginning of inspiration.

Alpha angle: The transition from phase II to III.
The alpha angle can be used to assess the ventilation/perfusion of the lung. V/Q mismatches will have an alpha angle greater than 90 degrees.

Beta angle: The transition from phase III to 0.
The beta angle can be used to assess rebreathing. If rebreathing occurs, the angle is greater than 90 degrees.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A 25-year-old male came with complaints of acute abdominal pain. A plain X-ray abdomen erect was taken which is shown below. What is your diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Pneumoperitoneum

The above X-ray clearly shows the presence of subdiaphragmatic free gas in the right upper quadrant. This indicates pneumoperitoneum.

Causes of pneumoperitoneum include:

1. Bowel perforation

1. Peptic ulcer
2. Ischemic bowel
3. Necrotizing enterocolitis.

2. Small bowel perforation

1. Trauma
2. Penetrating injuries

3. During surgery / laparoscopy

Signs of pneumoperitoneum:

• Bowel-related signs

• Double wall sign (also known as Rigler's sign or gas-relief sign)
• Telltale triangle sign (also known as triangle sign)

• Peritoneal ligament-related signs

• Football sign
• Falciform ligament sign
• Lateral umbilical ligament sign (also known as inverted "V" sign)
• Urachus sign

• Right upper quadrant signs

• Cupola sign
• Fissure for ligamentum teres sign
• Hepatic edge sign
• Lucent liver sign
• Morison's pouch sign (doge cap sign)
• Periportal free gas sign

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 32-year-old patient with a history of chronic alcohol abuse presents to the clinic with complaints of oral ulcers and a burning sensation in the mouth. A picture of the patient's oral cavity is provided, which reveals several white patches on the tongue and inner cheek. Based on this presentation, what is the likely diagnosis for this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Leukoplakia

Leukoplakia is defined as a non-scrapable white patch in the oral cavity that cannot be characterized as any other disease and is considered a premalignant lesion.

•

Risk factors:

• Tobacco, alcohol, chronic irritation

•

Appearance:

• White plaques on tongue, buccal mucosa
• Cannot be scraped off (distinguishes from candidiasis)

•

Pathology:

• May show dysplasia → risk of malignant transformation

Why not other options:

• Erythroplakia: Red lesion, higher malignant potential
• Submucosal fibrosis: Fibrosis with restricted mouth opening, not white patches
• Malakoplakia: Rare granulomatous condition, not typical oral white lesions

questions.text: Replacing alanine by which amino acid, will increase UV absorbance of protein at 280nm wavelength?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Tryptophan

Replacing alanine with tryptophan will increase UV absorbance of protein at 280nm wavelength

The amino acids which absorb 250-290nm (maximum at 280nm) UV light are Tryptophan (Maximum Absorption), Tyrosine, Phenylalanine.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A 42-year-old man sustains a head injury following which blood accumulates around his eyes, leading to periorbital swelling. This presentation is due to disruption of a specific anatomical attachment. Which structural attachment is responsible for this condition??
questions.explanation: The condition described is "raccoon eyes" (periorbital ecchymosis), which often follows a head injury involving the scalp's loose areolar tissue layer. The scalp has five layers: Skin, Connective tissue, Aponeurosis (galea aponeurotica), Loose areolar tissue, and Periosteum. When bleeding occurs in the loose areolar tissue, the blood can track anteriorly into the eyelids. This happens because the epicranial aponeurosis has no bony attachment anteriorly; its fibers instead blend with the orbicularis oculi muscle. Conversely, the periosteum (Option B) is firmly attached at the sutures, which would prevent such extensive tracking of fluid. Cellulitis (Option C) is a bacterial skin infection that presents with warmth, redness, and fever, rather than immediate post-traumatic blood collection. The "raccoon eyes" sign is a critical clinical indicator of a basal skull fracture or severe scalp trauma, facilitated specifically by the lack of an anterior bony attachment of the aponeurosis
questions.learning: The condition described is "raccoon eyes" (periorbital ecchymosis), which often follows a head injury involving the scalp's loose areolar tissue layer.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Kussmaul’s sign is a clinical feature of:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Constrictive pericarditis

Kussmaul’s sign is a paradoxical rise (or failure to fall) in jugular venous pressure (JVP) during inspiration due to impaired right ventricular filling. It is a classic finding in constrictive pericarditis, where the rigid pericardium restricts ventricular expansion.

Why not the other options?

• B. Hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy: Characterized by a systolic murmur that increases with Valsalva; Kussmaul’s sign is not a feature.
• C. Anteroseptal myocardial infarction: May cause LV failure or arrhythmias but does not typically produce Kussmaul’s sign.
• D. Dilated cardiomyopathy: Causes elevated JVP in heart failure, but Kussmaul’s sign is not characteristic.
questions.learning: Constrictive pericarditis Kussmaul’s sign is a paradoxical rise (or failure to fall) in jugular venous pressure (JVP) during inspiration due to impaired right ventricular filling.

questions.text: I-125 labelled albumin is used for measurement of:

I-125 labelled albumin is the most commonly used substance for the measurement of plasma volume.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 55-year-old female patient presented with a 4x3 cm lump in the right upper outer quadrant, with no axillary lymph node involvement. Mammography revealed BIRADS 4b staging. She underwent breast conservation surgery, and the final HPE report showed high nuclear grade DCIS with necrosis and 10 mm margin clearance. What is the further management?
options: Follow up 6 monthly for 2 years and then yearly follow up
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Adjuvant radiotherapy

The next step in the management in this patient with ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS) would be adjuvant radiotherapy, according to the University of Southern California/Van Nuys Prognostic Index (USC/VNPI).

The USC/VNPI  is a scoring system that evaluates the following four factors to predict recurrence in patients with DCIS who are undergoing conservative treatment:

• Tumor size
• Margin width
• Pathological classification (based on nuclear grade, and presence or absence of comedonecrosis)
• Age

This index also provides recommendations for managing patients based on the calculated score.

• Tumor size of 4cm (40mm) - score 2
