questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 45-year-old patient with chronic cough, weight loss, and night sweats is suspected to have tuberculosis. A sputum sample is cultured on Löwenstein–Jensen (LJ) medium. If the organism grows, what staining property would it characteristically exhibit?
questions.explanation: The patient's clinical symptoms (chronic cough, weight loss, night sweats) are highly suggestive of pulmonary tuberculosis caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis. M. tuberculosis is characterized by its unique waxy cell wall containing high concentrations of mycolic acids. This structure makes the organism resistant to traditional Gram staining (Options A and B). Instead, it is identified using Acid-Fast staining (such as the Ziehl-Neelsen stain), where the bacteria retain the primary carbol fuchsin dye even after washing with acid-alcohol. Growth on Löwenstein-Jensen (LJ) medium, which shows rough, tough, and buff-colored colonies, confirms the diagnosis. Therefore, "acid fast" is the definitive staining characteristic for these mycobacteria. This property is essential for the rapid identification of TB in sputum samples
questions.learning: The patient's clinical symptoms (chronic cough, weight loss, night sweats) are highly suggestive of pulmonary tuberculosis caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A patient with recurrent attacks of gout was started on a therapy that inhibits the synthesis of uric acid. His symptoms were reduced after therapy. Which drug was he started on?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Allopurinol

Allopurinol which inhibits uric acid synthesis is the likely drug that was added to the regimen.

It is a purine antimetabolite and a competitive inhibitor of the xanthine oxidase enzyme. It prevents the conversion of hypoxanthine and xanthine to uric acid reducing plasma uric acid levels. The metabolite of allopurinol called oxypurinol is a non-competitive inhibitor of xanthine oxidase.

It is used in the treatment of hyperuricemia in patients with gout and also in patients with hematological malignancies about to undergo chemotherapy.

Other options:

Option A: Probenecid is a uricosuric agent that promotes the excretion of uric acids by inhibiting the organic anion transporter, particularly URAT-1 in the renal tubule. It is used to decrease the body pool of urate in patients with chronic gout. It is used as an adjuvant to allopurinol in chronic gout and hyperuricemia. Plenty of fluids are given to avoid urate calculi formation.

Option B: Colchicine is an antimitotic drug that is used in the treatment of acute gout. It acts by inhibiting microtubule and spindle formation. Side effects are nausea, vomiting, myelosuppression, aplastic anemia, and rhabdomyolysis.

Option C: Diclofenac is a commonly used NSAID that has analgesic, antipyretic, and anti-inflammatory activities. It acts by inhibiting the cyclooxygenase-2 enzyme. Side effects are rashes, fluid retention, edema, and renal function impairment.
questions.learning: Allopurinol Allopurinol which inhibits uric acid synthesis is the likely drug that was added to the regimen. It is a purine antimetabolite and a competitive inhibitor of the xanthine oxidase enzyme.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: During the management of labor, oxytocin may be administered as an intravenous bolus. What adverse effect is commonly associated with giving oxytocin by this route?
questions.explanation: Oxytocin is a potent uterotonic agent used for labor induction and the prevention of postpartum hemorrhage. While it is vital for obstetric care, rapid intravenous bolus administration can lead to significant hemodynamic changes. Specifically, oxytocin has a direct relaxant effect on vascular smooth muscle, which can cause sudden, transient peripheral vasodilation. This results in acute maternal hypotension, often accompanied by tachycardia and increased cardiac output. Hypertension (Option B) is more commonly associated with other uterotonics like ergometrine. Neither hyperglycemia (Option C) nor hypoglycemia (Option D) are recognized side effects of oxytocin administration. To minimize the risk of cardiovascular collapse or profound hypotension, oxytocin is standardly administered as a slow intravenous infusion rather than a rapid bolus. Clinicians must be particularly cautious in patients with pre-existing cardiac disease or hypovolemia, as the rapid drop in blood pressure can compromise maternal safety and fetal perfusion. Monitoring of maternal vitals is essential during any oxytocin administration in the peripartum period
questions.learning: Oxytocin is a potent uterotonic agent used for labor induction and the prevention of postpartum hemorrhage. While it is vital for obstetric care, rapid intravenous bolus administration can lead to significant hemodynamic changes.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which is the most common organism causing acute bacterial prostatitis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. E.coli

The most common organism causing acute bacterial prostatitis (ABP) is Escherichia coli.

It is commonly caused by an ascending urethral infection or reflux of infected urine into prostatic ducts. Sexually transmissible infections and other urinary pathogens, such as Staphylococcus aureus and Streptococcus faecalis may also be responsible.

The patient presents with fever, perineal pain, chills and rigor, and dysuria. Per rectal examination will reveal a tender, boggy prostate. Care should be taken to avoid aggressive palpation or prostatic massage as it can lead to bacterial dissemination and sepsis.

Urine examination and culture should be done. Urine examination reveals threads in urine.

Management:

Patients with systemic signs of infection should be admitted for IV antibiotics, hydration, and monitoring of laboratory parameters.

Patients who have no signs of systemic infection, who can tolerate oral intake, and who have no urinary retention can be treated with oral antibiotics. Antibiotics are given for 2-6 weeks to ensure the eradication of the infection as antibiotics don't penetrate the prostate capsule easily.

For outpatient therapy: Ciprofloxacin 500 mg oral every 12 hours or levofloxacin 500 mg OD or trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole double-strength tablet oral every 12 hours can be used.

For hospitalized patients: Intravenous ciprofloxacin or levofloxacin with or without an aminoglycoside (gentamicin or tobramycin) or intravenous beta-lactam with or without an aminoglycoside. Gram-positive infections are treated with cephalosporins (cephalexin, cefazolin) or dicloxacillin and vancomycin.
questions.learning: E.coli The most common organism causing acute bacterial prostatitis (ABP) is Escherichia coli. It is commonly caused by an ascending urethral infection or reflux of infected urine into prostatic ducts.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: Which type of learning is demonstrated when a medical intern is guided step by step on how to correctly elicit the knee reflex?
questions.explanation: In medical education, learning objectives are categorized into three domains. Psychomotor learning (Option B) involves the acquisition of physical skills and manual dexterity, such as the correct technique for using a reflex hammer to elicit a knee jerk. This type of learning requires the coordination of cognitive understanding with physical performance. Cognitive learning (Option A) focuses on the acquisition of knowledge, facts, and theoretical concepts. Affective learning (Option C) pertains to the development of attitudes, professional values, and empathy. Repeated learning (Option D) is a method of study but not a recognized educational domain. Because the intern is being taught a specific procedural skill that requires physical action and precision, it is the classic example of psychomotor development. Clinical rotations are designed to bridge the gap between classroom cognitive knowledge and hands-on psychomotor proficiency. Therefore, mastering clinical examination techniques is a core psychomotor task
questions.learning: In medical education, learning objectives are categorized into three domains. Psychomotor learning (Option B) involves the acquisition of physical skills and manual dexterity, such as the correct technique for using a reflex hammer to elicit a knee jerk.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: A patient presents to the emergency department soon after a road traffic accident with intense superficial pain due to injuries. Which nerve fibre is responsible for the conduction of this pain?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. A delta

The clinical history of acute superficial pain refers to fast pain or first pain. It is transmitted by A delta (δ) fibers.

Pain can be carried by either Aδ fiber (fast pain/ epicritic pain) or by C fiber (slow pain/protopathic pain)

Fast pain is a rapid response and mediates the ability to localize the site and intensity of the noxious stimulus. it occurs when glutamate is released following the stimulation of A delta fibers.

Slow pain on the other hand can also be burning, dull and poorly localized. It is transmitted by C nociceptor fibers which release substance P.

Option D: C fibres (dorsal root) are associated with pain and temperature with a conduction velocity of 0.5-2 m/s while C fibres (sympathetic) carry the postganglionic sympathetic function and conduct at a velocity of 0.7-2.3 m/s.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 64-year-old woman was brought by her son, during a cataract outreach camp. She gives a history of trauma to her left eye, one year back and a complete loss of vision in that eye since then. Her left eye image is given below. What is the next line of management ?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Keratoplasty

The above image shows a dense white opacity which results due to the scarring of more than half of the stroma. It is characteristic of Leucomatous corneal opacity  and the treatment of choice is keratoplasty.

Depending on the density, corneal opacities are graded as nebula, macula and leucoma.

* Nebular corneal opacity (fog or mist):

* Hard-to-see corneal scar, due to superficial scars involving Bowman's layer and superficial stroma.

* Slit-lamp detection is required.

* A thin, diffuse nebula covering the pupillary area interferes more with vision than the localised leucoma away from the pupillary area. Nebula produces more discomfort due to blurred image (irregular astigmatism).

* Macular corneal opacity:

* Semi-dense opacity that can be seen with proper illumination.

* Due to scarring involving about half the corneal stroma.

* Leucomatous corneal opacity (leucoma simplex):

* White scar that is easily seen just by looking at the eye.

* Due to scarring of more than half of the stroma

* Adherent leucoma:

* It results when healing occurs after perforation of the cornea with incarceration of iris

Secondary changes in corneal opacity which may be seen in long-standing cases include hyaline degeneration, calcareous degeneration, pigmentation and atheromatous ulceration.

Treatment:

* Keratoplasty is the treatment of choice in leucomatous corneal opacities.

* Optical iridectomy may be performed in cases with central adherent leucomas

* Phototherapeutic keratectomy (PTK) performed with excimer laser is useful only in superficial (nebular) corneal opacities.

* Corneal tattooing is a treatment option in patients with corneal opacities, who have lost their vision or who do not expect to recover it. It improves cosmetic appearance by altering the white colour of the opacity and blending it to normal eye colour.
questions.learning: Keratoplasty — The above image shows a dense white opacity which results due to the scarring of more than half of the stroma. It is characteristic of Leucomatous corneal opacity and the treatment of choice is keratoplasty.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: ICER is used as an Economic model in which of the following Health Management Techniques:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Cost effectiveness analysis

In health economics, decision makers often need to determine which health intervention provides the best value for money. One important method used for this purpose is Cost-Effectiveness Analysis (CEA). It compared the cost of an intervention along with the health outcomes achieved.

ICER (Incremental Cost-Effectiveness Ratio) is a key measure in cost-effectiveness analysis, used to compare the additional cost per additional unit of health outcome (e.g., cost per life-year or QALY gained) between two interventions. ICER is used for evaluating vaccination programs, cancer screening programs, new drug therapies, public health interventions.
questions.learning: Cost effectiveness analysis — In health economics, decision makers often need to determine which health intervention provides the best value for money. One important method used for this purpose is Cost-Effectiveness Analysis (CEA).

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text:
Which of the following findings are seen in a high-resolution CT scan of fungal pneumonia?

1. Interlobular septations
2. Peripheral wedge-shaped consolidation
3. Pleural effusion
4. Cavitatory lesions with surrounding ground glass opacities
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 1, 2, 3

High-resolution computed tomography (HRCT) of fungal pneumonia shows interlobular septations, peripheral wedge-shaped consolidation, and pleural effusion. HRCT of fungal pneumonia shows a nodule (not a cavity) with surrounding ground-glass opacities.

A nodule surrounded by ground-glass attenuation on HRCT imaging is seen in aspergillosis, candidiasis, Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia, coccidioidomycosis, and paracoccidioidomycosis. Cavitation on HRCT is seen in cases of community-acquired pneumonia due to Mycobacterium tuberculosis, S. aureus, and gram-negative bacilli.

Aspergillosis is a fungal disease caused by Aspergillus sp. Pulmonary aspergillosis has been categorized into saprophytic, allergic, and invasive forms.

HRCT findings of various types of aspergillosis are as follows:

• Aspergilloma (saprophytic) shows a mass with soft-tissue attenuation, which is separated from the thoracic wall by airspace called the air crescent sign. Multiple nodules and bilateral involvement may be seen.
• Allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis (ABPA-allergic) shows hypodense mucous plugs.
• Angioinvasive aspergillosis shows multiple nodules surrounded by a halo of ground-glass attenuation (‘halo sign’) or pleural-based wedge-shaped areas of consolidation.

The following is an HRCT image of aspergilloma showing the air crescent sign:

The following CT image of aspergilloma shows the halo sign:

Candidiasis pneumonia caused by Candida sp. in immunocompromised patients shows multiple bilateral nodular opacities, areas of consolidation, and ground-glass opacities on HRCT.  Pleural effusion, thickening of the bronchial walls, and cavitation are less commonly seen.

Paracoccidioidomycosis (PCM), is a disease caused by Paracoccidioides brasiliensis. On HRCT, ground-glass opacities, nodules, the ‘halo’ and ‘reversed halo’ signs, interlobular septal thickening, airspace consolidation, cavitation, and fibrosis.
questions.learning: 1, 2, 3 High-resolution computed tomography (HRCT) of fungal pneumonia shows interlobular septations, peripheral wedge-shaped consolidation, and pleural effusion.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A patient presented with unilateral nasal obstruction associated with watery nasal discharge and bleeding. A diagnosis of inverted papilloma is made. Which of the following is true about this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Benign and invasive

Inverted papilloma is a benign and invasive tumor.

Inverted papilloma (Ringertz tumor or transitional cell papilloma or Schneiderian papilloma) is a benign neoplasm of the non-olfactory mucosa of the nose (also called the Schneiderian membrane) and paranasal sinuses. The lateral wall of the nose in the middle meatus is the most common site of origin.

The hyperplastic papillomatous tissue grows into the stroma. It is common in the 4th to 7th decades of life with a male preponderance. Clinical features are unilateral nasal obstruction, nasal discharge, and epistaxis. It is almost always unilateral. It can invade sinuses or the orbit, resulting in proptosis, diplopia, and lacrimation.

An examination of the nose or endoscopy shows a polypoidal mass resembling simple nasal polyps. A computed tomography(CT) scan and/or magnetic resonance imaging(MRI) show the location and extent of the lesion.

MRI is used to differentiate associated secretions in the sinus from the actual tumor mass. A biopsy is essential for diagnosis.

Medial maxillectomy is the treatment of choice, done preferably via endoscopy. Malignancy has been observed in up to 15% of the cases.

Pearl PF1087: Inverted Papilloma

* Inverted papilloma is also known as transitional cell papilloma or Ringertz tumor or Schneiderian papilloma

* It is the most common benign tumor of the nasal cavity

* It is a premalignant condition with 10-15% chances of turning malignant

* Etiology: Human papilloma virus has been implicated in its etiology

* Origin: Arises from the lateral wall of the nose from the non-olfactory epithelium of nose

* Clinical features:

* More common in males

* The age group most commonly affected is 40-70 years

* Unilateral nasal obstruction, nasal discharge, and epistaxis are the main presenting symptoms

* It is a locally invasive tumor and can invade orbit and paranasal sinuses.

* Proptosis, diplopia, and lacrimation can result from orbital invasion

* Findings:

* It is seen as a pale polypoidal mass resembling a simple nasal polyp

* Investigations: A biopsy is needed for diagnosis

* Treatment: Medial maxillectomy via lateral rhinotomy or midfacial degloving approach

* Radiotherapy can lead to malignancy

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A biopsy from a bronchial mass in a 55-year-old shows a neuroendocrine tumor. Which of the following statements regarding neuroendocrine tumors is incorrect?
options: Tumor cells show salt and pepper chromatin
Neuroendocrine tumors arising from different organs have identical microscopic features
Electron microscopy shows dense-core neurosecretory granules
Tumor cells may appear as small round blue cells forming rosettes
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Neuroendocrine tumors arising from different organs have identical microscopic features

Neuroendocrine tumors share common features like salt-and-pepper chromatin and neurosecretory granules, but their microscopic architecture varies by organ (e.g., lung, pancreas, GI tract).

They can show different patterns such as trabecular, insular, or rosette formation.

Hence, they are not identical across organs, making option B incorrect.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: In relation to the orbital wall, where are the canaliculi located as they open into the lacrimal sac?
questions.explanation: The lacrimal drainage system is strategically located at the medial aspect of the orbit. Tears enter the system through the superior and inferior puncta, travel through the canaliculi, and eventually empty into the lacrimal sac. The lacrimal sac sits within the lacrimal fossa, which is formed by the lacrimal bone and the frontal process of the maxilla, both located on the medial orbital wall. The canaliculi typically join to form a common canaliculus before entering the lateral wall of the lacrimal sac, but this entire complex is situated at the medial canthus. The lateral wall (Option A) contains the lacrimal gland, which produces tears, but not the drainage sac. The superior (Option C) and inferior (Option D) walls form the roof and floor of the orbit, respectively, and do not house the primary lacrimal drainage structures. Clinically, knowledge of this medial location is vital during procedures like dacryocystorhinostomy (DCR) or when managing medial canthal trauma to avoid permanent damage to the tear drainage pathway
questions.learning: The lacrimal drainage system is strategically located at the medial aspect of the orbit. Tears enter the system through the superior and inferior puncta, travel through the canaliculi, and eventually empty into the lacrimal sac.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: A patient presented with severe watery diarrhea resembling that of rice gruel stool. Damage of which structure is likely to have resulted in this diarrhea?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Zona occludens

The given clinical picture of a patient having rice gruel stools is suggestive of the diagnosis of ‘cholera’. Vibrio cholerae in addition to the cholera toxin (CT) produces some additional toxins such as,

• Zonula occludens toxin, which alters the intestinal permeability by acting on intestinal epithelial cell tight junctions (which are also called zonula occludens)
• Accessory cholera enterotoxin.

Zonula occludens:

• Also known as tight junctions
• Characteristically surround the apical margins of the cells in epithelia such as the intestinal mucosa, the walls of the renal tubules, and the choroid plexus.
• Also important to the endothelial barrier function and endothelium-dependent vasodilation.
• Made up of ridges- half from one cell and a half from another cell- which adhere so strongly that there is no space between the cells.
• Three families of transmembrane proteins are involved:

1. Occludin
2. Junctional adhesion molecule
3. Claudins

• Paracellular pathway - these tight junctions permit the passage of ions, solutes, and intracellular signaling molecules in between adjacent cells.

Other options:

B) Gap junctions:

• The gap between the two cells in these types of junctions is about 4nm.
• These junctions are formed by units called connexons, which are present in the membrane of each cell.
• Each connexon is made up of six protein subunits called connexins.
• They permit substances to pass between the cells, without entering the ECF.
• The pore diameter is around 0.8 to 1.4  nm, which permits the passage of ions, sugars, amino acids, and other solutes which weigh up to 1000 Da.
• They also permit rapid propagation of electrical activity from cell to cell, as well as the exchange of various chemical messengers and intracellular signaling molecules.

C) Adherent junctions:

• Adherent junctions or Zonula adherens is a continuous structure on the basal side of the zonula occludens.
• It contains cadherins.

D) Hemidesmosomes:

• They look like half-desmosomes.
• They attach cells to the underlying basal lamina and are connected intracellularly to intermediate filaments.
• They contain integrins.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A child presents with bone pain and hepatosplenomegaly. A trephine biopsy and aspirate show the following finding. Which of the following is the most likely enzyme deficient in this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Glucocerebrosidase

The given clinical scenario of a child with bone pain, hepatosplenomegaly, and biopsy showing Gaucher's cell with a characteristic crumpled tissue paper appearance is suggestive of Gaucher's disease. The deficient enzyme is glucocerebrosidase (also known as beta-glucosidase).

Gaucher's disease is an inborn error of metabolism caused due to a deficiency of beta-glucocerebrosidase. It is the most common lysosomal storage disorder and the mode of inheritance is autosomal recessive. There is an accumulation of lipid-laden macrophages in the spleen, liver, and other tissues.

There are three clinical subtypes - type I (chronic non-neuronopathic), type II (acute neuronopathic), and type III (intermediate). Clinical features include anemia, thrombocytopenia, hepatosplenomegaly, and neurological features depending on the subtype.

Gaucher's cells - These are formed as a result of the accumulation of massive amounts of glucocerebrosides within the phagocytes. The cells have a fibrillary cytoplasm and give a crumpled tissue paper appearance.

Option A: Deficiency of hexosaminidase A is seen in Tay-Sachs disease. The deficiency of beta-hexosaminidase A and B causes Sandhoff's disease. Clinical features are seizures, macrocephaly, and hyperacusis.

Option C: Deficiency of sphingomyelinase leads to Niemann-Pick disease. It is characterized by the presence of foam cells in the bone marrow. There may be pulmonary infiltrates leading to lung failure.

Option D: Pompe's disease (type 2 glycogen storage disease) occurs due to alpha 1,4-glucosidase (acid maltase) deficiency. It is the only glycogen storage disease that is a lysosomal storage disease and causes lysosomal glycogen accumulation in cardiac, skeletal, and smooth muscle cells. The clinical symptoms of Pompe disease are hypotonia (floppy infant), skeletal muscle weakness, hepatomegaly, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, and macroglossia.
questions.learning: Glucocerebrosidase — The given clinical scenario of a child with bone pain, hepatosplenomegaly, and biopsy showing Gaucher's cell with a characteristic crumpled tissue paper appearance is suggestive of Gaucher's disease.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A 72-year-old man came with complaints of unilateral knee pain. X-ray examination showed reduced joint space. Pathological findings shown below are of:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Osteoarthritis

The scenario of unilateral knee pain, the radiograph findings of reduced joint space, and the histopathology findings of loss of articular cartilage suggest osteoarthritis.

Osteoarthritis is a type of joint disease characterized by degeneration of cartilage leading to synovial joint destruction. Individuals with age > 50 years and overweight are usually affected.

The disease typically involves the knee and initially affects a single joint; eventually, both knees are affected. Pain is the predominant symptom and worsens with use. Other symptoms such as joint stiffness, swelling, giving away or locking can be present. Fixed flexion deformity can be seen in these patients.

A radiograph of the knee joint, the anteroposterior and lateral view is useful to establish a diagnosis. The characteristic findings are the diminution of joint space, subchondral sclerosis, subchondral cysts, osteophytes, and soft tissue calcifications.

Histopathology shows characteristic loss of the articular cartilage, congestion, fibrosis and inflammatory cells.

Management is as follows

• Conservative measures such as weight loss, exercise, physiotherapy for strengthening of the quadriceps muscle, analgesics for pain relief and usage of walking sticks for reducing the load of joints.
• Intraarticular injections of corticosteroids and hyaluronidase are useful.
• Operative measures such as osteotomy and total knee replacement surgery.

Other options:

Option B: Tuberculosis of the knee is more common in childhood with pain and limping being the common symptoms. X-rays show an enlargement of the epiphysis. The characteristic histopathologic findings are caseating and noncaseating granulomas with surrounding epithelioid and multinucleate giant cells.

The below image shows caseating granuloma with Langhans giant cells:

Option C: Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) of the knee is less common. It is usually seen in females in the 4th to 5th decades. It presents as symmetrical polyarthritis of the proximal finger joints, tenosynovitis, early morning stiffness and pain. Histopathological features include synovial cell hyperplasia and proliferation with inflammatory infiltrates and rheumatoid nodules. These are necrotising granulomas surrounded by fibrinoid necrosis.

The below image shows rheumatoid nodules:

Option D: Lyme disease is a tick-borne infection with skin lesions and flu-like symptoms. It presents with asymmetric inflammatory polyarthritis of the large joints when left untreated.
questions.learning: Osteoarthritis — The scenario of unilateral knee pain, the radiograph findings of reduced joint space, and the histopathology findings of loss of articular cartilage suggest osteoarthritis.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 14-year-old rape victim is 22 weeks pregnant and she would like to terminate her pregnancy. Which of the following is done under the MTP Act?
options: Opinion of 1 doctor is enough upto 24 weeks
Termination allowed between 20-24 weeks only if detrimental to mother's life
Can terminate pregnancy upto 24 weeks for sexual assault
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Can terminate pregnancy upto 24 weeks for sexual assault

According to the MTP Act with 2021 amendments, pregnancy can be terminated upto 24 weeks of gestation in victims of rape and incest, fetal anomalies, or congenital malformations.
questions.learning: Can terminate pregnancy upto 24 weeks for sexual assault According to the MTP Act with 2021 amendments, pregnancy can be terminated upto 24 weeks of gestation in victims of rape and incest, fetal anomalies, or congenital malformations.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: The image shows a skull fracture. The most likely causative weapon is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Heavy blunt object

Depressed skull fractures occur when a heavy blunt object with a small striking surface (e.g., hammer, stone, iron rod) strikes the skull. The fractured bone is driven inward, often producing a round or circular depressed defect that may resemble the shape of the weapon.

• The image shows a localized circular depressed fracture.
• Such injuries are classically produced by heavy blunt weapons with a limited impact surface.
• Examples include:

• Hammer
• Stone
• Iron rod
• Crowbar

Why not the other options?

• A. Bullet: A firearm injury typically shows internal or external beveling, often with radiating fractures and other ballistic features. Beveling cannot be reliably appreciated from this image alone.
• C. Sharp-edged weapon: Produces cut or chop fractures, which are usually linear or V-shaped rather than circular.
• D. Pointed weapon: Produces puncture or stab defects, not a depressed skull fracture.
questions.learning: Heavy blunt object Depressed skull fractures occur when a heavy blunt object with a small striking surface (e.g., hammer, stone, iron rod) strikes the skull.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 65-year-old male patient presents with a left groin swelling for a few years. The swelling increases in size on standing and decreases while lying on the bed. On examination, the swelling has a positive cough impulse. What is the most appropriate management for this patient?
options: Reduction of content, repair of the defect and reinforcement with a mesh
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Reduction of content, repair of the defect and reinforcement with a mesh

The given clinical scenario is an uncomplicated inguinal hernia.  An uncomplicated inguinal hernia is repaired by the reduction of the content, repair of the defect and reinforcement with mesh placement(Lichtenstein mesh repair).

A hernia is a protrusion of the contents outside the cavity containing it. Groin hernias arising lateral to the inferior epigastric artery are indirect and hernia arising medial to it are direct inguinal hernias. Hernias have two cardinal features- reducibility and cough impulse. A Lichtenstein mesh repair is currently one of the most frequently used methods for treating an inguinal hernia. It is done for the reconstruction of the inguinal floor in adults. It is an anterior tension-free mesh repair that reduces the chances of recurrence of a hernia. A piece of prosthetic nonabsorbable mesh is used to fit the canal to bridge the defect in this repair.

Other surgical methods used to repair a hernia are:

Bassini repair is done for the reconstruction of the inguinal floor in adults. In this method, a mesh is not used. It is associated with a high recurrence and is not used frequently now. It is used only in cases of hernial strangulation and peritonitis where the use of a mesh is not preferred. It is performed by suturing the transversus abdominis and internal oblique musculoaponeurotic arches/conjoined tendons to the inguinal ligament.  Shouldice repair is a multilayered repair, where the posterior wall of the inguinal canal is strengthened by continuous sutures. It involves double-breasting of the transversalis fascia. It is associated with a very low recurrence rate. These are herniorraphies (Option C)

Herniotomy is used to treat inguinal hernia in a child which occurs due to the presence of a patent processus vaginalis. Therefore in herniotomy, the repair of the inguinal ring is not done. (Option B)

McVay repair (Cooper's ligament repair) is used for the correction of direct inguinal hernia, large indirect hernia, recurrent hernia, femoral hernias (particularly suited for strangulated femoral hernias). In this method, the transversus abdominis aponeurosis is approximated to Cooper's ligament.

Stoppa-Rives repair is used for the repair of large, recurrent, or bilateral hernias. In this method, a sub-umbilical midline incision is given to place a large mesh into the preperitoneal space.

Pearl PF0034: Boundaries of Hesselbach’s triangle

* Lateral - inferior epigastric artery

* Medial - lateral border of rectus abdominis

* Inferior - inguinal ligament

Direct inguinal hernia emerges through Hesselbach’s triangle (Hence situated medial to inferior epigastric artery)

Indirect inguinal hernia enters deep inguinal ring (Hence it is lateral to inferior epigastric artery)

Pearl PF1778: Types of indirect inguinal hernia

* Bubonocele – Hernia limited to the inguinal canal.

* Funicular – Hernia stops just above the testis.

* Complete/scrotal – Hernia reaches bottom of scrotum.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: The specimen in the below image was obtained from a woman's stomach. Which specialist is recommended alongside a surgeon in this case?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Psychiatrist

The given image of a trichobezoar suggests a diagnosis of trichophagia, which mandates a detailed evaluation by a psychiatrist.

Trichophagia is the compulsive eating of hair associated with trichotillomania. In trichophagia, people also ingest the hair that they pull. Complications include trichobezoars, malnutrition, and intestinal obstruction.

Trichotillomania is a chronic psychiatric disorder characterized by repetitive hair pulling, leading to variable hair loss. There is increased tension prior to the hair pulling and a relief of tension or gratification after the hair pulling. It is seen more common in females.
questions.learning: Psychiatrist — The given image of a trichobezoar suggests a diagnosis of trichophagia, which mandates a detailed evaluation by a psychiatrist. Trichophagia is the compulsive eating of hair associated with trichotillomania.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The arrow in the image denotes which of the following muscles?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Extensor carpi radialis longus

The arrow shows extensor carpi radialis longus.

It originates from the distal third of the lateral supracondylar ridge of the humerus and inserts at the second metacarpal (radial side). It is innervated by the radial nerve, C6, and C7.

The vascular supply is by radial recurrent artery and it is responsible for the extension and abduction of the wrist joint.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following are symptoms of genital tuberculosis? 1. Postmenopausal bleeding 2. Infertility 3. Chronic pelvic pain 4. Oligomenorrhoea Select the correct answer using the code given below.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 2, 3 and 4

Female Genital Tuberculosis (FGTB) is an important cause of infertility in countries where tuberculosis is endemic. It usually results from hematogenous spread of Mycobacterium tuberculosis from a primary focus (commonly the lungs) and most frequently involves the fallopian tubes, followed by the endometrium.

• 1. Postmenopausal bleeding ✗

• Postmenopausal bleeding is not a typical feature of genital tuberculosis and should raise suspicion for endometrial carcinoma or other uterine pathology.

• 2. Infertility ✓

• Infertility is the most common presenting symptom of genital tuberculosis due to tubal damage and endometrial involvement.

• 3. Chronic pelvic pain ✓

• Chronic pelvic pain is common because of chronic inflammation, adhesions, and tubo-ovarian disease.

• 4. Oligomenorrhoea ✓

• Menstrual disturbances such as oligomenorrhea, hypomenorrhea, amenorrhea, or occasionally menorrhagia may occur due to endometrial involvement.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: The most common manifestation of congenital toxoplasmosis is ______
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Chorioretinitis

Chorioretinitis is the most common manifestation of congenital toxoplasmosis.

The characteristic triad of congenital toxoplasmosis is chorioretinitis, hydrocephalus, and diffuse intracranial calcifications. Clinical manifestations apart from the triad include hydrops fetalis, intrauterine growth retardation, prematurity, peripheral retinal scars, persistent jaundice, and mild thrombocytopenia.

Congenital toxoplasmosis occurs when a pregnant woman acquires the infection during gestation. The organism may cross to the fetus transplacentally or at the time of vaginal delivery. The severity of the disease in the neonate is greater if the woman gets infected early in her pregnancy. The causative agent is Toxoplasma gondii, an obligate intracellular protozoan.

The diagnosis is made by the detection of IgM anti-toxoplasma antibodies. IgG can cross the placenta is hence, cannot confirm infection in the infant. IgM immunosorbent agglutination assay (ISAGA) and IgA ELISA are the most useful diagnostic tests.

Spiramycin can be administered for cases of acute infection in early pregnancy to reduce vertical transmission. It does not cross the placenta and therefore cannot be used to treat an infected fetus. Pyrimethamine-sulfonamide (to be avoided in the first trimester) is used when a fetal infection is confirmed or in maternal infections after 18 weeks.
questions.learning: Chorioretinitis Chorioretinitis is the most common manifestation of congenital toxoplasmosis. The characteristic triad of congenital toxoplasmosis is chorioretinitis, hydrocephalus, and diffuse intracranial calcifications.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which of the following clotting factors would have decreased gamma carboxyglutamate residue in a patient on warfarin therapy?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Factor 2

Factor 2 would have decreased gamma carboxyglutamate residue in a patient on warfarin therapy.

Activation of coagulation factors II, VII, IX, X is done by carboxylation of their glutamate residues. This is done by the enzyme γ-glutamyl carboxylase with the reduced form of vitamin K as a co-factor.

This reduced form of vitamin K needs to be constantly recycled back from its oxidized form for the reaction to continue. This recycling is done by the enzyme vitamin K epoxide reductase. This enzyme is inhibited by warfarin.

Hence, warfarin indirectly inhibits the γ-carboxylation of vitamin K dependent clotting factors - Factors II, VII, IX, X by directly inhibiting vitamin K epoxide reductase. Thus leading to decreased gamma carboxyglutamate residue in these factors.
questions.learning: Factor 2 Factor 2 would have decreased gamma carboxyglutamate residue in a patient on warfarin therapy. Activation of coagulation factors II, VII, IX, X is done by carboxylation of their glutamate residues.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: What marker is regularly monitored in the management of ectopic pregnancy?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. β-hCG

The marker used in the monitoring of ectopic pregnancy is β-hCG

Human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG) is a glycoprotein. It can be detected in the maternal serum or urine as early as 8–9 days post-fertilization. Maximum levels in blood and urine are found between 60 - 70 days of pregnancy. It disappears from circulation within 2 weeks following delivery.

Ectopic pregnancy has decreased levels of hCG as compared to normal pregnancy hCG, and it is used as a marker for medical management of ectopic pregnancy. Following conservative surgery or medical treatment, estimation of serum β-hCG level should be done weekly until the β-HCG values go down.

Medical management is indicated when the patient is asymptomatic and hemodynamically stable. It involves the systemic or local use of chemotherapeutic drugs:

* Drugs used: Methotrexate (50 mg/m2, single dose intramuscularly)

* Regular monitoring of serum β-hCG

Medical management is likely to be successful when

* Initial serum hCG level is <3,000 IU/L.

* Ectopic mass is less than 4 cm.

* Fetal cardiac activity is absent.

* Intra-abdominal hemorrhage is absent.

Surgical management of ectopic pregnancy includes laparoscopic salpingostomy, salpingectomy, and microsurgical laparotomy.
questions.learning: β-hCG The marker used in the monitoring of ectopic pregnancy is β-hCG Human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG) is a glycoprotein. It can be detected in the maternal serum or urine as early as 8–9 days post-fertilization.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 28-year-old woman presents with continuous diarrhea, abdominal discomfort, bloating, and weight loss over the past two weeks. She reports recent camping in a rural area and consumption of untreated stream water. On examination, her temperature is normal, and mild tenderness is noted in the right upper quadrant. Stool analysis reveals trophozoites and cysts, with microscopic observation showing the characteristic “falling leaf” motility. Which organism is most likely responsible for her symptoms?
questions.explanation: The history of drinking untreated stream water during a camping trip, followed by bloating, flatulence, and "greasy" or continuous diarrhea, is the classic presentation for Giardiasis. The pathognomonic laboratory finding for Giardia lamblia is the observation of pear-shaped trophozoites with a "falling leaf" motility on a wet mount of fresh stool. Giardia trophozoites use their ventral sucking discs to attach to the intestinal mucosa, leading to malabsorption and weight loss. Salmonella typhi (Option A) causes enteric fever, characterized by high fever and "pea soup" diarrhea, which is inconsistent with the patient's normal temperature. Entamoeba histolytica (Option B) causes amoebic dysentery, typically presenting with bloody stools and trophozoites that may contain ingested RBCs, rather than "falling leaf" motility. Cryptosporidium parvum (Option D) also causes waterborne diarrhea, especially in immunocompromised individuals, but is identified by acid-fast staining of oocysts, not by the distinctive flagellated motility of Giardia. Thus, Giardia lamblia is the only diagnosis fitting all clinical and microscopic clues
questions.learning: The history of drinking untreated stream water during a camping trip, followed by bloating, flatulence, and "greasy" or continuous diarrhea, is the classic presentation for Giardiasis.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Identify the lesion in the histopathological image of retina.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Drusen

The below given image shows extracellular eosinophilic deposits between retinal pigment epithelium(RPE) and bruch's membrane which is suggestive of drusens.

Drusens are seen in dry age related macular degeneration(ARMD) and are composed of lipids, complement factors and other cellular components.

Age related Macular degeneration(ARMD) also known as senile macular degeneration is a chronic and progressive bilateral degenerative disorder of the macula that affects older individuals >50 yrs.

It is the leading cause of blindness in elderly in developed countries and its risk factors include smoking, exposure to sunlight, hypertension, female gender and nutritional deficiencies.

ARMD generally starts as dry ARMD which is characterized by the presence of drusen and gradually progresses to the advanced form known as wet ARMD whose hallmark is choroidal neovascularization with additional findings such as geographic atrophy of retinal pigmentatory epithelium (RPE) and photoreceptors at the macula.

Clinical features include loss of central vision, distorted vision(lines seen as wavy) and sudden painless loss of vision as seen in wet ARMD.

On fundus fluorescein angiography (FFA) the Druscens shows hyperfluorescent spots arranged in ‘stars in the sky’ appearance.

Disease management is by:

• Preventative measures to delay progression such as cessation of smoking, intake of good nutrition and supplementation of vitamins C,E and zinc.
• Treatment modalities with intravitreal Anti-VEGF injection- Bevacizumab (avastin) and Ranibizumab (Lucentis), photodynamic therapy (PDT) and submacular surgery.

The below given images show drusens in macular area and FFA depicting the 'stars in sky appearance' of drusens respectively.

Option B: Hard exudates are composed of lipoproteins and lipid laden macrophages. They are yellow waxy looking and arranged in clumps or circinate patterns. They are seen in diabetic retinopathy, hypertensive retinopathy and coat’s disease.

The below given image is that of Hard Exudates.

Option C: Cotton wool spots also known as soft exudates are small whitish fluffy lesions which represent areas of nerve infarcts in the nerve fiber layer of the retina. They are seen in central retinal vein occlusion (CRVO), hypertensive retinopathy, diabetic retinopathy, toxaemic retinopathy of pregnancy and papilledema.

Option D:Cystoid Macular edema(CME) is a collection of fluid between the outer plexiform layer(Henle's layer) and the inner nuclear layer of the retina.

In CME, on fundoscopy a honeycomb appearance and on FFA, flower petal pattern can be seen. Optical coherence tomography(OCT) of CME shows loss of foveal depression and intraretinal cystoid spaces.

The below given OCT image shows intraretinal cystoid spaces seen in CME.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 23-year-old man develops eye pain, redness, and photophobia two days after sustaining an ocular injury from leaves and thorns while gardening. Based on this history and presentation, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Fungal keratitis (keratomycosis) must be the primary suspicion in any patient presenting with a corneal ulcer following trauma with "vegetative matter" such as leaves, thorns, or wood. Agricultural workers and gardeners are at the highest risk. The most common organisms are Aspergillus and Fusarium. Clinical signs often include a "dry" looking ulcer with "feathery" margins and satellite lesions. Option A (Simplex keratitis) typically features a dendritic ulcer and is a viral reactivation rather than trauma-induced. Option B (Bacterial keratitis) is more acute and usually follows general trauma, appearing more "suppurative". Option D (Acanthamoeba) is strongly linked to contaminated contact lens solutions or swimming in fresh water. Fungal keratitis is notoriously difficult to treat because antifungal drugs have poor corneal penetration. Diagnosis is confirmed by corneal scrapings showing fungal hyphae on KOH mount. Treatment requires long-term topical antifungals such as Natamycin or Voriconazole
questions.learning: Fungal keratitis (keratomycosis) must be the primary suspicion in any patient presenting with a corneal ulcer following trauma with "vegetative matter" such as leaves, thorns, or wood.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 23 yr old gravida 1, para 0 at 25 weeks gestation, presents with right upper quadrant pain, nausea, and vomiting for the past 2 days. BP-104/72mm Hg, PR-72bpm. There is generalized edema. Peripheral smear shows hemolysis. Lab values are given below. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis? Leukocyte count: 10,500/mm3 Platelet count: 62000/mm3 Hematocrit: 26% AST: 90 IU/L
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. HELLP Syndrome

The most likely diagnosis in this patient is HELLP syndrome.

The typical presentation of right upper quadrant pain, nausea, vomiting, lab findings of thrombocytopenia, low hematocrit, and peripheral smear finding of hemolysis, point towards a diagnosis of  HELLP ( Hemolysis, Elevated Liver enzymes, Low Platelets) syndrome.

Although related to preeclampsia, hypertension and proteinuria may be absent or minimal in HELLP syndrome.

Tennessee criteria used in the diagnosis of HELLP syndrome :

* Platelet count <1 lakh,

* AST >70 IU/L,

* LDH >600 IU/L

Risk factors for HELLP syndrome include

* Preeclampsia

* abnormal placentation

* family history of HELLP syndrome

* elevated levels of fetal mRNA for FLT l (vascular endothelial growth factor rfi receptor 1) and

* Multiparity

* Maternal age >34 years

* European descent

* History of previous poor pregnancy outcomes

Laboratory evaluation in HELLP:

* Complete blood cell (CBC) count: Thrombocytopenia, anemia with possible reticulocytosis

* Coagulation studies: Normal prothrombin time, 50% may have prolonged activated partial thromboplastin time

* Peripheral smear: Schistocytes, helmet cells, and burr cells secondary to microangiopathic hemolytic anemia

* Serum aspartate aminotransferase/alanine aminotransferase (AST/ALT) levels: Elevated secondary to liver dysfunction

* Lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) level: Elevated secondary to liver dysfunction or hemolysis

* Elevated blood urea nitrogen (BUN)/creatinine with acute renal failure

* Bilirubin level: Increased secondary to hemolysis

* Haptoglobin level: Decreased secondary to hemolysis

* Fibrinogen levels: Low secondary to increased coagulation

* D-dimer: Increased due to fibrinolysis/DIC

HELLP syndrome may lead to the development of DIC which manifests as increased fibrin split products and decreased fibrinogen levels.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Mid-year population is the denominator in?
questions.explanation: The mid-year population is commonly used as the denominator in rates that measure events occurring in the entire population over a year. The best example is the Crude Death Rate (CDR). CDR is calculated as: The mid-year population (usually estimated on 1st July) represents the average population at risk during the year, making it the most appropriate denominator. Why other options are wrong: (B) CFR (Case Fatality Rate) : Denominator = number of diagnosed cases, not total population (C) MMR (Maternal Mortality Ratio) : Denominator = live births, not population (D) NMR (Neonatal Mortality Rate) : Denominator = live births, not population
questions.learning: The mid-year population is commonly used as the denominator in rates that measure events occurring in the entire population over a year. The best example is the Crude Death Rate (CDR).

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A young patient is admitted with a history of fever for 5 days. BP is 90/60 mmHg, PR-120 bpm, RR-24 breaths/min, GCS score-10; laboratory tests show leucocytosis with neutrophilia and serum creatinine level of 2.6 mg/dL. An intern doctor wants to calculate the qSOFA score to predict prognosis and hospitalization duration. Which of the following comprises the qSOFA score?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. SBP, RR, GCS score

qSOFA score comprises of SBP, RR, and GCS.

qSOFA score (quickSOFA) is a bedside prompt that may identify patients with suspected infection who are at greater risk for a poor outcome outside the intensive care unit (ICU).

It uses three criteria, assigning one point each for

• low blood pressure (SBP≤100 mmHg),
• high respiratory rate (≥22 breaths/min),
• altered mentation (GCS score, <15).

The score ranges from 0 to 3 points. The presence of 2 or more qSOFA points is a simple prompt to identify infected patients outside the ICU who are likely to develop sepsis. This is a simplified derivative of SOFA score. The primary method to evaluate the risk of organ dysfunction (sepsis) in patients with suspected infection is by determining the Sequential (sepsis-related) Organ Failure Assessment (SOFA) score, which includes assessment of:

• Circulation - Systolic BP and need for vasopressors; platelet count
• Respiration - PaO2/FiO2 and need for mechanical ventilation
• Mentation - Glasgow Coma Scale score
• Hepatic function - Bilirubin level
• Renal function - Creatinine level

Organ dysfunction is defined by a SOFA score of ≥2.

The SOFA score is limited by its requirement of multiple laboratory tests which makes it complex and time-consuming. In order to simplify the scoring process, the "Sepsis - 3" task force recommended the quick sepsis-related organ dysfunction assessment "qSOFA" score.

SOFA vs. qSOFA:

• SOFA is a more comprehensive and accurate scoring system, which is particularly superior to qSOFA in the ICU setting.
• qSOFA is a simplified derivative of SOFA for bedside assessment of individuals at risk for sepsis, particularly useful outside the ICU setting (i.e. ward/emergency department). However, note that it was originally designed as a predictive tool that calculates the risk of death from sepsis rather than a diagnostic tool.

Thereby, the best description of sepsis based on "Sepsis-3" task force recommendations would be as follows:

• Suspected or documented infection with SOFA score of ≥2  or
• Suspected or documented infection with qSOFA score of ≥2

Another score that has been used is the National Early Warning Score (NEWS). It ranges from 0 to 20 and is based on respiratory rate, oxygen saturation, use of supplemental O2, temperature, systolic blood pressure, pulse rate, and level of consciousness. ≥5 out of 20 is considered a positive score.

Other scoring systems for sepsis:

The Systemic Inflammatory Response Syndrome (SIRS) score is no longer recommended as is it not specific to infection.

The Logistic Organ Dysfunction System (LODS) score is not recommended as it is complex and has too many variables.
questions.learning: SBP, RR, GCS score qSOFA score comprises of SBP, RR, and GCS. qSOFA score (quickSOFA) is a bedside prompt that may identify patients with suspected infection who are at greater risk for a poor outcome outside the intensive care unit (ICU).

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The blood supply to the structure marked in the image is by:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Anterior cerebral artery

The marked structure is fornix which is supplied by the anterior cerebral artery.

The anteromedial central branches from the anterior cerebral artery supply the fornix along with optic chiasma, lamina terminalis, hypothalamus, para-olfactory areas, and cingulate gyrus.
questions.learning: Anterior cerebral artery — The marked structure is fornix which is supplied by the anterior cerebral artery. The anteromedial central branches from the anterior cerebral artery supply the fornix along with optic chiasma, lamina terminalis, hypothalamus,…

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: In cases of suspected ectopic pregnancy, which hormone is typically measured?
questions.explanation: The primary biochemical marker used in the diagnosis and monitoring of suspected ectopic pregnancy is Beta-human chorionic gonadotropin (beta-hCG). In a normal intrauterine pregnancy, beta-hCG levels typically double approximately every 48 hours. An abnormally slow rise or a plateau in beta-hCG levels is highly suspicious for an ectopic pregnancy or a non-viable intrauterine pregnancy. Estrogen (Option A) and LH (Option D) are not useful for pregnancy localization or viability. Progesterone (Option B) can occasionally be used to assess pregnancy viability (very low levels suggest a non-viable state), but it is not as sensitive or specific as serial beta-hCG measurements combined with ultrasound. The "discriminatory zone" refers to the beta-hCG level at which an intrauterine gestational sac should be visible on transvaginal ultrasound; failure to see a sac above this level strongly suggests an ectopic location
questions.learning: The primary biochemical marker used in the diagnosis and monitoring of suspected ectopic pregnancy is Beta-human chorionic gonadotropin (beta-hCG). In a normal intrauterine pregnancy, beta-hCG levels typically double approximately every 48 hours.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which is the best confirmatory method to ensure the central line is in the jugular vein?
questions.explanation: Following the insertion of a central venous line, such as in the internal jugular or subclavian vein, a chest X-ray is the gold standard confirmatory method. It serves two vital purposes: verifying the correct anatomical position of the catheter tip (ideally at the junction of the superior vena cava and right atrium) and ruling out immediate iatrogenic complications like a pneumothorax. While blood color (Option C) and blood pH (Option B) can provide clues about whether a vessel is arterial or venous, they are subjective and unreliable for definitive confirmation. ETCO2 (Option D) is used to confirm endotracheal tube placement, not central line position. Furthermore, if an insertion attempt fails on one side, an X-ray or ultrasound should be performed before attempting the opposite side to prevent bilateral complications. Thus, radiological verification remains the best confirmatory step
questions.learning: Following the insertion of a central venous line, such as in the internal jugular or subclavian vein, a chest X-ray is the gold standard confirmatory method.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Identify the finding seen in this hysterosalpingogram:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Bilateral hydrosalpinx

Bilateral hydrosalpinx is observed in the given image of hysterosalpingogram.

Hydrosalpinx is often bilateral and occurs following acute salpingitis. The tubes are retort shaped due to dilatation of the ampulla and filled with a clear fluid. The interstitial end of the tube is open whereas the fimbrial end is indrawn and closed. This permits the dye to enter but not exit the tube during hysterosalpingography.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 50-year-old male who is a chronic smoker presented to the hospital with intermittent claudication pain of both thigh and buttock region on walking about 500 m. Which of the following is a likely diagnosis?
options: Arterial disease involving the superficial femoral artery
Arterial disease involving the profunda femoris artery
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Arterial disease with aortoiliac involvement

The given clinical scenario is suggestive of arterial disease with aortoiliac involvement. Classically, the muscle group affected by claudication is one anatomical level below the level of arterial disease.

Intermittent claudication is a feature of chronic arterial disease or occlusion of the artery.  Aortoiliac disease affects the infrarenal aorta and iliac arteries.

Management involves smoking cessation, lifestyle modifications, and treatment of underlying diabetes or hyperlipidemia if present.

For claudication, cilostazol or pentoxyfilline is used. Cilostazol is superior to pentoxyfilline.

Surgical options include aortoiliac bypass, aortobifemoral bypass, percutaneous transluminal angioplasty (PTA), which can be with or without stent placement, and thromboendarterectomy.

Correlation of clinical findings to the Site of Disease

Aortoiliac obstruction

Claudication in buttocks, thighs, and calves

Bruit over the aortoiliac region

Impotence (Leriche's syndrome)

Iliac obstruction

Claudication of thigh and calf, unilaterally

Absence of femoral and distal pulses

Bruit over iliac region

Femoropopliteal obstruction

Claudication in calf

Femoral pulse felt but distal pulses absent

Distal obstruction

Ankle pulses absent

Claudication in calf and foot

Femoral and popliteal pulses palpable
questions.learning: Arterial disease with aortoiliac involvement — The given clinical scenario is suggestive of arterial disease with aortoiliac involvement. Classically, the muscle group affected by claudication is one anatomical level below the level of arterial disease.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient with a severe history of a road traffic accident shows clinical signs suggestive of raised intracranial pressure on examination. What is the recommended treatment in this situation?
options: Initiate anticoagulant therapy to prevent blood clot formation.
questions.explanation: In the acute management of a head injury patient exhibiting signs of elevated Intracranial Pressure (ICP)—such as altered consciousness, pupillary changes, or Cushing's triad—the immediate medical priority is to reduce the pressure. "Mannitol" is an osmotic diuretic that is the standard first-line pharmacological treatment for acutely lowering ICP. It works by creating an osmotic gradient that draws water out of brain tissue into the vascular space. Antibiotics (Option A) and anticoagulants (Option B) are not primary treatments for acute intracranial hypertension and can even be contraindicated in cases of traumatic hemorrhage. While surgical intervention (Option C) like a decompressive craniectomy may be necessary later, medical stabilization with mannitol is often the required "bridge" to imaging and surgery. Other emergency measures include elevating the head of the bed to 30 degrees and controlled hyperventilation if herniation is imminent
questions.learning: In the acute management of a head injury patient exhibiting signs of elevated Intracranial Pressure (ICP)—such as altered consciousness, pupillary changes, or Cushing's triad—the immediate medical priority is to reduce the pressure.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following findings from a pleural fluid aspirate will suggest an exudative pleural effusion? Normal values Total S.Protein:6-8 gm% S.LDH: 140-280 IU S. glucose:140-200
options: Pleural fluid protein = 4.5 gm% and LDH= 150 IU
Pleural fluid protein=4.5 gm% and glucose= 30mg%
Pleural fluid protein=3.5gm% and glucose=90 mg%
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Pleural fluid protein = 4.5 gm% and LDH= 150 IU

Light's criteria does not include glucose in it and hence all other options can be ruled out which makes option 'A' as the answer.

In this question, the ratio of pleural fluid protein(4.5gm%) to the normal serum protein (7gm%) is 0.64 and the Pleural Fluid LDH (150 IU) to Normal Serum LDH(200 IU) is 0.75 which satisfies Light's criteria.

Light’s criteria is used to distinguish between exudative and transudative pleural effusions.

An exudative pleural effusion satisfies at least one of the following criteria.

* Pleural fluid protein / serum protein > 0.5

* Pleural fluid LDH / serum LDH > 0.6

* Pleural fluid LDH more than 2/3rds upper limit of normal for serum
questions.learning: Pleural fluid protein = 4.5 gm% and LDH= 150 IU Light's criteria does not include glucose in it and hence all other options can be ruled out which makes option 'A' as the answer.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Identify the site of the lesion.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Left occipital lobe

The visual field defect shows right homonymous hemianopia with macular-sparing, which is caused by lesions of the left occipital lobe (contralateral/crossing of fibers).

Such lesions are generally due to the occlusion of the posterior cerebral artery. These are commonly seen in head injury and may be associated with visual hallucinations, denial of blindness (Anton syndrome), and the Riddoch phenomenon (only moving visual targets are perceived). These lesions generally spare the central vision/macular vision. The anatomical reason for this sparing is attributed to the uniqueness in the blood supply. While the part of the occipital lobe representing the peripheral field vision is supplied by the posterior cerebral artery, the area at the tip of the calcarine cortex, representing the central macular vision is supplied by a branch of the middle cerebral artery.
questions.learning: Left occipital lobe — The visual field defect shows right homonymous hemianopia with macular-sparing, which is caused by lesions of the left occipital lobe (contralateral/crossing of fibers).

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: Which of the following factors is not considered in the FRAX score assessment?
questions.explanation: The FRAX (Fracture Risk Assessment Tool) score is used to calculate the 10-year probability of a major osteoporotic fracture based on individual clinical risk factors. While Body Mass Index (BMI) (Option C) is a core component, it is calculated using weight and height; however, absolute height (Option A) is not a standalone factor in the risk calculation. Smoking status (Option B) and current or past glucocorticoid intake (Option D) are well-established clinical risk factors included in the tool. Other factors considered include age, sex, prior fracture history, rheumatoid arthritis, secondary osteoporosis, and alcohol intake. The tool is designed to identify patients who may benefit from pharmacological intervention to prevent fractures. While height is measured to calculate BMI, it does not serve as an independent predictor of bone mineral density or fracture risk within the FRAX algorithm. Therefore, "height" is the correct choice as the factor not directly assessed as an independent risk variable
questions.learning: The FRAX (Fracture Risk Assessment Tool) score is used to calculate the 10-year probability of a major osteoporotic fracture based on individual clinical risk factors.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Which among the following statements is true about keratosis obturans?
options: Failure of migration of desquamated epithelium along posterior meatal wall
Widening of meatus and facial nerve palsy might be seen
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. All of the above

All of the above statements are true regarding keratosis obturans.

Keratosis obturans occurs due to failure of migration of desquamated epithelial cells along the posterior meatal wall (Option A).

It is usually seen between the ages of 5-20 years and is commonly unilateral. Clinical features include severe otalgia and difficulty in hearing. It is associated with systemic conditions like bronchiectasis and chronic sinusitis (Option C).

On otoscopic examination, there is a thickening of the tympanic membrane and a keratin plug appearing like a pearly white mass occluding the canal. The keratin that is shed from the entire circumference of the deep ear canal appears to have an onion skin arrangement. There is also hyperemia of canal skin, sometimes with ulcerations and granulations.

Sometimes, the extent of bone erosion is such that it leaves the facial nerve exposed to injury and subsequent paralysis (Option B). Extensive erosion of the bone can also result in automastoidectomy.

Treatment involves the removal of the plug by syringing or instrumentation. Any recurrence can be prevented with the use of keratolytic such as 2% salicylic acid.
questions.learning: All of the above All of the above statements are true regarding keratosis obturans. Keratosis obturans occurs due to failure of migration of desquamated epithelial cells along the posterior meatal wall (Option A).

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A child presents with recurrent upper respiratory tract infections (URTIs) and laboratory findings reveal absence of B cells, T cells, and NK cells, along with ADA deficiency. What is the most likely underlying immunodeficiency disorder responsible for these findings?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Severe combined immunodeficiency disorder

Adenosine deaminase deficiency causes accumulation of toxic purine metabolites leading to lymphocyte apoptosis.

This results in absence of B cells, T cells, and NK cells with severe combined immune dysfunction.

ADA deficiency

↓

↑ Deoxyadenosine → ↑ dATP

↓

Inhibition of ribonucleotide reductase

↓

↓ DNA synthesis

↓

Failure of lymphocyte development

↓

↓ T cells + ↓ B cells + ↓ NK cells

↓

Severe Combined Immunodeficiency (SCID)

Patients present early with recurrent, severe infections involving multiple systems.

Bruton disease lacks B cells only, DiGeorge has T-cell deficiency, and MPO deficiency does not cause combined lymphocyte loss.

| Disorder | Defect | B cells | T cells | NK cells

| -------- | ------ | ------- | ------- | --------

| Bruton's | BTK mutation |  ↓ | ✔️ Normal | ✔️ Normal

| MPO deficiency | Neutrophil enzyme | ✔️ Normal | ✔️ Normal | ✔️ Normal

| SCID (ADA) | Purine metabolism |  ↓ |  ↓ |  ↓

| DiGeorge | Thymic aplasia | ✔️ Normal |  ↓ | ✔️ Normal

| Type | Cells affected

| ---- | --------------

| ADA deficiency | ↓ T, ↓ B, ↓ NK

| IL-2R mutation | ↓ T, ↓ NK, normal B

| RAG mutation | ↓ T, ↓ B, normal NK

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 55-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with severe unilateral eye pain, headache, and blurred vision after watching a movie in a dark theatre. On examination, the eye is red, cornea is hazy, and pupil is mid-dilated and non-reactive. What is the first line of management?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Mannitol + Pilocarpine

Sudden eye pain and decreased vision after being in a dark environment (movie theater) suggests acute angle-closure glaucoma (AACG).

• Darkness → pupillary dilation (mid-dilated pupil)
• Leads to pupillary block → iris bows forward → angle closure
• Rapid rise in IOP

First-line management:

• Mannitol (IV): Rapidly lowers IOP by osmotic dehydration
• Pilocarpine: Causes miosis → opens angle by pulling iris away from trabecular meshwork

Why not others:

• Moxifloxacin: Antibiotic, no role
• Atropine: Causes mydriasis → worsens angle closure
• Lubricants: No role in IOP reduction

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Which of the following correctly identifies the storage medium used for preserving a corneal graft and the type of suture material shown in the image below?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. McCarey Kaufman medium; Nylon

Successful corneal transplantation (keratoplasty) requires proper donor cornea preservation and appropriate suture material for graft fixation.

Corneal preservation media: McCarey–Kaufman (MK) medium

• Short-term storage (≈ 48–96 hours) at 4°C
• Commonly used in eye banks (especially in resource-limited settings)

Suture material in keratoplasty: Nylon (10-0 monofilament)

• Non-absorbable
• Minimal tissue reaction
• Provides long-term tensile strength → ideal for corneal graft suturing

Why other options are incorrect:

• Vicryl: Absorbable → loses strength → not suitable for cornea
• Prolene: Non-absorbable but less commonly used than nylon in cornea
• Silk: Causes more tissue reaction → avoided in ocular surgery
questions.learning: McCarey Kaufman medium; Nylon Successful corneal transplantation (keratoplasty) requires proper donor cornea preservation and appropriate suture material for graft fixation.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: Which type of intracranial hemorrhage is most likely shown in the image below?
questions.explanation: A subdural hematoma occurs due to tearing of bridging veins, leading to accumulation of venous blood between the dura mater and arachnoid mater. On NCCT, it appears as a crescent-shaped hyperdensity that can cross suture lines, a key distinguishing feature. Why other options are incorrect: (A) Extradural hemorrhage: Shows a biconvex (lens-shaped) hyperdense lesion and does not cross suture lines. (B) Subarachnoid hemorrhage: Appears as diffuse hyperdensity in sulci and basal cisterns, not a localized crescent-shaped collection. (D) Intraparenchymal hemorrhage: Seen as a hyperdense lesion within brain tissue, often with surrounding edema. Thus, based on standard imaging features, the correct diagnosis is subdural hematoma
questions.learning: A subdural hematoma occurs due to tearing of bridging veins, leading to accumulation of venous blood between the dura mater and arachnoid mater. On NCCT, it appears as a crescent-shaped hyperdensity that can cross suture lines, a key distinguishing feature.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: When can a patient with dengue hemorrhagic shock be discharged?
options: No episode of fever for more than 24 hours with paracetamol
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. After the return of appetite

A patient with dengue hemorrhagic shock can be discharged after the return of appetite.

Criteria for the discharge of patients recovering from dengue:

• Absence of fever for at least 24 hours without the use of antipyretic drugs
• Platelet count >50,000/cu.mm
• Return of appetite
• Adequate urine output
• Visible clinical improvement
• Minimum of 2-3 days after recovery from shock
• No respiratory distress from pleural effusion or ascites
