questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Allelic exclusion during B-cell maturation is ensured by:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. V(D)J rearrangements

Allelic exclusion ensures that each B cell expresses a single antigen receptor specificity by allowing productive rearrangement of only one immunoglobulin heavy-chain allele and one light-chain allele.

• During B-cell development in the bone marrow, V(D)J recombination rearranges variable (V), diversity (D), and joining (J) gene segments.
• Once a functional Ig heavy chain is produced, further rearrangement of the other allele is inhibited, ensuring single antibody specificity.

Why not other options:

B) Alternative splicing: Produces different forms of Ig (IgM vs IgD) from the same transcript. Does not ensure single allele expression.

C) Alternative polyadenylation: Determines membrane-bound vs secreted antibody forms. Not related to allelic exclusion.

D) Somatic hypermutation: Occurs after antigen stimulation in germinal centers to increase antibody affinity. Not involved in initial allele selection.
questions.learning: V(D)J rearrangements Allelic exclusion ensures that each B cell expresses a single antigen receptor specificity by allowing productive rearrangement of only one immunoglobulin heavy-chain allele and one light-chain allele. • During B-cell development in…

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Apparent volume of distribution of a drug is very high (6L/kg). Which of the following is true regarding the distribution of that drug?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Sequestered in body tissues

In the present case, the volume of distribution of the drug is 6L/kg (420 L in a normal adult with reference weight 70kg) which is very high when compared to the total body water of 42L. Therefore, it can be implied that the drug is having high sequestration in tissues.

The apparent volume of distribution (Vd) is an imaginary volume throughout which the drug is distributed if the plasma concentration remains constant throughout.

Vd = Dose administered IV/ plasma concentration

The difference in the volume of distribution based on drug type:

• Low Vd

• Restricted to the intravascular compartment
• Seen in drugs with high molecular weight (e.g., heparin) or high protein binding (e.g., warfarin - 9.8L)

• Medium Vd

• Lipid insoluble drugs (e.g., gentamicin - 20L) do not enter the cells and are distributed in the extracellular fluid volume
• Small water-soluble molecules (e.g., ethanol - 42L) are distributed in the total body water

• High Vd

• Sequestered and accumulated in the tissues
• Small lipophilic molecules (e.g., chloroquine - 13000L)
questions.learning: Sequestered in body tissues — In the present case, the volume of distribution of the drug is 6L/kg (420 L in a normal adult with reference weight 70kg) which is very high when compared to the total body water of 42L.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A 60-year-old male came to the emergency department after sustaining a fall. X-Ray showed a fractured neck of the femur and was operated on for the same. On post-operative day 2, he experienced a sharp, severe, constant, burning pain over his right back. On examination, the lesion is as seen below. The area is tender to light touch with a rash over the area. What is the most appropriate treatment for this patient ?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Valacyclovir

This patient had a traumatic accident. He then developed burning pain followed by a rash localized on the right back unilaterally suggestive of herpes zoster.Oral valacyclovir is the most appropriate treatment in the given options.

Herpes zoster is due to varicella-zoster virus from the dorsal root ganglia of a sensory nerve following initial infection with varicella(chickenpox) during childhood. The risk of VZV reactivation is greatest in those with advanced age due to waning cell-mediated immunity. Recent trauma also increases risk due to traumatic sensory nerve stimulation.

It manifests as dermatomal pain (burning, throbbing, stabbing, pruritic) that precedes the rash by days or weeks followed by a unilateral dermatomal rash that begins as erythematous papules, grouped vesicles, and crusts within 7-10 days. The characteristic feature is cut-off at the mid-line. Mucous membranes within the affected dermatome are also involved. The lymph nodes are tender and enlarged.

Treatment involves starting oral aciclovir 800mg five times a day for 7-10 days or valacyclovir 1g t.i.d for 7 days when the patient presents with < 72hrs of rash.

The commonest and most intractable sequel of zoster is post‐herpetic neuralgia, generally defined as persistence or recurrence of pain more than a month after the onset of zoster, but better considered after 3 months.

Other Options:

* Option A: Oral amitryptiline, a tricyclic antidepressant is used to treat postherpetic neuralgia. It is not used in the acute phase of herpes zoster.

* Option B: Pain control is required however, the topical corticosteroid can lead to an increased risk of secondary bacterial infections.

* Option C : Muprocin is used for bacterial infections.
questions.learning: Valacyclovir — This patient had a traumatic accident. He then developed burning pain followed by a rash localized on the right back unilaterally suggestive of herpes zoster.Oral valacyclovir is the most appropriate treatment in the given options.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which of the following is not used in heart failure?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Trimetazidine

Trimetazidine is not used in heart failure.

Trimetazidine is a newer antianginal drug that is a pFOX inhibitor which partially inhibits the fatty acid oxidation pathway in the myocardium. This decreases the oxygen requirement of the heart.

Nesiritide (natriuretic peptide), sacubitril (neprilysin inhibitor) and metoprolol (beta-blocker) are used in the treatment of heart failure.
questions.learning: Trimetazidine Trimetazidine is not used in heart failure. Trimetazidine is a newer antianginal drug that is a pFOX inhibitor which partially inhibits the fatty acid oxidation pathway in the myocardium.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which of the following drugs has dual activity against hepatitis B and HIV both?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Tenofovir

Tenofovir is an acyclic nucleotide analog used in the treatment of hepatitis B and HIV.

The preferred first-line regimen for managing HIV-1 and hepatitis B co-infection is tenofovir + lamivudine + dolutegravir.

Tenofovir is an acyclic nucleotide analog that is used as first-line therapy for the treatment of chronic hepatitis B and lamivudine-resistant chronic hepatitis B. It is also a potent antiretroviral agent used in the treatment of HIV infection.

In patients with hepatitis B, tenofovir is more potent at suppressing HBV DNA and is active against both wild-type and lamivudine-resistant HBV. It is given as an oral once-daily dose of 300 mg for 48 weeks. Tenofovir therapy provides histologic improvement, reduction in fibrosis score, and regression of cirrhosis in patients. Side effects include acute renal failure and low blood phosphate levels.

Tenofovir, an Nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor (NRTI) is used to treat HIV by inhibiting the reverse transcriptase enzyme. It converts to tenofovir diphosphate in cells, competing with dATP to incorporate into viral DNA. This causes chain termination due to the absence of a 3'-hydroxyl group, halting viral DNA synthesis and reducing replication.

Other options :

Option B: Nevirapine is a non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor (NNRTI). Nevirapine PLUS twice-daily zidovudine is administered for six weeks, after which either nevirapine is given as a single drug or the same combination is continued for another 6 weeks in high-risk infants with mothers who are:

* HIV positive, not on ART

* Mother diagnosed with HIV 72 hours after delivery.

* On ART with viral load > 1000 copies/mL

* With unknown viral load, hasn't been on ART for >4 consecutive weeks.

Option C: Abacavir is a nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor (NRTI) approved for the treatment of HIV-1 infectionThe most serious adverse effect is a hypersensitivity syndrome characterized by fever, maculopapular rash, abdominal pain, gastrointestinal upset, malaise, and fatigue.

Option D: Enfuvirtide is an entry (fusion) inhibitor that binds to the transmembrane gp41 of HIV-1 and blocks its entry into the host cells. It is the only approved parenteral antiretroviral drug, and therefore, injection-site reactions like pain, erythema, induration, and nodules/cysts development are most frequently seen.
questions.learning: Tenofovir Tenofovir is an acyclic nucleotide analog used in the treatment of hepatitis B and HIV. The preferred first-line regimen for managing HIV-1 and hepatitis B co-infection is tenofovir + lamivudine + dolutegravir.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: The fundoscopy findings of a known case of HIV with low CD4 counts in shown below. What is the treatment of choice for this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Ganciclovir

The above image depicts "sauce and cheese" retinopathy, which is characteristic of cytomegalovirus (CMV) retinitis. Ganciclovir is the treatment of choice.

CMV retinitis is the most probable diagnosis as the patient is immunocompromised (transplant recipient) and the fundoscopy shows patchy areas of retinal necrosis with irregular borders and overlying retinal hemorrhages.

CMV retinitis is mainly of 2 types

Central CMV retinitis

* Dense, white areas of retinal necrosis

* Retinal hemorrhage in the areas of necrosis

* Pizza pie or sauce and cheese appearance

Peripheral CMV retinitis

* Less demarcated

* Infection spreads along the vascular arcades in a brush fire-like fashion.

The serological assay is not informative in the case of the immunocompromised patient and PCR assay is the gold standard for diagnosis.
CMV mostly causes infection in immunocompromised patients such as transplant recipients and AIDS. The most common infections are interstitial pneumonitis, gastroenteritis, esophagitis, and retinitis. Apart from ganciclovir, valganciclovir, foscarnet, and cidofovir are approved for treatment of CMV retinitis in patients with AIDS.
questions.learning: Ganciclovir — The above image depicts "sauce and cheese" retinopathy, which is characteristic of cytomegalovirus (CMV) retinitis. Ganciclovir is the treatment of choice.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Identify the image representing the National Leprosy eradication program:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 2

The given image 2 represents the National Leprosy Eradication Programme (NLEP).

Characteristics of the NLEP emblem:

• The lotus in the NLEP emblem symbolizes beauty and purity.
• A partially affected thumb, a normal forefinger, and the shape of a house symbolize that leprosy can be cured and that a patient with leprosy can be a useful member of society.
• The rising sun symbolizes hope and optimism.
• The emblem captures the spirit of hope and positivity in the eradication of leprosy.

NLEP is a centrally sponsored health scheme of the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, Government of India.

Other options:

Option A: Poshan Abhiyaan: It aims to enhance key nutritional indicators for both children and women.

Option C: National Health Mission: It is a public health initiative focused on ensuring universal access to affordable, equitable, and high-quality healthcare services.

Option D: Ayushman Bharat: It provides nationwide medical coverage and cashless hospitalization benefits for enrolled families in both public and private hospitals.

The given image shows the correct logos for these programs

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text:
India is a country with different cultures and diverse languages. Which of the following steps should a physician take to address the patient for better outcomes?

1. Insist on good communication

2. Insist on communication only via an interpreter

3. Treat them regardless of their cultural perceptions

4. The physician should consider the patient's religion and cultural perception.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 1, 4

The physician should have good communication and consider the patient's religious, and cultural perceptions for better outcomes (statements 1 and 4 are correct).

Statement 1 is true since the proper usage of vocabulary that is easy for the patient to understand is essential for the patient. The doctor should clarify the patient's interpretation of the words used. Thus insisting on good communication is essential for better health outcomes.

Statement 2 is not true. An interpreter is needed if the patient is not a native speaker of the language spoken in that region. The interpreter can be a family member above the age of 16 or an independent interpreter. Communication gets affected with open-ended questioning getting lost in the double translation. The answer returned might not be adequate for the doctor and the consultation as such becomes longer than usual. The doctor will have to change to a more direct style of questioning to prevent any misunderstanding.

Statement 3 is not true while statement 4 is true. Personality, culture, and beliefs are important in creating trust between the doctor and patient and are an important component in the medical interview for a better outcome. The doctor must listen to the patients' concerns, and preferences.

Health communication may fail if the message is not adequate. A good message should have the following:

• It should be in line with the objective
• It needs to be meaningful
• Based on the felt needs
• Clear and understandable
• Specific and accurate
• Culturally and socially appropriate.
questions.learning: 1, 4 The physician should have good communication and consider the patient's religious, and cultural perceptions for better outcomes (statements 1 and 4 are correct).

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 2-year-old child was eating peanuts when he suddenly developed respiratory distress, cough, and was unable to speak. What is the initial treatment for this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Perform Heimlich maneuver

In a choking child (more than 1 year old) or an adult, the first step to be done is to perform Heimlich maneuver, which involves delivering abdominal thrusts.

The rescuer should stand or kneel behind the patient and wrap his arms around the patient’s waist. A fist is made with one hand and using the other hand, the fist is driven into the patient’s abdomen with a rapid, forceful upward thrust so as to dislodge the foreign body. This is continued until the foreign body is expelled or if the patient becomes unresponsive.

If the patient becomes unresponsive, immediately start CPR.

In a choking infant who is responsive, 5 back slaps between the shoulder blades and 5 downward thrusts on the chest are given in order to dislodge the foreign body.

If the patient becomes unresponsive, immediately start CPR.

Other Options:

Option A: The blind finger sweep should be avoided in infants to avoid pushing the object further inside the airway. However, it can be done for unresponsive adults with complete FBAO. With the patient's face up, the mouth is opened by grasping both the tongue and lower jaw and lifting the mandible. The index finger is inserted along the inside of the cheek and using a hooking action, the foreign body is dislodged and removed.

Option B: Endoscopic removal is wrong as an initial treatment because it's not an immediate life-saving measure and requires time to set up and organize. It can be attempted once the airway is stabilized.

Option C: Immediate X-ray is wrong as initial treatment because it delays essential life-saving intervention. Not all foreign bodies are radio-opaque (especially peanuts) and the patient needs immediate intervention for respiratory distress.
questions.learning: Perform Heimlich maneuver — In a choking child (more than 1 year old) or an adult, the first step to be done is to perform Heimlich maneuver, which involves delivering abdominal thrusts.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: In which of the following conditions is the Dystrophin protein completely absent?
questions.explanation: Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy (DMD) is an X-linked recessive disorder caused by a frameshift mutation in the DMD gene. This results in a complete absence of the protein dystrophin (Option B). Dystrophin is essential for maintaining the structural integrity of the muscle fiber's sarcolemma; its absence leads to progressive muscle necrosis and weakness. In Becker's Muscular Dystrophy (Option A), the mutation allows for the production of a truncated, partially functional dystrophin protein, resulting in a milder phenotype. Myasthenia gravis (Option C) and Lambert-Eaton syndrome (Option D) are autoimmune disorders affecting the neuromuscular junction (acetylcholine receptors or calcium channels) and do not involve dystrophin defects. Therefore, the absolute lack of this critical structural protein is pathognomonic specifically for Duchenne's. This leads to the characteristic clinical findings of pseudohypertrophy and Gowers' sign in young boys
questions.learning: Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy (DMD) is an X-linked recessive disorder caused by a frameshift mutation in the DMD gene. This results in a complete absence of the protein dystrophin (Option B).

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which of the following opportunistic systemic mycoses is characterized by rapid development of severe tissue necrosis and emerged as a specific complication associated with COVID-19 infection in India?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Mucormycosis

Mucormycosis is an opportunistic invasive fungal infection caused by fungi belonging to the order Mucorales (most commonly Rhizopus arrhizus/oryzae). It is characterized by angioinvasion, leading to vascular thrombosis, tissue ischemia, and rapidly progressive tissue necrosis. During the COVID-19 pandemic, India witnessed a large surge in COVID-19-associated mucormycosis (CAM), particularly in patients with uncontrolled diabetes and corticosteroid use.

Why not the other options?

• A. Histoplasmosis ✗: Caused by Histoplasma capsulatum; acquired by inhalation of spores from bird/bat droppings; does not typically cause rapidly progressive tissue necrosis.
• C. Coccidioidomycosis ✗: A dimorphic fungal infection endemic to the southwestern United States; not associated with COVID-19-related outbreaks in India.
• D. Sporotrichosis ✗: A subcutaneous fungal infection acquired by traumatic inoculation (e.g., rose thorn injury).
questions.learning: Mucormycosis Mucormycosis is an opportunistic invasive fungal infection caused by fungi belonging to the order Mucorales (most commonly Rhizopus arrhizus/oryzae).

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: What is the surgery done to widen the cartilaginous part of the external auditory canal called?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Meatoplasty

The surgery done to widen the cartilaginous part of the external auditory canal is meatoplasty.

Meatoplasty is a surgical procedure that involves the removal of a crescent-shaped portion of conchal cartilage to widen the external auditory meatus. It is performed in combination with all canal wall-down procedures like modified radical and radical mastoidectomies, for easy access to the mastoid cavity for periodic inspection and cleaning.

It is also done as an isolated procedure in elderly people with sagging auricles. A sagging auricle causes obstruction to the meatus leading to the retention of wax and difficulty in hearing.

Other options:

Option B: Tympanoplasty is the surgical reconstruction to correct damage in the middle ear and restore the integrity of the tympanic membrane for improved hearing. It is ossicular reconstruction only or ossicular reconstruction with myringoplasty.

Option C: Myringoplasty refers to the reconstruction of the tympanic membrane only.

Option D: Otoplasty is the correction of external ear/deformities of the pinna.
questions.learning: Meatoplasty — The surgery done to widen the cartilaginous part of the external auditory canal is meatoplasty. Meatoplasty is a surgical procedure that involves the removal of a crescent-shaped portion of conchal cartilage to widen the external auditory meatus.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which of the following is an opsonin?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. C3b

C3b functions as an opsonin.

Opsonization is the process of coating a foreign particle and preparing it for phagocytosis. The substances involved in this process are called opsonins and include:

• Mannose-binding lectin
• C3b, C4b, C5b
• IgM and Fc receptor of IgG
• CRP
• Fibrinogen

Elie Metchnikoff was the first person to describe the process of phagocytosis, and is hence known as the Father of Innate Immunity.
questions.learning: Opsonization is the process of coating a foreign particle and preparing it for phagocytosis. The substances involved in this process are called opsonins and include: • Mannose-binding lectin • C3b, C4b, C5b • IgM and Fc receptor of IgG • CRP • Fibrinogen…

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which enzyme is deficient in Von Gierke's disease?
questions.explanation: Von Gierke's disease, also known as Glycogen Storage Disease Type I (GSD I), is the most common form of GSD . it is caused by a deficiency of the enzyme glucose-6-phosphatase (Option D). This enzyme is critical because it catalyzes the final step of both glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis, converting glucose-6-phosphate into free glucose in the liver and kidneys. Without it, glucose cannot be released into the bloodstream, leading to severe fasting hypoglycemia, hepatomegaly (due to glycogen accumulation), hyperuricemia, and lactic acidosis. Liver glycogen phosphorylase deficiency (Option A) causes GSD Type VI (Hers disease). Muscle glycogen phosphorylase deficiency (Option B) causes GSD Type V (McArdle disease). Glycogen debranching enzyme deficiency (Option C) results in GSD Type III (Cori disease). Therefore, the absence of glucose-6-phosphatase is the biochemical hallmark that distinguishes Von Gierke's from other glycogen storage disorders
questions.learning: Von Gierke's disease, also known as Glycogen Storage Disease Type I (GSD I), is the most common form of GSD . it is caused by a deficiency of the enzyme glucose-6-phosphatase (Option D).

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A healthcare worker sustains a needle-stick injury from a syringe used on a confirmed HIV-positive patient. To definitively determine whether she has acquired HIV infection, which diagnostic test should be used?
questions.explanation: Western blot is the gold standard confirmatory test for definitive diagnosis of HIV infection. It detects specific antibodies against individual HIV proteins (gp120, gp41, p24), and a positive result definitively confirms HIV infection. It is used as a confirmatory test after a reactive ELISA result. Why other options are wrong: (A) p24 antigen is incorrect because p24 antigen detection is useful during the early window period before antibody development. It is a marker of early/acute infection but is not used as a definitive confirmatory diagnostic test for established HIV infection. (B) PCR is incorrect because although PCR detects HIV RNA/DNA with high sensitivity and is useful in window period and infants, it is not the standard definitive confirmatory test used in routine clinical practice for diagnosing HIV infection following needle-stick injury. (C) HIV ELISA is incorrect because ELISA is a screening test, not confirmatory. It has high sensitivity but lower specificity, meaning false positives can occur. It always requires confirmation by Western blot before definitive diagnosis is established
questions.learning: Western blot is the gold standard confirmatory test for definitive diagnosis of HIV infection. It detects specific antibodies against individual HIV proteins (gp120, gp41, p24), and a positive result definitively confirms HIV infection.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A male child with coarse facies, macroglossia, thick lips with hepatosplenomegaly presents with copious mucous discharge from the nose. The most probable underlying diagnosis is ________
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Hurler disease

The given clinical scenario of a child with coarse facies, macroglossia, thick lips, hepatosplenomegaly, and copious discharge from the nose is suggestive of Hurler's disease.

It is the severe form of mucopolysaccharidoses type 1 (MPS 1), an autosomal recessive disorder caused by a defect in α-L iduronidase, leading to the accumulation of heparan sulfate and dermatan sulfate. The child usually presents between 6 and 24 months with hepatosplenomegaly, coarse facial features (shown below), corneal clouding, large tongue, prominent forehead, joint stiffness, short stature, and skeletal dysplasia.

Most patients have recurrent upper respiratory tract and ear infections, noisy breathing, and persistent copious nasal discharge. Radiograph shows skeletal dysplasia, called dysostosis multiplex - thick ribs, ovoid vertebral bodies, enlarged and trabeculated diaphyses of the long bones with irregular metaphysis and epiphysis.

Macrocephaly, enlarged J-shaped sella, premature closure of lambdoid sagittal sutures, and shallow orbits are seen with disease progression. Obstructive airway disease, cardiac complications, and respiratory infections are the common causes of death.

The image below shows the radiograph shows enlarged diaphyses of the metacarpal and phalanges.

Other options:

Option B: Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome is an overgrowth syndrome characterized by macrosomia, macroglossia, hemihypertrophy, omphalocele, and renal anomalies. It is associated with an increased risk of Wilms tumor, hepatoblastoma, rhabdomyosarcoma, neuroblastoma, and adrenal cortical carcinoma.

Option C: Proteus syndrome is a disturbance of cellular growth involving ectodermal and mesodermal tissues, caused by mutation in the AKT1 gene. They present with hemimegalencephaly, asymmetric overgrowth of the extremities, verrucous cutaneous lesions, thickening of the bone, and excessive growth of muscles.

Option D: A child with untreated congenital hypothyroidism may have stunted growth, short extremities, narrow palpebral fissures, swollen eyelids, depressed nasal bridge, thick broad protruded tongue, and short and thick neck, dry and scaly skin.
questions.learning: Hurler disease — The given clinical scenario of a child with coarse facies, macroglossia, thick lips, hepatosplenomegaly, and copious discharge from the nose is suggestive of Hurler's disease.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Injury of the lower brachial plexus leads to Klumpke's paralysis. What is the characteristic clinical finding seen in this lesion?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Claw hand

The characteristic clinical finding in Klumpke's paralysis is a complete claw hand.

Klumpke's paralysis is caused by injury of the lower trunk of the brachial plexus-mainly T1 and partially C8, due to traction injury of the lower trunk that may be seen in undue abduction of the arm (outstretched arm grabbing an object during a fall from height) or birth injury (traction of the extended arm during delivery)

This leads to paralysis of the intrinsic muscles of the hand (T1) that are responsible for flexion at metacarpophalangeal joints (MCP) and extension at proximal and distal interphalangeal joints(PIP and DIP). The unopposed action of extensor digitorum at MCP causes hyperextension. The unopposed action of flexor digitorum superficialis and profundus at PIP and DIP causes flexion. Thus giving rise to the characteristic claw hand.

Other changes include anesthesia and analgesia along the ulnar border of the forearm, vasomotor changes, absence of sweating, and trophic changes in long-standing cases. If the C8 is also damaged, the extent of anesthesia will be greater and will involve the medial side of the forearm, hand, and medial two fingers.

Horner's syndrome (option D) may occur in one-third of the cases due to injury of sympathetic fibers to the head and neck that leave the spinal cord through nerve T1.

The following image shows a complete claw hand in Klumpke's paralysis:

Other options:

Option A: Policeman tip deformity, also known as waiter's tip hand or porter's tip hand, is a finding of Erb's palsy due to injury of the upper trunk of the brachial plexus involving C5 and C6. The hand is adducted, medially rotated, and hangs by the side with the elbow extended and pronated.

The following image shows policeman tip deformity in Erb's palsy:

Option B: Wrist drop is a feature of radial nerve injury in the axilla, radial groove, anterolateral side of the lower arm, or injury of the deep branch in the cubital fossa.

Option D: Horner's syndrome is caused due to the disruption of sympathetic supply to the face. It causes ptosis, miosis, anhydrosis, enophthalmos, and loss of ciliospinal reflex of the affected eye. It may occur in some cases of Klumpke's paralysis and is not a characteristic finding.

The following image shows the ocular manifestation of Horner syndrome:

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A 28-yr old man has recently finished a half- marathon. He complains of pain along the anterior and medial aspect of the tibia which increases on jogging & walking for a long time. Plain X-Ray radiograph of the leg was found to be normal. What is the probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Shin splint

The given clinical scenario, with a history of lower limb overuse (marathon running) and pain along the medial tibial border which increases with activity (jogging and long walks), along with a normal radiograph, suggests medial tibial stress syndrome (MTSS), also known as shin splints.

MTSS is a stress injury of the tibia which occurs due to the frequent overuse of lower limbs. It is commonly seen in athletes and military personnel.

Exercise-induced pain along the distal two-thirds of the medial tibial border is typical. Since it is a stress injury, the radiograph of the leg appears normal.

Management is mainly conservative with rest and activity modification with less repetitive and load-bearing exercises.
questions.learning: Shin splint — The given clinical scenario, with a history of lower limb overuse (marathon running) and pain along the medial tibial border which increases with activity (jogging and long walks), along with a normal radiograph, suggests medial tibial stress…

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Deficiency of which enzyme leads to the development of Maple Syrup Urine Disease (MSUD)?
questions.explanation: Maple Syrup Urine Disease (MSUD) is an autosomal recessive metabolic disorder caused by a deficiency in the branched-chain alpha-ketoacid dehydrogenase (BCKAD) complex. This enzyme complex is responsible for the oxidative decarboxylation of the ketoacids derived from the three branched-chain amino acids (BCAAs): Leucine, Isoleucine, and Valine. A defect here leads to the accumulation of these BCAAs and their toxic alpha-ketoacid byproducts, which impart a characteristic sweet, maple syrup odor to the patient's urine and earwax. Isovaleryl CoA dehydrogenase deficiency (Option B) causes Isovaleric Acidemia, which presents with a "sweaty feet" odor. Pyruvate carboxylase (Option C) and Acetyl CoA carboxylase (Option D) are involved in gluconeogenesis and fatty acid synthesis, respectively, and are not related to BCAA metabolism. MSUD is a pediatric emergency; if untreated, the leucine accumulation causes severe cerebral edema and neurological damage. Treatment involves a strict life-long diet restricted in BCAAs and specialized medical formulas
questions.learning: Maple Syrup Urine Disease (MSUD) is an autosomal recessive metabolic disorder caused by a deficiency in the branched-chain alpha-ketoacid dehydrogenase (BCKAD) complex.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: In rural areas, one ASHA worker is assigned to serve a population of how many individuals?
questions.explanation: Under the National Health Mission (NHM) of India, the ASHA (Accredited Social Health Activist) is a trained female community health volunteer. The standard norm is to have one ASHA worker per 1,000 population in rural areas. In tribal, hilly, or desert areas with sparse populations, this norm may be relaxed to one ASHA per habitation or a smaller population group. The ASHA acts as a bridge between the community and the public health system, promoting institutional deliveries, immunization, and basic first aid. Other rural health norms include one Sub-centre per 5,000 people (3,000 in difficult areas) and one Primary Health Centre (PHC) per 30,000 people (20,000 in difficult areas). Options A, B, and C do not represent the standard population allocation for an ASHA. Because 1,000 is the national standard for her coverage area, it is the correct answer for public health management questions
questions.learning: Under the National Health Mission (NHM) of India, the ASHA (Accredited Social Health Activist) is a trained female community health volunteer. The standard norm is to have one ASHA worker per 1,000 population in rural areas.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: All of the following statements are true about a PHC except
options: There is 1 PHC per 30,000 population in plain areas
Type A PHC conducts < 20 deliveries per month.
Provides maternal and child health care, family planning and MTP
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Is the first referral unit

A PHC is not a first referral unit (FRU). FRUs are centres that provide round-the-clock services for emergency obstetric and newborn care and manage emergencies that any well-equipped hospital is required to provide. CHCs, district hospitals, sub-divisional hospitals, etc. are FRUs.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A boy born to a normal father and mother had Hemophilia. Detailed history taking revealed that the mother's side had a family history of similar affected individuals. The children born to this boy are likely to have which of the following (provided mother is unaffected)?
options: All boys and girl children equally affected
50% boys affected and no girl children unaffected
No boy affected and all girl children are carrier
25% boy affected and 25% girl children are carrier
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. No boy affected and all girl children are carrier

• Hemophilia is an X-linked recessive disorder affecting males who inherit the mutant X chromosome.
• An affected male transmits his X chromosome to all daughters and Y chromosome to all sons.
• Hence, none of the sons are affected as they receive the father’s Y chromosome.
• All daughters receive the mutant X, making 100% daughters carriers; effectively, 50% of total children are carrier females.

Genotype setup:

• Affected male (boy): XʰY
• Assume wife is normal: XᴴXᴴ

Punnett Square:

Mother

Xᴴ      Xᴴ

Father Xʰ  XᴴXʰ   XᴴXʰ

Y    XᴴY    XᴴY

Interpretation:

• Daughters (XᴴXʰ) → All are carriers (100%)
• Sons (XᴴY) → All are normal (0% affected)

Final conclusion:

• No male child affected
• All female children are carriers

questions.text: A woman who has just delivered a full-term baby vaginally suddenly develops profuse postpartum hemorrhage associated with severe lower abdominal pain. She becomes hypotensive and tachycardic. On examination, the uterine fundus is not palpable abdominally, and a fleshy mass is felt protruding through the vagina with the placenta still attached. What is the immediate next step?
options: Remove placenta and reposition the uterus
Put uterus inside without removing the placenta
Shift to OT and insert the uterus back
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Put uterus inside without removing the placenta

These findings are classic for Uterine Inversion. Uterine inversion occurs when the uterine fundus collapses inward and turns inside out, sometimes protruding through the cervix or vagina.

Major causes

| ----- | ---------

| Excess traction on umbilical cord | Pulls fundus downward

| Fundal pressure | Forces uterus inward

| Placenta attached at fundus | Facilitates inversion

The first step is immediate manual repositioning of the uterus- Johnson maneuver

Uterine inversion

↓

Do NOT remove placenta

↓

Immediate manual repositioning

↓

Placenta removed after uterus replaced

Removing the placenta before repositioning may:

• Increase hemorrhage
• Worsen uterine inversion

C) Shift to OT first

Immediate bedside repositioning is required because delay increases mortality.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 60-year-old woman who underwent a renal transplant two months earlier now presents with high-grade fever, severe breathlessness, and a dry, hacking cough. Chest radiography shows diffuse bilateral interstitial infiltrates, and urine microscopy reveals cells with an “owl- eye” appearance. Which infectious agent is most likely responsible for her condition?
questions.explanation: In immunocompromised patients, particularly those who have recently undergone an organ transplant, Cytomegalovirus (CMV) is a leading cause of opportunistic infection. CMV pneumonia classically presents with high fever, hacking cough, and interstitial lung infiltrates. The pathognomonic finding described—cells with an "owl-eye" appearance—refers to large cells containing large, dark, basophilic intranuclear inclusion bodies surrounded by a clear halo. This is the hallmark histological feature of CMV. Adenovirus (Option A) can cause respiratory infections but shows different inclusion patterns. Influenza (Option C) and RSV (Option D) are common viral causes of pneumonia but do not produce the characteristic "owl-eye" nuclear inclusions. CMV remains the most significant viral pathogen in the transplant population, and its identification is critical for initiating antiviral therapy like ganciclovir. Therefore, Cytomegalovirus is the correct causative agent
questions.learning: In immunocompromised patients, particularly those who have recently undergone an organ transplant, Cytomegalovirus (CMV) is a leading cause of opportunistic infection.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: The test kit shown in the image below works on the principle of:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Immunochromatography

The above image shows a HbsAg card test kit which works on the principle of immunochromatography.

In immunochromatography, a nitrocellulose membrane is used to absorb the antigen from a specimen. The membrane is impregnated with anti-HBsAg antibody and colloidal gold dye. The specimen (serum) travels through the membrane by capillary action. If the serum contains HBaAg, a coloured reaction (in the form of a band) appears directly on the membrane at the test site. These assays are rapid and include a built-in internal control.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient presents with joint pain, fatigue, and abnormal liver function tests. Genetic testing is performed due to these symptoms and a relevant family history. Which gene mutation is most commonly associated with hemochromatosis?
questions.explanation: Hereditary Hemochromatosis is an autosomal recessive iron-overload disorder. It results from a mutation in the HFE gene (most commonly the C282Y mutation), which leads to excessive intestinal iron absorption. This excess iron is deposited in organs, particularly the liver, heart, and joints, causing the described symptoms of fatigue, joint pain (arthropathy), and liver dysfunction (cirrhosis). PTEN (Option B) is a tumor suppressor gene associated with Cowden syndrome and various cancers. The ATP7B gene (Option C) mutation is responsible for Wilson's disease, which involves copper overload. The MRP2 protein (Option D) is involved in bilirubin transport and is defective in Dubin-Johnson syndrome. Therefore, the HFE gene is the definitive genetic marker for hereditary hemochromatosis. Early diagnosis is critical, as the condition can be effectively managed with regular therapeutic phlebotomy to prevent permanent organ damage
questions.learning: Hereditary Hemochromatosis is an autosomal recessive iron-overload disorder. It results from a mutation in the HFE gene (most commonly the C282Y mutation), which leads to excessive intestinal iron absorption.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A female patient presents with complaints of pain over the anterolateral aspect of thigh after normal vaginal delivery. Which is the nerve injured in this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Lateral cutaneous nerve

The given clinical scenario of a patient with symptoms of pain over the anterolateral aspect of the thigh is suggestive of meralgia paresthetica. It is due to compression neuropathy or neuroma of the lateral femoral cutaneous nerve of the thigh.

The lateral cutaneous nerve of the thigh arises from the posterior divisions of the ventral rami of L2 and L3, and it supplies the skin of the anterior and lateral surfaces of the thigh up to the knee.

It is prone to injury especially as it leaves the pelvis deep to the inguinal ligament just medial to the anterior superior iliac spine. The angulation of the nerve as it crosses the iliac crest makes it vulnerable to compression during hip extension which may increase angulation and tension on the nerve. This leads to impaired sensation, pain and paraesthesia on the anterolateral aspect of thigh, in the distal end of the cutaneous distribution of this nerve. The symptoms don't cross the midline, nor extend below knee or behind hamstrings laterally

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: An alcoholic patient presented with itchy lesions as shown in the image, He also has a red-colored beefy tongue. Which of the following histories would you like to additionally ask/ elicit in this patient?
options: Ask for diarrhea and history of memory loss
Ask for diarrhea, thiamine deficiency features, and detailed dietary history
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Ask for diarrhea and history of memory loss

An alcoholic patient with a red-colored beefy tongue, itching and the characteristic Casal's necklace, shown in the image, is suggestive of pellagra. It is caused by niacin/vitamin B3 deficiency. Hence, one should ask for a history of diarrhea and memory loss in this case.

Pellagra presents with 4 Ds: Diarrhea, Dermatitis, Dementia, and if untreated, Death. Early symptoms of pellagra are loss of appetite, generalized weakness and irritability, abdominal pain, and vomiting. Photosensitive dermatitis is seen over sun-exposed areas. Diarrhea occurs due to proctitis or malabsorption. Bright red glossitis (beefy tongue) and Casal’s necklace (a pigmented, scaly skin rash that forms a ring around the neck) follow. Depressive psychosis and dementia also commonly occur.

Corn/ maize/ jowar based diets are the main causes of niacin deficiency. Corn/maize lacks niacin and tryptophan. The excess leucine in jowar and maize disrupts the conversion of tryptophan to niacin. Niacin deficiency is also seen in alcoholism. Hence, additional histories of diarrhea and memory loss will aid in supporting the diagnosis of pellagra (along with dietary history).

Treatment includes oral supplementation with 100–200 mg of nicotinamide or nicotinic acid three times daily for 5 days.

Option B: Thiamine deficiency (vitamin B1) features include CVS manifestations like heart failure and edema (wet beriberi), peripheral neuritis (dry beriberi), and Wernicke encephalopathy (in alcoholics).

Option C: Dermatitis seen in pellagra is due to dietary deficiency of niacin and so allergy history is not relevant.

Option D: Conjunctivitis is not a feature of niacin deficiency.
questions.learning: Ask for diarrhea and history of memory loss — An alcoholic patient with a red-colored beefy tongue, itching and the characteristic Casal's necklace, shown in the image, is suggestive of pellagra.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Revised Which of the following is not a component of qSOFA score?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. LDH- Lactate dehydrogenase

Lactate dehydrogenase is not a component of the qSOFA score.

qSOFA scoring is a simplified derivative of SOFA for bedside assessment that is particularly useful outside the ICU setting as it does not require laboratory values.

The qSOFA assigns one point for each component and suggests potentially life-threatening sepsis when at least two of the following parameters are met.

* Altered mental status (GCS <15)

* Systolic blood pressure ≤ 100 mmHg

* Respiratory rate ≥ 22 breaths/min.

A qSOFA score of ≥2 is associated with a significant risk of death or prolonged ICU stay.

SOFA is a more comprehensive and accurate scoring system which is particularly superior to qSOFA in the ICU setting. This includes:

* Circulation - Systolic BP & need for vasopressors and platelet count

* Respiration - PaO2/FiO2 & need for mechanical ventilation

* Mentation - Glasgow coma score

* Hepatic function - Bilirubin

* Renal function - Creatinine

Organ dysfunction is identified by a SOFA score of ≥ 2
questions.learning: LDH- Lactate dehydrogenase Lactate dehydrogenase is not a component of the qSOFA score. qSOFA scoring is a simplified derivative of SOFA for bedside assessment that is particularly useful outside the ICU setting as it does not require laboratory values.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: What is the ideal thickness of lead aprons for personnel working in a radiology department?
questions.explanation: In the field of radiation protection, the goal is to reduce occupational exposure as much as possible (ALARA principle). For the majority of diagnostic radiology workers, a lead apron with a thickness of 0.5 mm lead equivalent is considered the ideal standard. This thickness provides an excellent balance between radiation attenuation and the physical comfort of the wearer; a 0.5 mm apron can block approximately 95–99% of the scattered X-ray radiation encountered in typical diagnostic settings. While a 1 mm apron (Option B) would provide even higher protection, it is significantly heavier and can cause orthopedic issues with prolonged use. 0.75 mm (Option C) and 2 mm (Option D) are not standard requirements for general diagnostic work. Proper storage (hanging rather than folding) is also essential to prevent the lead from cracking. Consistent use of these personal protective devices, along with thyroid shields and lead glasses, is mandatory for ensuring the long-term safety of radiology personnel
questions.learning: In the field of radiation protection, the goal is to reduce occupational exposure as much as possible (ALARA principle). For the majority of diagnostic radiology workers, a lead apron with a thickness of 0.5 mm lead equivalent is considered the ideal standard.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: The diagram below shows the pressure-volume curves for 3 different lungs. Which of the following is the best representation of compliance between the three lungs?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. B>A>C

• The pressure-volume relationship is the fundamental relation between the work of breathing and lung mechanics.
• The diagram depicts the change in volume with respect to the change in intrapleural pressure, which is compliance. Here, the change is more (steep curve) with B and least (flat curve) with C.
• The “stiffer” lung displays a more horizontal curve (C), meaning that it takes a greater pressure to achieve the same inflation volume compared with a normal lung (A). These lungs are called less compliant.
• Curve (B) is more compliant as it takes lesser pressure to achieve the same inflation volume compared to normal (A).

Applied aspect:

Compliance is increased in emphysema. The mechanism is shown in the flow chart below.

Compliance is decreased in case of pulmonary edema or fibrosis.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Based on the image of the anal region showing a painful abscess commonly resulting from obstruction of an anal gland, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The provided image and clinical description identify a perianal abscess (Option C). This is the most common type of anorectal abscess, occurring when an anal crypt gland becomes blocked and subsequently infected. It presents as a very painful, red, and swollen lump immediately adjacent to the anal verge. Hemorrhoids (Option A) are swollen vascular cushions; while they can be painful if thrombosed, they do not present as an acute fluctuant abscess. A pelvirectal abscess (Option B) is deeper and more severe, often presenting with systemic symptoms and high-seated rectal pain rather than a visible external lump. A pilonidal sinus (Option D) occurs in the natal cleft between the buttocks, further away from the anus. The primary treatment for a perianal abscess is immediate incision and drainage. Over 50% of these cases may eventually develop a fistula-in-ano. Therefore, the visual evidence of a localized abscess confirms the diagnosis
questions.learning: The provided image and clinical description identify a perianal abscess (Option C). This is the most common type of anorectal abscess, occurring when an anal crypt gland becomes blocked and subsequently infected.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Which of the following methods is regarded as the gold standard for the measurement of intraocular pressure?
questions.explanation: The Goldmann Applanation Tonometer (GAT) is universally recognized as the gold standard for the measurement of intraocular pressure (IOP). It operates on the Imbert-Fick principle, which states that the pressure inside a sphere is equal to the force needed to flatten a fixed area of its surface. GAT is highly accurate and is the reference against which all other tonometers are calibrated. Option A (Gonioscope) is used to examine the drainage angle of the eye, not measure pressure. Option C (Hertel's) is used to measure the degree of proptosis (eyeball protrusion). Option D (Tonopen) is a portable handheld device useful for bedridden patients or irregular corneas but is not as accurate as GAT. GAT measurements can be influenced by central corneal thickness (CCT); therefore, clinicians often adjust readings based on pachymetry. Accurate IOP measurement is fundamental in the diagnosis and management of glaucoma to prevent irreversible optic nerve damage

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: In a patient, after administration of Noradrenaline injection, the heart rate started to decrease. What is the reason behind it?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Stimulation of baroreceptors

The decrease in heart rate (bradycardia) after noradrenaline (norepinephrine) injection is due to the stimulation of baroreceptors (baroreceptor reflex, also known as the baroreflex).

When noradrenaline is administered, it causes vasoconstriction via alpha-1 receptors, leading to an increase in blood pressure. This increase in blood pressure activates the baroreceptors in the carotid sinus and aortic arch, which through the baroreflex mechanism, leads to increased vagal tone and decreased sympathetic outflow to the heart, resulting in a compensatory decrease in heart rate (reflex bradycardia).

Baroreceptors are stretch receptors in the walls of the heart and blood vessels. Baroreceptors are stimulated by the stretching of the walls of the respective vessels when there is an increased volume or pressure in the vessel. They are important in the immediate management of blood pressure.

The afferents from the baroreceptors activate the Nucleus tractus solitarius (NTS) which in turn activates the caudal ventrolateral medulla (CVLM). The CVLM, on activation, releases gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA) which is inhibitory to the rostral ventrolateral medulla (RVLM). The RVLM is the major excitatory source of the sympathetic nervous system. As it is inhibited, there is sympathetic inhibition thus reducing the blood pressure.

The NTS also simultaneously activates the vagal motor neurons causing bradycardia.

Other options:

Option A: (Stimulation of alpha-2 receptors): While alpha-2 receptor stimulation can cause a decrease in sympathetic outflow, this is not the primary mechanism for the heart rate decrease seen with noradrenaline administration. Alpha-2 effects are more relevant for drugs like clonidine.

Option B: (Stimulation of beta-1 receptors): Beta-1 stimulation would actually cause an increase in heart rate (tachycardia), not a decrease. While noradrenaline does have some beta-1 activity, its alpha effects predominate.

Option D: (Inhibition of Baroreceptor): The baroreceptors are stimulated, not inhibited, by the increase in blood pressure. Inhibition of baroreceptors would actually lead to an increase in heart rate.

Pearl PF0543: Factors Affecting Heart Rate

Heart rate is accelerated by

• Decreased activity of arterial baroreceptors
• Increased activity of atrial stretch receptors
• Inspiration
• Excitement
• Anger
• Pain
• Hypoxia
• Exercise
• Thyroid hormones
• Fever

The Heart is slowed by

• Increased activity of arterial baroreceptors
• Expiration
• Grief
• Stimulation of pain fibers in trigeminal nerve
• Increased intracranial pressure
questions.learning: Stimulation of baroreceptors — The decrease in heart rate (bradycardia) after noradrenaline (norepinephrine) injection is due to the stimulation of baroreceptors (baroreceptor reflex, also known as the baroreflex).

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text:
A patient presents with dull aching pain in both legs. He gives a history of prolonged standing and tortuous veins in the legs. Which of the following tests are done for saphenofemoral incompetence?

1. Brodie Trendelenburg Test
2. Morrissey's test
3. Fegan's test
4. Modified Perthes test
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 1, 2

Brodie Trendelenburg test and Morrissey's test are performed to test the incompetence of the saphenofemoral valve. Fegan’s method is used to detect perforator incompetence while Modified Perthe’s test is a test for deep vein thrombosis (DVT).

Brodie Trendelenburg test - Lay the patient down and elevate the leg. Empty the vessels and tie a tourniquet below the SFJ. Ask the patient to stand up:

• Trendelenburg’s test part l - Here the tourniquet is released. A rapid filling from above shows saphenofemoral incompetence.
• Trendelenburg’s test part ll - Here the tourniquet is not released. A gradual filling from below to upwards indicates perforator incompetence.

Morrissey’s cough impulse test - The limb is elevated to empty the varicose veins. Now it is put to bed and the patient is asked to cough forcibly. An expansile cough impulse is felt at the saphenous opening if the saphenofemoral valve is incompetent. Similarly, a bruit may be heard on auscultation. The patient is asked to cough. A cough impulse at the saphenofemoral junction indicates SFJ incompetence.

Fegan’s method - Mark the places of excessive bulges within the varicosities. Ask the patient to lie down and empty the varicose vessels. Palpate along the marked area to look for gaps and pits in the deep fascia, which indicates perforator incompetence.

Modified Perthe’s test - A tourniquet is tied around the upper part of the thigh to prevent reflux down the vein and the patient is asked to walk around. In the presence of normal communicating and deep veins, the varicose veins will shrink. If there is any block, the veins will get more distended. An increase in pain and prominence of dilated veins indicate DVT.
questions.learning: 1, 2 Brodie Trendelenburg test and Morrissey's test are performed to test the incompetence of the saphenofemoral valve. Fegan’s method is used to detect perforator incompetence while Modified Perthe’s test is a test for deep vein thrombosis (DVT).

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: During an autopsy, what is commonly used to preserve blood?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. NaF

10 mg/ml of sodium or potassium fluoride and potassium oxalate (anti-coagulant) is used to preserve blood.

Other preservatives used in toxicology postmortem include:

* Saturated NaCl solution: Avoided in poisoning from corrosive acids, alkalis, corrosive sublimate, and aconite.

* Fluoride should be added to urine, CSF, and vitreous humor if alcohol estimation is required and if analysis for cocaine, cyanide, and CO is being done.

A preservative is not necessary if :

* The viscera can be analyzed in 24 hours

* If the sample can be stored in a refrigerator or icebox

* Bone, hair, nails specimens

* Lung for inhaled poisons

* The viscera should not be preserved in formaldehyde because extraction of non-volatile poisons becomes difficult.

In cases of chronic poisoning with heavy metals such as lead, arsenic, mercury, antimony, copper, etc., the shaft of a long bone, strands of scalp hair, fingernails or toenails, and a wedge of the quadriceps muscle should also be taken for sampling.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Consider the following pharmacological agents: 1. Liothyronine 2. Levothyroxine 3. Carbimazole 4. Sodium ipodate Which of the above may be included in the treatment of myxoedema coma?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 1 and 2

Myxedema coma is a life-threatening form of severe hypothyroidism. Treatment includes intravenous levothyroxine (T4), with or without liothyronine (T3), along with IV hydrocortisone (until adrenal insufficiency is excluded), supportive care, and correction of precipitating factors.

Why not the other options?

• 3. Carbimazole: Antithyroid drug used for hyperthyroidism; contraindicated in myxedema coma.
• 4. Sodium ipodate: Used historically in thyrotoxic crisis to inhibit T4→T3 conversion; has no role in myxedema coma.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: According to the WHO Medical Eligibility Criteria (MEC-1), in which of the following conditions can combined oral contraceptives (OCPs) be safely used?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. HIV

Combined Oral Contraceptive Pills contain:

• Estrogen (Ethinyl estradiol)
• Progestin (e.g., Levonorgestrel)

They are widely used for birth control and menstrual regulation.

Medical Eligibility Criteria (MEC) categorizes the safety of contraceptive methods based on underlying medical conditions. The MEC classification system has four categories:

●        MEC 1: Method is absolutely safe for use

●        MEC 2: Safe for use but has certain limitations (benefits outweigh risks)

●        MEC 3: Relatively contraindicated (risks outweigh benefits)

●        MEC 4: Absolutely contraindicated (method should not be given)

HIV infection without complications is classified as MEC 1 for combined oral contraceptive pills.

For HIV-positive women:

COCs are MEC-1 (safe to use).

Reasons:

• Do not worsen HIV disease progression
• Do not significantly increase viral replication

Diabetes Mellitus - Often MEC-2 or MEC-3, especially with vascular complications.

Hyperlipidemia - COCs may increase lipid levels, so usually MEC-2 or MEC-3.

Hypertension - Estrogen-containing pills may increase thrombotic risk, so classified as MEC-3 or MEC-4 depending on severity.

Benefits of COCs

| Benefit | Effect

| ------- | ------

| Regulates menstrual cycles | Reduces irregular bleeding

| Decreases dysmenorrhea | Less painful periods

| Reduces risk of ovarian cancer | Long-term protection

| Reduces risk of endometrial cancer | Endometrial suppression
questions.learning: HIV Combined Oral Contraceptive Pills contain: • Estrogen (Ethinyl estradiol) • Progestin (e.g., Levonorgestrel) They are widely used for birth control and menstrual regulation.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A patient presents with a fish bone lodged in the pyriform sinus. During attempted removal, which nerve is most at risk of injury?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Internal laryngeal nerve (ILN)

A fish bone in the pyriform sinus puts the internal laryngeal nerve (ILN) at risk during removal because it provides sensory innervation to the supraglottic larynx and pyriform fossa.

• Internal laryngeal nerve (branch of superior laryngeal nerve):

• Purely sensory above the vocal cords
• Supplies pyriform sinus, epiglottis, laryngeal inlet

• It pierces the thyrohyoid membrane → lies close to the pyriform fossa

• Injury leads to:

• Loss of protective cough reflex
• Risk of silent aspiration

Why not other options:

• External laryngeal nerve (ELN): Motor to cricothyroid, not in pyriform sinus
• Recurrent laryngeal nerve (RLN): Supplies below vocal cords, deeper course

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: How is the ApoB gene differentially processed in the liver and intestine such that ApoB-100 is synthesized in the liver, whereas ApoB-48 is produced in the intestine?
questions.explanation: The production of different forms of Apolipoprotein B (ApoB-100 and ApoB-48) from the same gene is a classic example of RNA editing. In the liver, the APOB mRNA is translated into the full-length ApoB-100 protein, which is essential for VLDL and LDL. However, in the intestine, a specific enzyme (cytidine deaminase) changes a single base in the mRNA (converting a Cytidine to a Uridine). This creates a premature stop codon (UAA), resulting in a truncated protein that is only 48% of the full length, known as ApoB-48. Gene splicing (Option B) involves removing introns. Alternative polyadenylation (Option C) changes the length of the 3' tail. Gene rearrangements (Option D) occur in immune cells for antibody diversity. RNA editing allows the body to produce tissue-specific proteins with distinct functional roles from a single genetic sequence. This mechanism is critical for lipid transport, as ApoB-48 is required specifically for the assembly and secretion of chylomicrons in the gut
questions.learning: The production of different forms of Apolipoprotein B (ApoB-100 and ApoB-48) from the same gene is a classic example of RNA editing. In the liver, the APOB mRNA is translated into the full-length ApoB-100 protein, which is essential for VLDL and LDL.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A pre-menopausal woman is diagnosed with lymph node-positive, early invasive breast cancer. IHC reveals ER +, PR +, and HER-2-neu 1+. Which of the following drug will you provide for this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Tamoxifen

The given clinical scenario suggests early invasive breast cancer in a pre-menopausal woman, which is lymph node-positive, hormone receptor-positive (ER/PR +), and Her-2/neu negative (Her-2/neu IHC score of 1+ is considered negative). Hence Tamoxifen is the drug of choice.

Treatment of early-stage breast cancer (T1-2 N0-1 M0) includes:

Breast conservation surgery (BCS) + ALND or SLNB + Radiotherapy

• BCS is followed by radiotherapy
• Mastectomy is done if BCS is contraindicated.
• Clinical N0 status-sentinel lymph node biopsy (SLNB) at the time of surgery.
• Clinical N1 status-ultrasound-guided fine-needle aspiration (FNA): axillary lymph node dissection (ALND) if positive and sentinel lymph node biopsy (SLNB) if negative.

Endocrine therapy: for hormone receptor (ER/PR) positive

• For Premenopausal women-tamoxifen (selective estrogen receptor modulator, SERM)
• For post-menopausal women (usually >50 years)-anastrozole (Aromatase inhibitor)
• Tamoxifen has an agonistic action on the endometrium, leading to an increased risk of endometrial cancers Hence, it is not used in post-menopausal women.

Anti-Her-2 therapy: for Her-2/neu positive breast cancer

• Trastuzumab is given
• Her-2/neu IHC interpretation:

•   0 or 1+ = Negative
•   2+ = Equivocal cases ->        confirmed with Fluorescence    in situ hybridization (FISH)      analysis
•   3+ = Positive

Chemotherapy

Indicated for:

• Lymph nodes positive
• Lymph nodes negative but tumor size of >1 cm
• Lymph nodes negative and tumor size of >0.5 cm with

• Blood vessel/Lymph vessel invasion
• ER/PR –ve
• Her-2/neu overexpression
• High grade

• Triple-negative breast carcinoma
• High recurrence score after Oncotype Dx

The table below shows the summary of the adjuvant treatment approach:

Tumor hormone receptor status (ER, PR)

Tumor HER status
Positive
Negative

Positive
Endocrine therapy + chemotherapy + trastuzumab
Chemotherapy + trastuzumab

Negative
Endocrine therapy ± chemotherapy
Chemotherapy
questions.learning: Tamoxifen — The given clinical scenario suggests early invasive breast cancer in a pre-menopausal woman, which is lymph node-positive, hormone receptor-positive (ER/PR +), and Her-2/neu negative (Her-2/neu IHC score of 1+ is considered negative).

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient with hypertension is found to have laboratory abnormalities including hypernatremia, hypokalemia, and metabolic alkalosis. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Conn’s syndrome (primary hyperaldosteronism) is the classic diagnosis for a hypertensive patient with hypernatremia, hypokalemia, and metabolic alkalosis. Excess aldosterone secretion, usually from an adrenal adenoma, leads to increased sodium reabsorption (causing hypertension and hypernatremia) and increased renal excretion of potassium and hydrogen ions. Addison’s disease (Option B) is the opposite; it presents with hypotension, hyponatremia, and hyperkalemia. Diabetes Insipidus (Option C) causes hypernatremia due to free water loss but is not associated with hypertension, hypokalemia, or metabolic alkalosis. Cushing’s disease (Option D) primarily involves excess cortisol; while it can cause hypertension, it does not typically present with this specific triad of electrolyte and acid-base disturbances unless there is very severe ectopic ACTH production. Therefore, primary aldosterone overproduction is the most probable physiological explanation for these laboratory findings
questions.learning: Conn’s syndrome (primary hyperaldosteronism) is the classic diagnosis for a hypertensive patient with hypernatremia, hypokalemia, and metabolic alkalosis.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 56-year-old woman, with a history of burn injury to her lower limb 5 years ago, now presents with an ulcer developing in the burn scar (as shown in the image). What is the most probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The development of a new ulcer within a long-standing, chronic burn scar (especially 5 years or more after the initial injury) is highly diagnostic for a Marjolin’s Ulcer. This is a type of aggressive squamous cell carcinoma that arises in areas of chronic inflammation or previous trauma. Venous ulcers (Option B) typically occur in the "gaiter area" above the medial malleolus and are associated with varicose veins. Arterial ulcers (Option C) occur on distal pressure points and are extremely painful. Cellulitis (Option D) is an acute bacterial skin infection and would not present as a chronic, non-healing ulcer in an old scar. Marjolin's ulcers are characterized by their rapid growth, everted edges, and a high risk of regional lymph node metastasis compared to standard skin cancers. The definitive diagnostic step is a wedge biopsy of the ulcer edge. Management requires wide surgical excision with adequate margins, often involving skin grafting or amputation depending on the location and depth of invasion
questions.learning: The development of a new ulcer within a long-standing, chronic burn scar (especially 5 years or more after the initial injury) is highly diagnostic for a Marjolin’s Ulcer.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: What is the most common indication for performing a Posterior Colpotomy? (NEET PG 2016)
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Drainage of Pelvic Abscess

Posterior colpotomy is a surgical incision made through the posterior vaginal fornix into the pouch of Douglas (rectouterine pouch). The most common indication is Drainage of pelvic abscess, especially tubo-ovarian or pelvic cul-de-sac abscesses

Advantages:

• Provides direct access to the pouch of Douglas
• Avoids abdominal incision
• Allows dependent drainage of pus or fluid collections

Other occasional uses:

• Culdocentesis
• Vaginal sterilization procedures
• Access during certain gynecologic surgeries

The posterior fornix lies closest to the rectouterine pouch, making it the safest vaginal route to access the peritoneal cavity.
questions.learning: Drainage of Pelvic Abscess Posterior colpotomy is a surgical incision made through the posterior vaginal fornix into the pouch of Douglas (rectouterine pouch).

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: What is the causative agent in a 55-year-old man presenting with fever, progressive fatigue, hypotension, tachycardia, and the peripheral blood smear findings shown?
questions.explanation: The peripheral blood smear provides two definitive diagnostic clues for Plasmodium falciparum malaria. First, the presence of multiple delicate ring-form trophozoites within single red blood cells is characteristic. Second, the pathognomonic finding is the banana-shaped (crescentic) gametocyte, which is unique to P. falciparum. Plasmodium vivax (Option A) would show enlarged RBCs with Schuffner's dots and more amoeboid trophozoites. Plasmodium malariae (Option D) classically shows "band-form" trophozoites. Plasmodium ovale (Option C) shows oval-shaped RBCs with fimbriated edges. Clinically, P. falciparum is the most dangerous species, capable of causing cerebral malaria, hypotension, and rapid systemic failure as seen in this febrile patient. Therefore, because the crescent-shaped gametocyte is a definitive morphological marker for this species, Plasmodium falciparum is the correct etiological factor
questions.learning: The peripheral blood smear provides two definitive diagnostic clues for Plasmodium falciparum malaria. First, the presence of multiple delicate ring-form trophozoites within single red blood cells is characteristic.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient with hypertensive episodes, with an MRI abdomen showing a suprarenal mass, is planned for surgery. A 24-hour urine shows elevated metanephrine levels. What drug will be given preoperatively and also intraoperatively?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Phenoxybenzamine

Phenoxybenzamine is a nonselective irreversible α-blocker used preoperatively in pheochromocytoma to prevent catecholamine-induced hypertensive crises.

Phenoxybenzamine = irreversible α-blocker

Blocks α₁ and α₂ receptors

Causes vasodilation

Preoperative

• Classically Phenoxybenzamine (α-blocker) → given days before surgery

Intraoperative BP control

• Need short-acting, titratable drug
• Nicardipine (IV CCB) is preferred:

• Rapid onset
• Easily adjustable
• Controls hypertensive surges during tumor manipulation

Question asks: “preoperative AND intraoperative”

• Among options, Phenoxybenzamine seems most appropriate due to its traditional use-case in pheochromocytoma.
questions.learning: Phenoxybenzamine Phenoxybenzamine is a nonselective irreversible α-blocker used preoperatively in pheochromocytoma to prevent catecholamine-induced hypertensive crises.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 2-year-old child presents with fever and lymphadenopathy. Histopathological examination (H&E) shows hallmark cells, and a diagnosis of anaplastic large cell lymphoma is made. Which chromosomal translocation is most commonly associated with this condition?
questions.explanation: Anaplastic Large Cell Lymphoma (ALCL) is highly associated with the t(2;5)(p23;q35) chromosomal translocation. This translocation results in the fusion of the nucleophosmin (NPM) gene on chromosome 5 with the anaplastic lymphoma kinase (ALK) gene on chromosome 2. The resulting NPM-ALK fusion protein leads to the constitutive activation of ALK tyrosine kinase, which drives malignant cell proliferation. Histologically, ALCL is identified by "hallmark cells"—large pleomorphic cells with characteristic horseshoe-shaped nuclei. Option A (t(8;14)) and Option B (t(8;22)) are associated with Burkitt lymphoma, involving the MYC gene. Option D (t(14;18)) is the hallmark of follicular lymphoma, involving BCL2 overexpression. Therefore, the t(2;5) translocation is the definitive genetic finding for ALK-positive anaplastic large cell lymphoma

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A one-month-old child presents with recurrent pneumonia and no cyanosis. On examination, a continuous murmur is heard below the left clavicle and a bounding pulse is present. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. PDA (Patent Ductus Arteriosus)

Patent ductus arteriosus is a congenital left-to-right shunt in which the ductus arteriosus fails to close after birth, leading to continuous blood flow from the aorta to the pulmonary artery.

• Continuous “machinery” murmur best heard below the left clavicle
• Bounding pulses and wide pulse pressure due to runoff of blood into pulmonary circulation
• Recurrent respiratory infections and signs of heart failure due to increased pulmonary blood flow
• Usually no cyanosis initially (acyanotic congenital heart disease)

Pathophysiology:

• Persistent connection between aorta and pulmonary artery → left-to-right shunt
• Increased pulmonary blood flow → pulmonary congestion → recurrent pneumonia

Contrast:

• ASD: fixed split S2, no continuous murmur
• VSD: pansystolic murmur at left lower sternal border
• Coarctation of aorta: radio-femoral delay, upper limb hypertension, weak lower limb pulses

The doctor, based on history, suspects that the child maybe suffering from an infection due to Shigella over cholera and proceeds to give ciprofloxacin as the antibiotic. Among the options given, the presence of fever favours the suspicion towards Shigella as the infectious agent, for which ciprofloxacin is the drug of choice.

The presence of vomiting and absence of rectal pain favour cholera and abdominal pain is present in both the diseases.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which specific monoclonal antibody is used in the treatment of cancer?
questions.explanation: Rituximab is a chimeric monoclonal antibody that specifically targets the CD20 antigen found on the surface of B-lymphocytes. It is a cornerstone in the treatment of various B-cell malignancies, including Non-Hodgkin’s Lymphoma and Chronic Lymphocytic Leukemia. By binding to CD20, it triggers cell lysis through antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity and complement-dependent pathways. Omalizumab (Option A) is used for severe allergic asthma and chronic urticaria by targeting IgE. Denosumab (Option B) targets RANKL and is used for osteoporosis and giant cell tumors of the bone, but it is not primarily classified as a direct anti-cancer cytotoxic agent in this context. Methotrexate (Option D) is a conventional folic acid antagonist chemotherapy drug, not a monoclonal antibody. Rituximab’s ability to selectively deplete B-cells makes it effective not only in oncology but also in autoimmune disorders like rheumatoid arthritis. Therefore, among the monoclonal antibodies listed, Rituximab is the primary agent utilized for malignant cancer therapy
